<!-- question-1: body_md -->
\label{question:randomness}
When does randomization reduce query complexity across dimensions?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
\label{question:smoothness}
How much can higher-order smoothness reduce query
complexity under low-order access?
<!-- end question-2 -->
<!-- question-3: body_md -->
\label{question:oracle-information}
How closely can gradient-only algorithms match
function-value guarantees?
<!-- end question-3 -->
<!-- question-4: body_md -->
\label{question:constraints}
How do constraints change the complexity of finding
stationary points?
<!-- end question-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:informal-low-dimensional-trapping}
For objective in $C^{p,\beta_p}$, there exist $0$-th order
deterministic trapping algorithms that find an
$\varepsilon$-stationary point in the unconstrained setting using $\mathcal{O}_{d,p}
    \bigl(\varepsilon^{-(d-1)}\bigr)$
queries and an $\varepsilon$-KKT point over $[0,1]^d$ using $    \mathcal{O}_{d,p}
    \bigl(\varepsilon^{-(d-1)/\nu}\bigr)$
queries.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
Let $\nu = p+\beta_p$. For $C^{p,\beta_p}(L_p)$ objectives, there exist trapping algorithms
using only exact gradient queries with the following guarantees.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Deterministic algorithms.}
An $\varepsilon$-stationary point in the unconstrained setting
can be found using
$\widetilde{\mathcal O}\!\left(
\varepsilon^{-\max\{d-1,\,\nu/(\nu-1)\}}\right)$ queries,
and an $\varepsilon$-KKT point over $[0,1]^d$ can be found using
$\widetilde{\mathcal O}\!\left(
\varepsilon^{-\max\{(d-1)/\nu,\,1/(\nu-1)\}}\right)$ queries.

\item \textbf{Randomized algorithms.}
With high probability, an $\varepsilon$-stationary point in the
unconstrained setting can be found using
$\widetilde{\mathcal O}\!\left(
\varepsilon^{-\max\{d-1,\,2\nu/(2\nu-1)\}}\right)$ queries,
and an $\varepsilon$-KKT point over $[0,1]^d$ can be found using
$\widetilde{\mathcal O}\!\left(
\varepsilon^{-\max\{(d-1)/\nu,\,2/(2\nu-1)\}}\right)$ queries.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:informal-lazy-trapping}
There are deterministic trapping-or-descent algorithms that return an
$\varepsilon$-stationary point when $\mathcal X=\mathbb R^d$, and an
$\varepsilon$-KKT point when $\mathcal X=[0,1]^d$, using respectively
$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{\mathrm{fval}}
&=
\mathcal O_{p,\beta_p}\!\left(
d^p+d^{p-1+\frac{\beta_p}{\nu-1}}
\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
\right),\qquad
N_{\mathrm{grad}}
=
\mathcal O_{p,\beta_p}\!\left(
d^{p-1}+d^{p-2+\frac{\beta_p}{\nu-1}}
\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
function-value queries and strict gradient-only queries.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:informal-drhs}
In sufficiently high dimension, every randomized algorithm using only
exact gradient queries requires
$$
\begin{cases}
\Omega(\varepsilon^{-\frac{7}{4}}),
    & f\in C^{2,1},\\[2mm]
\Omega_p(\varepsilon^{-\frac{5}{3}}),
    & f\in C^{p,1},\quad p\geq3,\\[2mm]
\Omega_p\!\left(
    \varepsilon^{-(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2p})}
\right),
    & f\in C^{1,1}\cap C^{p,1},\quad p\geq2,
\end{cases}
$$
queries to return an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point with constant
success probability. The hard instances can be chosen \(C^\infty\)
and coercive.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:holder}
Let \(p\ge 1\) be an integer, \(\beta\in(0,1]\), and \(L_p\ge 0\).
A function \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) belongs to
\(C^{p,\beta}(L_p)\) if \(f\in C^p(\mathbb R^d)\) and
\[
    \bigl\|\nabla^p f(x)-\nabla^p f(y)\bigr\|_{\mathrm{op}}
    \le
    L_p\|x-y\|_2^\beta
    \qquad
    \text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb R^d.
\]
We call \(p+\beta\) the corresponding fractional smoothness order and
write \(C^{p,\beta}\) when \(L_p\) is clear from context.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- assumption-1: body_md -->
\label{ass:lower-bounded}
The objective has a finite infimum:
\[
    f_\star
    :=
    \inf_{x\in\mathbb R^d} f(x)
    >
    -\infty.
\]
<!-- end assumption-1 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{the:main1}
Assume target function $f$ lies in $C^{p,\beta_p}(L_p)$.
For $\varepsilon>0$, $d = \Theta(1)$, there is a deterministic algorithm finding $\varepsilon$-stationary points, running within $k = \mathcal{O}(\log (\frac{1}{\varepsilon}))$-round, with
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin =14pt]
    \item $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-(d-1)})$ function value queries per iteration when $f$ is unconstrained but lower bounded,
    \item $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{ - \frac{d-1}{p+\beta_p}})$ function value queries per iteration when $f$ is constrained on $[0,1]^d$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
For $p\ge2$, Theorem~\ref{the:main1} requires only
$f\in C^{p,\beta_p}(L_p)$, without an additional
$C^{1,1}(L_1)$ assumption, and its query bounds do not depend on $L_1$.
This distinction matters because the highest-order H\"older
condition does not control the gradient Lipschitz constant.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:full-dimensional-hyperrectangle}
A hyperrectangle in $\mathbb R^d$ is a set
$R=\prod_{i=1}^d[a_i,b_i]$ with $a_i\le b_i$.
Its dimension is the number $k$ of indices satisfying $a_i<b_i$.
It is \emph{full-dimensional} if $k=d$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:trapping-certificate}
For $\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y\in\mathbb R^d$ and $\eta>0$, define
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:trapping-potential}
    \phi_{\boldsymbol x,\eta}(\boldsymbol y)
    :=f(\boldsymbol y)-f(\boldsymbol x)
      +\eta\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2.
\end{equation}
We say that $\boldsymbol y$ is \emph{$\eta$-unreachable from
$\boldsymbol x$} if $\phi_{\boldsymbol x,\eta}(\boldsymbol y)>0$,
and \emph{$\eta$-reachable} otherwise.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:trapping-implies-stationarity}
Let $R\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, compact, and convex,
$\boldsymbol x\in R$, and $\eta>0$.
If every point of $\partial R$ is $\eta$-unreachable from
$\boldsymbol x$, then $R$ contains a point $\boldsymbol z$ with
$\|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z)\|_2\le\eta$.
In the constrained setting, if $R\subseteq [0,1]^d$ and every point of
$\partial_{[0,1]^d} R$ is $\eta$-unreachable from $\boldsymbol x$, then $R$
contains a point $\boldsymbol z$ with
$\|G_\gamma(\boldsymbol z)\|_2\le\eta$ for every $\gamma>0$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $\boldsymbol z$ minimize $\phi_{\boldsymbol x,\eta}$ over $R$ and existence follows from compactness and continuity.
Its value is at most $\phi_{\boldsymbol x,\eta}(\boldsymbol x)=0$.
The boundary certificate therefore gives
$\boldsymbol z\in\operatorname{int}(R)$ in the unconstrained case,
and $\boldsymbol z\in\operatorname{int}_{[0,1]^d}(R)$ in the constrained case.
First-order optimality gives
$\nabla f(\boldsymbol z)+\eta\boldsymbol v+\boldsymbol n=0$
for some $\boldsymbol v\in
\partial\|\cdot-\boldsymbol x\|_2(\boldsymbol z)$ and
$\boldsymbol n\in N_R(\boldsymbol z)$.
The norm is continuous and convex, so the subgradient sum rule
applies, and $\|\boldsymbol v\|_2\le1$.

In the unconstrained case, $N_R(\boldsymbol z)=\{\boldsymbol 0\}$,
which gives $\|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z)\|_2\le\eta$.
For the constrained case, we verify that
$N_R(\boldsymbol z)=N_{[0,1]^d}(\boldsymbol z)$ whenever
$\boldsymbol z\in\operatorname{int}_{[0,1]^d}(R)$.
The inclusion $N_{[0,1]^d}(\boldsymbol z)\subseteq N_R(\boldsymbol z)$ follows
from $R\subseteq [0,1]^d$.
Conversely, if $\boldsymbol n\in N_R(\boldsymbol z)$ and
$\boldsymbol y\in [0,1]^d$, then for sufficiently small $t>0$,
$\boldsymbol z+t(\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol z)\in R$ by convexity
of the cube and local equality of $R$ and the cube.
Hence $t\langle\boldsymbol n,\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol z\rangle\le0$,
which proves the reverse inclusion.

Consequently, $\boldsymbol n\in N_{[0,1]^d}(\boldsymbol z)$ and
$\operatorname{proj}_{[0,1]^d}(\boldsymbol z+\gamma\boldsymbol n)=\boldsymbol z$.
For this $\boldsymbol n$, nonexpansiveness of projection gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-mapping-normal-residual}
\begin{split}
    \|G_\gamma(\boldsymbol z)\|_2
    &=\gamma^{-1}
      \|\operatorname{proj}_{[0,1]^d}(\boldsymbol z+\gamma\boldsymbol n)
      -\operatorname{proj}_{[0,1]^d}(\boldsymbol z-\gamma\nabla f(\boldsymbol z))\|_2\\
    &\le\|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z)+\boldsymbol n\|_2
     \le\eta.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
The first inequality holds for any $\boldsymbol z\in [0,1]^d$ and
$\boldsymbol n\in N_{[0,1]^d}(\boldsymbol z)$, independently of the trapping
certificate.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lmm:to_local_minima}
Let $\boldsymbol{y}\in E$ be an $\varepsilon_0$-approximate minimizer of $\phi_{\boldsymbol{x},\varepsilon}$ over $E$, \emph{i.e.},
\[
\phi_{\boldsymbol{x},\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{y}) \le \min\limits_{\boldsymbol{z}\in E}\phi_{\boldsymbol{x}, \varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{z})+\varepsilon_0.
\]
If $\boldsymbol{y}$ is $\varepsilon$-unreachable from $\boldsymbol{x}$, then every point $\boldsymbol{z}\in E$ is $\varepsilon'$-unreachable from $\boldsymbol{x}$, where
\[
\varepsilon'=\varepsilon+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{\mathrm{dist}(\boldsymbol{x},E)}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
For any point $\boldsymbol{z} \in E$, since $\phi_{\boldsymbol{x},\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{y}) \le \min\limits_{\boldsymbol{z}\in E}\phi_{\boldsymbol{x},\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{z})+\varepsilon_0$, we have 
\[f(\boldsymbol{z})  + \varepsilon\|\boldsymbol{z} - \boldsymbol{x}\| + \varepsilon_0 \geq f(\boldsymbol{y}) + \varepsilon\|\boldsymbol{y} - \boldsymbol{x}\|.  \]
Combining the fact that $\boldsymbol{y}$ is $\varepsilon$-unreachable from $\boldsymbol{x}$, we have
\begin{align*}
f(\boldsymbol{z}) ~\geq~& f(\boldsymbol{y})  + \varepsilon\|\boldsymbol{y} - \boldsymbol{x}\| - \varepsilon\|\boldsymbol{z} - \boldsymbol{x}\| - \varepsilon_0   \\
~\geq~& f(\boldsymbol{x})  - \varepsilon\|\boldsymbol{z} - \boldsymbol{x}\| - \varepsilon_0   \\
~\geq~& f(\boldsymbol{x})  - \varepsilon\|\boldsymbol{z} - \boldsymbol{x}\| -\frac{\varepsilon_0}{\mathrm{dist}(\boldsymbol{x},E)}  \|\boldsymbol{z} - \boldsymbol{x}\|.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Lemma~5 in \cite{hollender2023computational} is a special case of
Lemma~\ref{lmm:to_local_minima}. In their setting, a nice
\(\delta\)-net and \(L\)-smoothness yield an
\(\varepsilon_0\)-approximate minimizer of
\(\phi_{\boldsymbol{x},\varepsilon}\) over \(E\), where
\[
\varepsilon_0
=
\frac{\delta^2}{2}
\left(
L+\frac{2\varepsilon}{\mathrm{dist}(\boldsymbol{x},E)}
\right).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lmm:to_local_minima} then recovers their unreachability
parameter exactly. More generally, our lemma reduces the geometric
task of certifying that every point of \(E\) is unreachable to the
global minimization of the trapping function over \(E\), after which
the smoothness of \(f\) can be exploited to construct an accurate
approximate minimizer.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
In this work, we only concerns oracle complexity. No claim is made about the computational
cost of polynomial reconstruction or the subsequent global search.
This follows the standard evaluation-complexity convention for
\(\mathrm{AR}p\) methods
\cite{BGM+17,cartis2020sharp}, which counts evaluations of
\(f\) and its derivatives but excludes the internal cost of
approximately minimizing each regularized Taylor model.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:stationarity-from-model}
Let $R\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, compact, and convex,
let $\boldsymbol x\in R$, and let $\varepsilon>0$.
Suppose that $f$ and $P$ are continuously differentiable on a
neighborhood of $R$ and satisfy
$\|\nabla P-\nabla f\|_{\infty,R}\le\frac{\varepsilon}{8}$.
Every minimizer
$\boldsymbol z\in
\operatorname*{argmin}\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in R}\Psi(\boldsymbol y)$
has the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin =* ]
\item If every point of $\partial R$ is $(\frac{\varepsilon}{2})$-unreachable
from $\boldsymbol x$, then $\boldsymbol z\in\operatorname{int}(R)$
and $\|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z)\|_2\le\varepsilon$.

\item If $R\subseteq[0,1]^d$ and every point of
$\partial_{[0,1]^d}R$ is $(\frac{\varepsilon}{2})$-unreachable from
$\boldsymbol x$, then
$\boldsymbol z\in\operatorname{int}_{[0,1]^d}(R)$ and
$\|G_\gamma(\boldsymbol z)\|_2\le\varepsilon$ for every $\gamma>0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Since $\Psi$ is continuous and $R$ is nonempty and compact,
a global minimizer exists. Fix any such minimizer $\boldsymbol z$.
Because $\boldsymbol x\in R$ and $\Psi(\boldsymbol x)=0$,
we have $\Psi(\boldsymbol z)\le0$.

For every $\boldsymbol y\in R$, convexity keeps the segment from
$\boldsymbol x$ to $\boldsymbol y$ in $R$. Integrating
$\nabla P-\nabla f$ along this segment gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:model-increment-error}
\begin{split}
 &|P(\boldsymbol y)-P(\boldsymbol x)-f(\boldsymbol y)+f(\boldsymbol x)|=
 \left|\int_0^1
 \left\langle
 (\nabla P-\nabla f)
 (\boldsymbol x+t(\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x)),
 \boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x
 \right\rangle\,dt\right|
 \le\frac{\varepsilon}{8}\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Consequently, on the certified boundary,
$\Psi(\boldsymbol y)\ge
\phi_{\boldsymbol x,\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}(\boldsymbol y)
+\frac{\varepsilon}{8}\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2>0$.
Since $\Psi(\boldsymbol z)\le0$, the minimizer cannot lie on
that boundary. Thus $\boldsymbol z\in\operatorname{int}(R)$
in case~(i), and
$\boldsymbol z\in\operatorname{int}_{[0,1]^d}(R)$ in case~(ii).

The constrained first-order necessary condition for minimizing
the sum of the continuously differentiable function $P$ and
the convex distance penalty supplies vectors
$\boldsymbol v\in\partial\|\cdot-\boldsymbol x\|_2(\boldsymbol z)$
and $\boldsymbol n\in N_R(\boldsymbol z)$ such that
$\nabla P(\boldsymbol z)
+(3\varepsilon/4)\boldsymbol v+\boldsymbol n=\boldsymbol0$.
Here $\|\boldsymbol v\|_2\le1$, including when
$\boldsymbol z=\boldsymbol x$. Therefore,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:model-normal-residual}
    \|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z)+\boldsymbol n\|_2
    \le
    \|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z)-\nabla P(\boldsymbol z)\|_2
    +\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}\|\boldsymbol v\|_2
    \le\frac{7\varepsilon}{8}
    \le\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
In case~(i), $\boldsymbol z\in\operatorname{int}(R)$ implies
$N_R(\boldsymbol z)=\{\boldsymbol0\}$, so
\eqref{eq:model-normal-residual} proves the claimed gradient bound.

For case~(ii), we first show that
$N_R(\boldsymbol z)=N_{[0,1]^d}(\boldsymbol z)$.
The inclusion
$N_{[0,1]^d}(\boldsymbol z)\subseteq N_R(\boldsymbol z)$
follows from $R\subseteq[0,1]^d$.
Conversely, take $\boldsymbol n\in N_R(\boldsymbol z)$ and
$\boldsymbol y\in[0,1]^d$.
Since $\boldsymbol z\in\operatorname{int}_{[0,1]^d}(R)$,
the point $\boldsymbol z+t(\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol z)$
belongs to $R$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$.
The normal-cone inequality gives
$t\langle\boldsymbol n,\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol z\rangle\le0$.
Dividing by $t$ shows that
$\langle\boldsymbol n,\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol z\rangle\le0$.
As $\boldsymbol y$ was arbitrary,
$\boldsymbol n\in N_{[0,1]^d}(\boldsymbol z)$, proving the identity.

For every $\gamma>0$, the projection characterization now gives
$\operatorname{proj}_{[0,1]^d}
(\boldsymbol z+\gamma\boldsymbol n)=\boldsymbol z$.
Hence, by nonexpansiveness of projection,
\[
\begin{split}
 \|G_\gamma(\boldsymbol z)\|_2
 &=
 \frac{1}{\gamma}
 \left\|
 \operatorname{proj}_{[0,1]^d}
     (\boldsymbol z+\gamma\boldsymbol n)
 -
 \operatorname{proj}_{[0,1]^d}
     (\boldsymbol z-\gamma\nabla f(\boldsymbol z))
 \right\|_2\\
 &\le\|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z)+\boldsymbol n\|_2
 \le\varepsilon,
\end{split}
\]
where the last inequality follows from
\eqref{eq:model-normal-residual}.
This proves case~(ii).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{the:main_gradient}
Suppose that $f\in C^{p,\beta_p}(L_p)$. For $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, the following
\emph{total} gradient-query bounds hold, with $d,p,\beta_p,L_p$
and the initial-gap bound $\Delta$ fixed independently of
$\varepsilon$ whenever applicable.

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin = 2em]
\item \textbf{Unconstrained optimization.}
Given $\boldsymbol x^0$ and a known bound
$f(\boldsymbol x^0)-\inf f\le\Delta<\infty$, an
$\varepsilon$-stationary point can be found deterministically using
$\widetilde O\!\left(
\varepsilon^{-\max\{d-1,\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}\}}\right)$
gradient queries, or with randomization using
$\widetilde O\!\left(
\varepsilon^{-\max\{d-1,\frac{2\nu}{2\nu-1}\}}\right)$
gradient queries.

\item \textbf{Cube-constrained optimization.}
A point $\boldsymbol z\in[0,1]^d$ satisfying
$\|G_\gamma(\boldsymbol z)\|_2\le\varepsilon$ for every $\gamma>0$
can be found deterministically using
$\widetilde O\!\left(
\varepsilon^{-\max\{\frac{d-1}{\nu},\ \frac{1}{\nu-1}\}}\right)$
gradient queries, or with randomization using
$\widetilde O\!\left(
\varepsilon^{-\max\{\frac{d-1}{\nu},\ \frac{2}{2\nu-1}\}}\right)$
gradient queries.
\end{enumerate}
For any $\rho\in(0,1)$, the randomized algorithms succeed with
probability at least $1-\rho$ and their query bounds hold for every
random seed, with only logarithmic dependence on $1/\rho$.
Both implementations use $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ adaptive rounds.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:randomized-line-integration}
\label{lem:randomized-high-order-line-integration}
Let $\mathcal F$ be the sigma-field generated by the past
transcript, and let $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$
be $\mathcal F$-measurable. Suppose that the fixed objective $f$
belongs to $C^{p,\beta_p}(L_p)$ on a neighborhood of $[u,v]$.
Write $\ell:=\|v-u\|_2$.
Each of the following constructions uses one nonadaptive batch
of exact gradient queries on $[u,v]$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin =*]
\item \textbf{Deterministic integration.}
An estimate $I^{\mathrm{det}}$ satisfying
\[|I^{\mathrm{det}}-(f(v)-f(u))|\le\varepsilon_0\] can be computed
using $\mathcal O_p(1+(L_p\ell^\nu/\varepsilon_0)^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}})$
queries.

\item \textbf{Randomized integration.}
For any $\mathcal F$-measurable $\vartheta\in(0,1)$, an estimate
$\widehat I$ can be computed using
$\mathcal O_p(1+(L_p\ell^\nu/\varepsilon_0)^{\frac{2}{2\nu-1}}
[\log(2/\vartheta)]^{\frac{1}{2\nu-1}})$ queries such that
$\mathbb E[\widehat I\mid\mathcal F]=f(v)-f(u)$ and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-line-integration-accuracy}
 \mathbb P\!\left(
 |\widehat I-(f(v)-f(u))|\le\varepsilon_0
 \mid\mathcal F\right)\ge1-\vartheta.
\end{equation}
The random seeds are independent of one another and of
$\mathcal F$.
\end{enumerate}
If $L_p=0$, both estimates are exact. If $\ell=0$, both return
zero without queries.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Condition on $\mathcal F$ and assume $\ell>0$.
The function $g(t):=\langle\nabla f(u+t(v-u)),v-u\rangle$
satisfies $\int_0^1g(t)\,dt=f(v)-f(u)$, and its
$(p-1)$st derivative is $\beta_p$-H\"older with constant
$L_p\ell^\nu$.

Partition $[0,1]$ into $n$ equal subintervals $J_j$ and let
$P_j$ be the local degree-$(p-1)$ interpolant of $g$, using
left-endpoint constants when $p=1$. Taylor approximation and
interpolation stability give
$\|g-P_j\|_{\infty,J_j}
=\mathcal O_p(L_p\ell^\nu n^{-(\nu-1)})$.
Integrating the interpolants gives a deterministic estimate
with error of the same order. For $p=1$, the sharper bound is
$L_p\ell^\nu n^{-\beta_p}/(1+\beta_p)$.

For the randomized rule, draw independent uniform points
$U_j\in J_j$, using fresh seeds, and set
\[
 \widehat I_n
 :=\sum_{j=1}^n\left[
 \int_{J_j}P_j(t)\,dt+\frac{g(U_j)-P_j(U_j)}{n}
 \right].
\]
The residual corrections make this estimate conditionally
unbiased. Conditional Hoeffding's inequality bounds its error
by $\mathcal O_p(L_p\ell^\nu
n^{-(\nu-1/2)}\sqrt{\log(2/\vartheta)})$ with probability at
least $1-\vartheta$.
Choosing $n$ to meet the accuracy target gives the two claimed
query bounds. Each construction uses $\mathcal O_p(n)$
gradient queries, with all nodes selected before any new answer
is observed. The full proof, including the degenerate cases and
constants uniform in $\beta_p$, is given in
Appendix~\ref{app:4.1}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Conditional on the past transcript, each iteration selects all
query points before observing any new answers and thus uses
one nonadaptive batch.
Reconstruction and minimization require no further queries,
and all integration segments lie in $R_t$ by convexity.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{the:fresh-trapping-or-descent}
Under assumption~\ref{def:holder} and~\ref{ass:lower-bounded}, each of the following deterministic
algorithms returns $\boldsymbol z\in\mathcal X$ satisfying
$\|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z)\|_2\le\varepsilon$ when
$\mathcal X=\mathbb R^d$, or
$\|G_\gamma(\boldsymbol z)\|_2\le\varepsilon$ for every $\gamma>0$
when $\mathcal X=[0,1]^d$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin =*]
\item \textbf{Function values.}
The total number of function-value queries is
\[
\mathcal O_{p,\beta_p}\!\left(
d^p\left[
1+L_p^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
\Delta\,
\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
\right]
\right).
\]
\item \textbf{Gradients.}
The total number of gradient queries is
\[
\mathcal O_{p,\beta_p}\!\left(
d^{p-1}\left[
1+L_p^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
\Delta\,
\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
\right]
\right).
\]
\end{enumerate}
All queries lie in $\mathcal X$. If $\Delta=0$, both algorithms
return $\boldsymbol x^0$ without queries.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{the:lazy-trapping-or-descent}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{the:fresh-trapping-or-descent},
the following deterministic query bounds achieve the same output
guarantees.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin =*]
\item \textbf{Function values.}
The total number of function-value queries is
\[
\mathcal O_{p,\beta_p}\!\left(
d^p
+d^{p-1+\frac{\beta_p}{\nu-1}}
L_p^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
\Delta\,
\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
\right).
\]
\item \textbf{Gradients.}
The total number of gradient queries is
\[
\mathcal O_{p,\beta_p}\!\left(
d^{p-1}
+d^{p-2+\frac{\beta_p}{\nu-1}}
L_p^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
\Delta\,
\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
\right).
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:boundary-trapping-or-descent}
\label{lem:box-trapping-or-descent}
Suppose that $\Gamma\ne\varnothing$ and that a continuous
surrogate $\widehat\phi_x$ on $\Gamma$ satisfies
$\|\widehat\phi_x-\phi_{x,\frac{\varepsilon}{4}}\|_{\infty,\Gamma}
\le\frac{\varepsilon r}{16}$.
Let $\widehat y\in\Gamma$ satisfy
$\widehat\phi_x(\widehat y)
\le\min_\Gamma\widehat\phi_x+\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}$.
Then the following alternatives are exhaustive and disjoint.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\widehat\phi_x(\widehat y)>\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}$, then
every point of $\partial_XQ$ is $\frac{3\varepsilon}{8}$-unreachable
from $x$.
\item If $\widehat\phi_x(\widehat y)\le\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}$, then
$f(\widehat y)\le f(x)-\frac{5\varepsilon r}{32}
\le f(x)-\frac{\varepsilon r}{8}$.
\end{enumerate}
If $\Gamma=\varnothing$, the trapping certificate in the first
alternative holds vacuously.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:trapped-ball-localization}
\label{lem:box-trapped-ball-localization}
Let $Q:=Q_x(r)$.
Suppose that $\phi_{x,\frac{3\varepsilon}{8}}>0$ on
$\partial_XQ$, and that the known scalar polynomial $P_x$
satisfies
$\|\nabla P_x-\nabla f\|_{\infty,Q}
\le\frac{\varepsilon}{16}$.
Then Algorithm~\ref{alg:trap-localize} terminates after
finitely many offline operations, without further oracle queries,
and returns a point $z\in Q$ satisfying
\[
\begin{cases}
 \|\nabla f(z)\|_2\le\varepsilon,
 &X=\mathbb R^d,\\
 \|G_\gamma(z)\|_2\le\varepsilon
 \quad\text{for every }\gamma>0,
 &X=[0,1]^d.
\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:rand-fo-lower-bound}
For every integer \(p\geq2\), there is a constant \(c_p>0\) such that the
following holds.  If $ 0<\varepsilon
 \leq
 c_p\min\big\{
   (\Delta L_1)^{\frac{1}{2}},
\Delta^{\frac{p}{p+1}}L_p^{\frac{1}{p+1}}
 \big\},$
then there is a finite constant \(C_{p,\Delta,L_1,L_p}\) such that, for every
$ d\geq
 C_{p,\Delta,L_1,L_p}\varepsilon^{-\big(4+\frac{2}{p}\big)},$
one has
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-main-rate}
 T_{\varepsilon,\mathrm{FO}}^{\mathrm{rand}}
 \bigl(\mathcal F_{1,p}^{(d)}(\Delta,L_1,L_p)\bigr)
 \geq
 c_p\Delta\sqrt{L_1\gamma_p(\varepsilon)}\,
 \varepsilon^{-2}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
The hard functions may be chosen \(C^\infty\) and coercive.  The conclusion
holds for the exact value-and-gradient oracle and for an arbitrary
transcript-measurable terminal output.  It therefore also holds for the
weaker gradient-only oracle.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:drhs-high-accuracy-rate}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:rand-fo-lower-bound}, suppose in
addition that $ \varepsilon
 \leq
 \big(\frac{L_1^p}{L_p}\big)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}.$
Then
\[
 T_{\varepsilon,\mathrm{FO}}^{\mathrm{rand}}
 \bigl(\mathcal F_{1,p}^{(d)}(\Delta,L_1,L_p)\bigr)
 \geq
 c_p\Delta L_1^{\frac{1}{2}}L_p^{\frac{1}{2p}}
\varepsilon^{-\big(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2p}\big)}.
\]
In particular, the exponent of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ is \(\frac 7 4\) for \(p=2\) and \(\frac 5 3\) for \(p=3\).
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
For the class $\bigcap_{q=1}^p C^{q,1}(L_q)$,
\cite{zhou2026sharp} establishes a deterministic first-order
lower bound of order
$\Delta\sqrt{L_1\Gamma_p(\varepsilon)}\,\varepsilon^{-2}$, where
\[
\Gamma_p(\varepsilon)
:=
\sup_{r\ge1}
\min\left\{
L_1,\,
\frac{L_1}{\ell_1r^2},\,
\min_{2\le q\le p}
\left(
\frac{L_q\varepsilon^{q-1}r^{q-3}}{\ell_q}
\right)^{\frac1q}
\right\},
\]
with constants $\ell_q$ for $q\ge1$.
The parameter $r$ controls the hard function and is
optimized to balance the derivative bounds.

Theorem~\ref{thm:rand-fo-lower-bound} applies to randomized
first-order methods under
$C^{1,1}(L_1)\cap C^{p,1}(L_p)$.
For fixed positive smoothness constants and sufficiently small
$\varepsilon$, one has
$\Gamma_p(\varepsilon)\sim \gamma_p(\varepsilon)$
when $p=2,3$.
Thus our randomized lower bound matches the corresponding
deterministic scales in these cases.
For $p\ge4$, however,
$\Gamma_p(\varepsilon)
=\Theta_{p,L_1,\ldots,L_p}(\varepsilon^{\frac23})$,
whereas
$\gamma_p(\varepsilon)
=L_p^{\frac1p}\varepsilon^{\frac{p-1}{p}}$.

                                                 
Theorem~\ref{thm:rand-fo-lower-bound} gives a sufficient
dimension requirement of order
$\varepsilon^{-(4+\frac2p)}$ while the deterministic construction of \cite{zhou2026sharp} can be realized in
dimension $\mathcal O(\varepsilon^{-\frac74})$ for $p=2$
and $\mathcal O(\varepsilon^{-\frac53})$ for $p\ge3$.
These dimension estimates follow from its block sizes and phase count.
Whether the sufficient dimension threshold for our randomized
lower bound can be reduced remains open.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:drhs-without-l1}
For every integer \(p\geq2\), there are constants \(c_p,C_p>0\) such
that the following holds whenever
\(0<\varepsilon\leq
c_p\Delta^{p/(p+1)}L_p^{1/(p+1)}\):
\begin{equation*}
\label{eq:drhs-without-l1-rates}
\begin{aligned}
p=2,\quad
d&\geq
C_p\left(
 \frac{\Delta^{2/3}L_2^{1/3}}{\varepsilon}
\right)^5
&&\Longrightarrow&
T_{\varepsilon,\mathrm{FO}}^{\mathrm{rand}}
\bigl(\mathcal F_2^{(d)}(\Delta,L_2)\bigr)
&\geq
c_p\left(
 \frac{\Delta^{2/3}L_2^{1/3}}{\varepsilon}
\right)^{7/4},\\
p\geq3,\quad
d&\geq
C_p\left(
 \frac{\Delta^{p/(p+1)}L_p^{1/(p+1)}}{\varepsilon}
\right)^{13/3+1/p}
&&\Longrightarrow&
T_{\varepsilon,\mathrm{FO}}^{\mathrm{rand}}
\bigl(\mathcal F_p^{(d)}(\Delta,L_p)\bigr)
&\geq
c_p\left(
 \frac{\Delta^{p/(p+1)}L_p^{1/(p+1)}}{\varepsilon}
\right)^{5/3}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
The hard functions may be chosen \(C^\infty\) and coercive.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
The ungated term $-\Phi_1(z_1)$ initiates the first phase.
For $s\geq2$, the coupling
$-G_{s-1}(z_{s-1})\Phi_s(z_s)$ activates the forcing in
phase $s$ only when the preceding block approaches its target.
The quadratic terms remain present throughout, allowing
earlier queries to collect information about $A_s$.

Before $z_{s-1}$ enters $B(x_{s-1}^\star,3\rho)$,
both $G_{s-1}$ and $\nabla G_{s-1}$ vanish.
Hence the incoming coupling containing $\Phi_s$ contributes
nothing to either the function value or the gradient.
The vector $b_s$ also determines the center of the outgoing
gate $G_s$ when $s<N$.
This second information channel likewise vanishes while
$z_s\notin B(x_s^\star,3\rho)$.

Thus, before the preceding target is approached, these
couplings can reveal information about $b_s$ only through
a premature hit on the current target neighborhood.
The information argument below shows that such hits are
unlikely and that prior exploration of $A_s$ cannot eliminate
the query cost after $b_s$ is revealed.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
Let $s$ be the first phase with
$\|z_s-x_s^\star\|_2\geq2\rho$.
The incoming forcing in Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-hard-gradient}
is then fully active.
When $\|z_s\|_2\leq R$, its first two terms combine into
$A_s(z_s-x_s^\star)$.
The last term is a nonnegative multiple of
$z_s-x_s^\star$, since $\eta'\leq0$ and $\Phi_{s+1}>0$,
so it cannot cancel the outward radial component.
Hence
$\|\nabla_sF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}(z)\|_2
\geq\mu\|z_s-x_s^\star\|_2\geq2\varepsilon$.
When $\|z_s\|_2>R$, the last term vanishes and $A_sz_s$
dominates the bounded forcing by the choice of $R$.
Thus every $\varepsilon$-stationary point must approach
all targets within distance $2\rho$;
see Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-certification}.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{remark:str_oracle}
For the lower-bound proof, we additionally reveal \(b_1\) before the first candidate is
selected and, for \(s\geq2\), reveal \(b_s\) after the first candidate
that outer-hits phase \(s-1\) has been frozen but before its
value-and-gradient response is returned.  This only strengthens the
oracle, so a lower bound under this disclosure protocol also applies to
the original model.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:drhs-one-phase}
There is a numerical constant $C_0>0$ such that, if the dimension of each phase block
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-one-phase-dimension}
 M\geq C_0\left(
 Q^2+\kappa\left[
 Q+\log\frac{(Q+2)\mathsf L}{\delta}
 \right]\right),
\end{equation}
every procedure described above satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-one-phase-conclusion}
 \Pr_{(A,b)\sim\mathsf P_{\mathrm{ph}}}
 \left(
 \exists\,y\in\mathcal Y:
 \|y-x^\star\|_2<3\rho
 \right)\leq\delta.
\end{equation}
Moreover, $\mathsf P_0(\mathcal G)\geq\frac{7}{8}$,
and $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{ph}}$ is well defined and supported
on admissible pairs satisfying
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-admissible-data}.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:drhs-sequential}
Let
\((\mathbf A,\mathbf b)\sim
\mathsf P_{\mathrm{chain}}=\mathsf P_{\mathrm{ph}}^{\otimes N}\),
and let \(C_0\) be the constant furnished by
Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-one-phase}.  Set $ Q=T,
 \mathsf L=T,
 \delta=\frac1{12N}.$
If 
\[ M\geq C_0\left\{
   T^2+\kappa\left[
     T+\log\bigl(12NT(T+2)\bigr)
   \right]
 \right\},\]
then every deterministic exact value-and-gradient algorithm making at most
\(T-1\) oracle calls and returning a
                                    
point
\(z^{\mathrm{out}}\) satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-sequential-conclusion}
 \Pr_{(\mathbf A,\mathbf b)\sim\mathsf P_{\mathrm{chain}}}
 \left(
   \|z_s^{\mathrm{out}}-x_s^\star\|_2<3\rho
   \text{ for every }s\in[N]
 \right)
 \leq\frac1{12}.
\end{equation}
The output need not have been queried.  The same assertion holds for the
ambient extension \(F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}\).
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:drhs-certification}
For every \(M,N\geq1\), every admissible phase realization, every
\(d\geq NM\), and every \((z,u)\in\mathbb R^d\),
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-certification-stationarity}
 \bigl\|\nabla F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}(z,u)\bigr\|_2
 \leq\varepsilon
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \|z_s-x_s^\star\|_2<2\rho
 \quad\text{for every }s\in[N].
\end{equation}
In particular, every \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point lies in the inner,
and hence also the outer, ball of every phase.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:drhs-regularity}
There exist constants \(C_{\mathrm{sm}},C_{\mathrm{gap}}<\infty\),
                                              
and
a constant \(C_q<\infty\) for each integer \(q\geq2\)
                                                 
with the following property.  For every \(M,N\geq1\), every admissible phase
realization, and every \(d\geq NM\), the function
\(F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}\) is \(C^\infty\) and coercive, and
\[
\operatorname{Lip}\bigl(\nabla F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}\bigr)\leq\frac{L_1}{2}+C_{\mathrm{sm}}\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Lip}\bigl(\nabla^qF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}\bigr)\leq C_q\frac{\mu^q}{\varepsilon^{q-1}},\qquad F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}(0)-\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^d}F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}(x)\leq C_{\mathrm{gap}}N\frac{\varepsilon^2}{\mu}.
\]
These constants are independent of
\(M,N,d,\mu,\frac{L_1}{2},\varepsilon\), and the phase realization.  For the fixed
order \(p\) in the theorem, we denote the corresponding constant in the
second inequality by \(C_p\).
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Choose \(c_p>0\) so that $ c_p\leq
 \min\left\{
   c_{\mathrm{acc},p},
   \frac{c_Nc_0\sqrt{c_{\mu,p}}}{4\sqrt2}
 \right\}.$
    
          
              
                        
                                           
            
    
Then the small-accuracy assumption of the theorem implies
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-calibrated-small-accuracy}, and hence the calibration above
gives \(N,t\geq1\).

We first record the routine consequences of the calibration.  Since
\(\gamma_p(\varepsilon)
 =\Theta_{p,\Delta,L_1,L_p}
 (\varepsilon^{(p-1)/p})\), the definitions of
\(N,\kappa,t,T\), and \(M\) give
\[
 N=O\bigl(\varepsilon^{-(1+1/p)}\bigr),
 \qquad
 T=O\bigl(\varepsilon^{-(3/2+1/(2p))}\bigr),
 \qquad
 M=O\bigl(\varepsilon^{-(3+1/p)}\bigr).
\]
Consequently,
\[
 d_0=NM
 =O_{p,\Delta,L_1,L_p}
   \bigl(\varepsilon^{-(4+2/p)}\bigr).
\]
Thus \(C_{p,\Delta,L_1,L_p}\) is chosen so that \(d\geq d_0\).

Now use the algorithm-independent hard distribution
\(\mathcal D_d\) .
Because \(C_{\mathrm{dim}}\geq C_0\), the choice of \(M\) in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-calibrated-dimension} satisfies the dimension hypothesis
of Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-sequential}.  Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-one-phase}
ensures that the phase law is supported on admissible pairs.  Moreover,
Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-regularity}, together with
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-constant-choice} and the definition of \(N\), immediately
gives
\[
 \operatorname{Lip}(\nabla F)\leq L_1,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Lip}(D^pF)\leq L_p,
 \qquad
 F(0)-\inf F\leq\Delta.
\]
Every realization is also \(C^\infty\) and coercive.  Hence
\(\mathcal D_d\) is supported on
\(\mathcal F_{1,p}^{(d)}(\Delta,L_1,L_p)\).

Fix a deterministic value-and-gradient algorithm making at most \(T-1\)
queries, and let
\(x^{\mathrm{out}}=(z^{\mathrm{out}},u^{\mathrm{out}})\) be its output.
Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-certification} gives
\[
 \left\{
   \|\nabla F(x^{\mathrm{out}})\|_2\leq\varepsilon
 \right\}
 \subseteq
 \bigcap_{s=1}^N
 \left\{
   \|z_s^{\mathrm{out}}-x_s^\star\|_2<2\rho
 \right\}
 \subseteq
 \bigcap_{s=1}^N
 \left\{
   \|z_s^{\mathrm{out}}-x_s^\star\|_2<3\rho
 \right\}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-sequential} and the pushforward definition of
\(\mathcal D_d\) therefore imply
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-distributional-conclusion}
 \Pr_{F\sim\mathcal D_d}
 \left(
   \|\nabla F(x^{\mathrm{out}})\|_2\leq\varepsilon
 \right)
 \leq\frac1{12}.
\end{equation}

It remains to calculate the query rate.  Both quantities inside the floors
in Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-calibrated-depth} are at least two, so
\(\lfloor a\rfloor\geq a/2\) gives
\begin{align}
 T=Nt
 &\geq
 \frac{c_Nc_0}{4}
 \frac{\Delta\mu}{\varepsilon^2}
 \sqrt{\frac{L_1}{2\mu}}=
 \frac{c_Nc_0\sqrt{c_{\mu,p}}}{4\sqrt2}
 \Delta\sqrt{L_1\gamma_p(\varepsilon)}\,
 \varepsilon^{-2}.
\label{eq:drhs-query-rate}
\end{align}

Finally, consider a randomized algorithm with hard query budget \(T-1\).
For every fixed realization \(\omega\) of its random seed, the resulting
algorithm is deterministic, so Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-distributional-conclusion}
applies.  Averaging over \(\omega\) gives
\[
 \mathbb E_{F\sim\mathcal D_d}
 \Pr_\omega\left(
   \|\nabla F(x^{\mathrm{out}}(F,\omega))\|_2
   \leq\varepsilon
 \right)
 \leq\frac1{12}.
\]
Therefore, for this randomized algorithm, there is a fixed
\(f\in\mathcal F_{1,p}^{(d)}(\Delta,L_1,L_p)\) such that
\[
 \Pr_\omega\left(
   \|\nabla f(x^{\mathrm{out}}(f,\omega))\|_2
   \leq\varepsilon
 \right)
 \leq\frac1{12}<\frac23.
\]
Thus no randomized algorithm with budget \(T-1\) satisfies the uniform
\(2/3\)-success requirement, and hence
\[
 T_{\varepsilon,\mathrm{FO}}^{\mathrm{rand}}
 \bigl(\mathcal F_{1,p}^{(d)}(\Delta,L_1,L_p)\bigr)
 \geq T.
\]
Combining this with Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-query-rate} and the choice of \(c_p\)
proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-main-rate}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
Let $S\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a known nonempty compact convex
set with nonempty interior.
For a scalar- or vector-valued map $F$, write $D^jF$ for its
$j$th Fr\'echet derivative, with $D^0F:=F$.
For scalar $f$, we identify $D^jf$ with the derivative tensor
$\nabla^jf$ and in particular,
$Df(\boldsymbol x)[\boldsymbol v]
=\langle\nabla f(\boldsymbol x),\boldsymbol v\rangle$.
Vector norms are Euclidean, derivative norms are the induced
multilinear operator norms, and
$\|D^jF\|_{\infty,S}
:=\sup\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in S}\|D^jF(\boldsymbol y)\|$.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- problem-1: body_md -->
\label{prob:apx-function-reconstruction}
Given $S$, the smoothness parameters $p,\beta,L_p$,
function-value or gradient data on $V$, and target
accuracies $\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1>0$, construct
an explicit model $\widehat f$ satisfying
\[
 \|\widehat f-f\|_{\infty,S}\le\varepsilon_0,
 \qquad
 \|\nabla\widehat f-\nabla f\|_{\infty,S}
 \le\varepsilon_1,
\]
where the second guarantee is required only when
derivative accuracy is requested.
For gradient-only data, a reference point
$\boldsymbol c\in S$ is specified, and the value guarantee
is instead
$\|\widehat f-f+f(\boldsymbol c)\|_{\infty,S}
\le\varepsilon_0$.
<!-- end problem-1 -->
<!-- problem-2: body_md -->
\label{prob:apx-global-minimization}
Given $S$, the smoothness parameters $p,\beta,L_p$,
function-value data $(V,\widetilde f)$ with error bound
$\tau$, a known continuous function $q:S\to\mathbb R$,
and a target accuracy $\delta>0$, compute
$\widehat{\boldsymbol y}\in S$ satisfying
\[
 (f+q)(\widehat{\boldsymbol y})
 -\min_{\boldsymbol y\in S}(f+q)(\boldsymbol y)
 \le\delta.
\]
The output must be computed from the supplied data
and known inputs, without further queries to $f$.
<!-- end problem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:holder-taylor-remainder}
Let $p\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, let $S\subset\mathbb R^d$ be convex,
and let $F\in C^{p,\beta}(L_p)$ on a neighborhood of $S$.
For $\boldsymbol c\in S$, let $T_p$ be the degree-$p$
Taylor polynomial of $F$ at $\boldsymbol c$.
Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-holder-taylor}
 \|D^j(F-T_p)(\boldsymbol c+\boldsymbol v)\|
 \le a_{p-j,\beta}L_p\|\boldsymbol v\|_2^{p-j+\beta},
 \qquad
 0\le j\le p,\quad \boldsymbol c+\boldsymbol v\in S.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Fix $0\le j\le p$ and put $k:=p-j$.
If $k=0$, then $D^pT_p=D^pF(\boldsymbol c)$, so the
claim follows directly from the H\"older condition on $D^pF$.

Suppose that $k\ge1$, and set
$\Delta_p(t):=D^pF(\boldsymbol c+t\boldsymbol v)
-D^pF(\boldsymbol c)$.
Convexity ensures that the segment
$[\boldsymbol c,\boldsymbol c+\boldsymbol v]$ lies in $S$.
Applying Taylor's integral formula to $D^jF$ and subtracting
$D^jT_p$ gives
\[
 D^j(F-T_p)(\boldsymbol c+\boldsymbol v)
 =\frac{1}{(k-1)!}\int\limits_0^1(1-t)^{k-1}
 \Delta_p(t)[\boldsymbol v^{\otimes k},\,\cdot^{\,j}]\,dt.
\]
Here the last $j$ arguments remain free.
The H\"older condition gives
$\|\Delta_p(t)\|\le L_pt^\beta\|\boldsymbol v\|_2^\beta$.
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|D^j(F-T_p)(\boldsymbol c+\boldsymbol v)\|
 &\le
 \frac{1}{(k-1)!}
 \int\limits_0^1(1-t)^{k-1}
 \|\Delta_p(t)\|\,\|\boldsymbol v\|_2^k\,dt\\
 &\le
 \frac{L_p\|\boldsymbol v\|_2^{k+\beta}}{(k-1)!}
 \int\limits_0^1(1-t)^{k-1}t^\beta\,dt\\
 &=a_{k,\beta}L_p\|\boldsymbol v\|_2^{k+\beta}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the last equality, repeated integration by parts gives
$\frac{1}{(k-1)!}
\int\limits_0^1(1-t)^{k-1}t^\beta\,dt
=\prod\limits_{i=1}^k\frac{1}{\beta+i}=a_{k,\beta}$.
Substituting $k=p-j$ proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:interpolation-error-decomposition}
Under the preceding setup, every such comparison polynomial
$T$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-common-interpolation-error}
\begin{aligned}
 \|\mathcal I-F\|_{\infty,C}
 &\le\|T-F\|_{\infty,C}+\Lambda_0(r_T+\tau),\\
 \|D\mathcal I-DF\|_{\infty,C}
 &\le\|DT-DF\|_{\infty,C}+\Lambda_1(r_T+\tau),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the second inequality additionally requires $F$
to be continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of $C$.

If $\Pi_p^d\subseteq\mathcal P$ and
$F\in C^{p,\beta}(L_p)$ on a neighborhood of $C$, then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-stable-local-error}
 \|\mathcal I-F\|_{\infty,C}
 \le(1+\Lambda_0)a_{p,\beta}L_p
 \operatorname{diam}(C)^{p+\beta}+\Lambda_0\tau.
\end{equation}
This includes $p=0$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Fix $T$ and set
$\boldsymbol e_i:=\widetilde F_i-T(\boldsymbol z_i)$.
By the triangle inequality,
$\|\boldsymbol e_i\|
\le\|\widetilde F_i-F(\boldsymbol z_i)\|
+\|F(\boldsymbol z_i)-T(\boldsymbol z_i)\|
\le\tau+r_T$.
Since interpolation reproduces each component of $T$, we have
$T=\sum\limits_{i=1}^nT(\boldsymbol z_i)\ell_i$.
Therefore,
\[
 \mathcal I-F
 =T-F+\sum\limits_{i=1}^n\boldsymbol e_i\ell_i.
\]
For every $\boldsymbol y\in C$, the second term has norm at most
$\sum\limits_{i=1}^n
\|\boldsymbol e_i\|\,|\ell_i(\boldsymbol y)|
\le(r_T+\tau)\Lambda_0$.
Taking the supremum over $\boldsymbol y\in C$ proves the
value bound.

For the derivative bound, differentiate the same identity.
Each $\boldsymbol e_i$ is constant, so
$D(\boldsymbol e_i\ell_i)
=\boldsymbol e_i(\nabla\ell_i)^{\mathsf T}$.
The induced operator norm of this rank-one map is
$\|\boldsymbol e_i\|\,\|\nabla\ell_i\|_2$.
Thus, for every $\boldsymbol y\in C$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|D\mathcal I(\boldsymbol y)-DF(\boldsymbol y)\|
 &\le
 \|DT(\boldsymbol y)-DF(\boldsymbol y)\|
 +\sum\limits_{i=1}^n
 \|\boldsymbol e_i\|\,\|\nabla\ell_i(\boldsymbol y)\|_2\\
 &\le
 \|DT-DF\|_{\infty,C}+(r_T+\tau)\Lambda_1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the supremum proves the derivative bound.

For \eqref{eq:apx-stable-local-error}, choose $T$ to be the
degree-$p$ Taylor polynomial of $F$ at any $\boldsymbol c\in C$.
Its components belong to $\mathcal P$ because
$\Pi_p^d\subseteq\mathcal P$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:holder-taylor-remainder} and
$\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol c\|_2\le\operatorname{diam}(C)$ give
$r_T\le\|F-T\|_{\infty,C}
\le a_{p,\beta}L_p\operatorname{diam}(C)^{p+\beta}$.
Substituting both bounds into the value estimate yields
\eqref{eq:apx-stable-local-error}.
For $p=0$, take $T=F(\boldsymbol c)$ and use the
H\"older continuity of $F$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:local-reconstruction}
Suppose that $F\in C^{p,\beta}(L_p)$ on a neighborhood of $S$.
There is a nonadaptively chosen node set $X_p\subset S$,
containing $\boldsymbol c$ and having
$|X_p|=\binom{d+p}{p}$, with the following property.
Supplied values satisfying
$\|\widetilde F_i-F(\boldsymbol z_i)\|\le\tau$
at its nodes determine a polynomial map $P$, with each
component in $\Pi_p^d$, such that
$P(\boldsymbol c)=\widetilde F_{\boldsymbol c}$ and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-local-vector-value-bounds}
 \|D^j(P-F)\|_{\infty,S}
 \le
 \frac{3}{2}a_{p-j,\beta}L_p\rho^{p-j+\beta}
 +\Lambda_j\tau,
 \qquad j=0,1.
\end{equation}
Here $\widetilde F_{\boldsymbol c}$ is the supplied value
at $\boldsymbol c$, so
$\|P(\boldsymbol c)-F(\boldsymbol c)\|\le\tau$.

For fixed $S,\boldsymbol c$ and exponents
$\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_p\in(0,1]$, the constructions admit
nested node sets
$X_0=\{\boldsymbol c\}\subset X_1\subset\cdots\subset X_p$
with $|X_j|=\binom{d+j}{j}$.
At degree $j\ge1$, the corresponding bound uses
$(j,\beta_j,L_j)$ whenever
$F\in C^{j,\beta_j}(L_j)$, and the stability constants
of the degree-$j$ node set.

At degree zero, the constant model
$P\equiv\widetilde F_{\boldsymbol c}$ satisfies
$\|P-F\|_{\infty,S}\le L_0\rho^\beta+\tau$
whenever $F\in C^{0,\beta}(L_0)$.
Its interpolation stability constants are
$\Lambda_0=1$ and $\Lambda_1=0$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
We construct a fixed interpolation pattern, contract its
nodes toward $\boldsymbol c$, and then bound separately
the approximation error and the effect of the supplied-value
errors.

\noindent\textbf{Reference nodes.}
Let
$A_p:=\{\boldsymbol\alpha\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^d:
|\boldsymbol\alpha|\le p\}$, where
$|\boldsymbol\alpha|:=\sum\limits_{k=1}^d\alpha_k$,
and set
$\Sigma_p:=\{\frac{\boldsymbol\alpha}{p}:
\boldsymbol\alpha\in A_p\}$.
These $\binom{d+p}{p}$ nodes include $\boldsymbol0$
and lie in the closed unit ball because
$\|\frac{\boldsymbol\alpha}{p}\|_2
\le\frac{|\boldsymbol\alpha|}{p}\le1$.

To verify unisolvence, define
$B_{\boldsymbol\alpha}(\boldsymbol w)
:=\prod\limits_{k=1}^d\binom{pw_k}{\alpha_k}$,
where
$\binom{t}{r}:=\frac{1}{r!}
\prod\limits_{i=0}^{r-1}(t-i)$ for $r\ge1$ and
$\binom{t}{0}:=1$.
At a node $\frac{\boldsymbol\zeta}{p}$,
$B_{\boldsymbol\alpha}(\frac{\boldsymbol\zeta}{p})
=\prod\limits_{k=1}^d\binom{\zeta_k}{\alpha_k}$.
This value vanishes unless
$\boldsymbol\alpha\le\boldsymbol\zeta$ coordinatewise,
and equals one when
$\boldsymbol\alpha=\boldsymbol\zeta$.
Ordering the indices by total degree gives a triangular
evaluation matrix with unit diagonal: among indices
of the same total degree, a nonzero entry requires
$\boldsymbol\alpha=\boldsymbol\zeta$.
The matrix is therefore invertible.
Since its size is $\dim\Pi_p^d$, these nodes are unisolvent.

Write $\Sigma_p=\{\boldsymbol\sigma_i\}_i$ and let
$\ell_i(\boldsymbol w)
=\sum\limits_{\boldsymbol\alpha\in A_p}
\lambda_{i,\boldsymbol\alpha}
\boldsymbol w^{\boldsymbol\alpha}$
be the associated Lagrange basis.
Define
$K_{d,p}:=\max\{1,\,
p\sum\limits_{i,\boldsymbol\alpha}
|\lambda_{i,\boldsymbol\alpha}|\}$.
For $R\ge1$ and $\|\boldsymbol w\|_2\le R$, we have
$|\boldsymbol w^{\boldsymbol\alpha}|
\le R^{|\boldsymbol\alpha|}$ and
$\|\nabla\boldsymbol w^{\boldsymbol\alpha}\|_2
\le|\boldsymbol\alpha|R^{|\boldsymbol\alpha|-1}$,
with zero derivative when $\boldsymbol\alpha=\boldsymbol0$.
The derivative estimate follows by bounding the Euclidean
norm of the coordinate derivatives by their absolute sum.
Summing over the coefficients gives
\[
 \sup\limits_{\|\boldsymbol w\|_2\le R}
 \sum\limits_i\|D^j\ell_i(\boldsymbol w)\|
 \le K_{d,p}R^{p-j},
 \qquad j=0,1.
\]

\noindent\textbf{Sampling nodes and stability.}
Choose $\eta>0$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-interpolation-spacing}
 \eta\le
 \min\left\{
 \operatorname{dist}(\boldsymbol c,\partial S),\,
 \rho(2K_{d,p})^{-\frac{1}{\beta}}
 \right\}.
\end{equation}
Set $\boldsymbol z_i:=\boldsymbol c+\eta\boldsymbol\sigma_i$.
The first condition places these nodes in $S$.
Their physical Lagrange basis consists of the functions
$\boldsymbol y\mapsto
\ell_i((\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol c)/\eta)$.
Since $\eta\le\rho$, the reference basis bound with
$R=\rho/\eta\ge1$ yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-contracted-stability}
 \Lambda_j
 \le
 \eta^{-j}K_{d,p}
 \left(\frac{\rho}{\eta}\right)^{p-j}
 =K_{d,p}\rho^{p-j}\eta^{-p},
 \qquad j=0,1.
\end{equation}
Construct the interpolant of the supplied values by
$P(\boldsymbol c+\boldsymbol v)
:=\sum\limits_i\widetilde F_i\ell_i(\boldsymbol v/\eta)$.
The origin node ensures
$P(\boldsymbol c)=\widetilde F_{\boldsymbol c}$.

\noindent\textbf{Approximation and data errors.}
Let $P_{\mathrm{ex}}$ be the interpolant at the same nodes
of the exact values $F(\boldsymbol z_i)$; it is used only
in the analysis.
Let $T_p$ be the degree-$p$ Taylor polynomial of $F$
at $\boldsymbol c$ and put
$r_T:=\max\limits_i
\|(F-T_p)(\boldsymbol z_i)\|$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:holder-taylor-remainder} gives
$r_T\le a_{p,\beta}L_p\eta^{p+\beta}$.
Since interpolation reproduces $T_p$, the difference
$P_{\mathrm{ex}}-T_p$ interpolates these nodal residuals.
The scaled basis bound gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-coefficient-bounds}
\begin{aligned}
 \|D^j(P_{\mathrm{ex}}-T_p)\|_{\infty,S}
 &\le
 \eta^{-j}K_{d,p}
 \left(\frac{\rho}{\eta}\right)^{p-j}r_T\\
 &\le
 K_{d,p}a_{p,\beta}L_p\eta^\beta\rho^{p-j}\\
 &\le
 \frac{1}{2}a_{p-j,\beta}L_p\rho^{p-j+\beta},
 \qquad j=0,1.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The last inequality uses
$K_{d,p}\eta^\beta\le\frac{1}{2}\rho^\beta$
and $a_{p,\beta}\le a_{p-j,\beta}$.
Adding the Taylor bound
$\|D^j(T_p-F)\|_{\infty,S}
\le a_{p-j,\beta}L_p\rho^{p-j+\beta}$
gives
$\|D^j(P_{\mathrm{ex}}-F)\|_{\infty,S}
\le\frac{3}{2}a_{p-j,\beta}L_p\rho^{p-j+\beta}$.

On the other hand,
$P-P_{\mathrm{ex}}
=\sum\limits_i(\widetilde F_i-F(\boldsymbol z_i))
\ell_i((\cdot-\boldsymbol c)/\eta)$.
The triangle inequality for values, and the rank-one
operator norm identity for derivatives, therefore give
$\|D^j(P-P_{\mathrm{ex}})\|_{\infty,S}
\le\Lambda_j\tau$ for $j=0,1$.
Adding these bounds proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:apx-local-vector-value-bounds}.

\noindent\textbf{Nested nodes.}
Choose a common $s>0$ such that $js$ satisfies
Eq.~\eqref{eq:apx-interpolation-spacing} at degree $j$
and exponent $\beta_j$, for every $1\le j\le p$.
There are finitely many positive upper bounds on $s$,
so such a choice exists.
Set
$X_j:=\{\boldsymbol c+s\boldsymbol\alpha:
\boldsymbol\alpha\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^d,\,
|\boldsymbol\alpha|\le j\}$.
These sets are nested, have the required cardinalities,
and satisfy $X_j=\boldsymbol c+(js)\Sigma_j$ for $j\ge1$.
The preceding construction and its error bound apply at
every degree with the corresponding physical Lagrange basis.
At degree zero,
$\|\widetilde F_{\boldsymbol c}-F(\boldsymbol y)\|
\le\|\widetilde F_{\boldsymbol c}-F(\boldsymbol c)\|
+\|F(\boldsymbol c)-F(\boldsymbol y)\|
\le\tau+L_0\rho^\beta$.
Its only basis function is the constant one, giving
$\Lambda_0=1$ and $\Lambda_1=0$.
All nodes depend only on the prescribed parameters and
the geometry of $S$, so all evaluations are nonadaptive.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:polynomial-reconstruction}
Suppose that $F\in C^{p,\beta}(L_p)$ on a neighborhood of $S$.
There is a constant $C_{p,\beta}>0$, depending only on $p,\beta$,
and a nonadaptively chosen node set $V\subset S$, containing
$\boldsymbol c$, with
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-two-accuracy-queries}
 |V|
 \le
 \binom{d+p}{p}
 \left[
 \max\left\{
 1,\,
 C_{p,\beta}d^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}(\sigma-1)
 \right\}
 \right]^d.
\end{equation}
There are explicit coefficient functions $L_{\boldsymbol v}$
that are $C^\infty$ on a neighborhood of $S$ and have
finite stability constants $\Lambda_0,\Lambda_1$.
For supplied values satisfying
$\|\widetilde F_{\boldsymbol v}-F(\boldsymbol v)\|\le\tau$
at every $\boldsymbol v\in V$, the model
$W:=\sum\limits_{\boldsymbol v\in V}
\widetilde F_{\boldsymbol v}L_{\boldsymbol v}$ satisfies
$W(\boldsymbol c)=\widetilde F_{\boldsymbol c}$ and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-vector-value-bounds}
 \|W-F\|_{\infty,S}
 \le\varepsilon_0+\Lambda_0\tau,
 \qquad
 \|DW-DF\|_{\infty,S}
 \le\varepsilon_1+\Lambda_1\tau.
\end{equation}
If $\sigma\le(\frac{4}{3})^{\frac{1}{\nu}}$, then
$\binom{d+p}{p}$ evaluations suffice, and each component
of $W$ belongs to $\Pi_p^d$.
All queries form one nonadaptive batch.
For exact data, $\tau=0$, the two budgets are attained and
$W(\boldsymbol c)=F(\boldsymbol c)$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We first construct the model from exact values and denote it
by $W^{\mathrm{ex}}$.
We then identify its linear dependence on the data and bound
the effect of perturbing those data.
Set $\sigma_0:=(\frac{4}{3})^{\frac{1}{\nu}}>1$.

\noindent\textbf{A single polynomial.}
If $\sigma\le\sigma_0$, take $W^{\mathrm{ex}}=P$ from
Proposition~\ref{prop:local-reconstruction} with exact data.
The definition of $\sigma$ gives
\[
 \frac{\|W^{\mathrm{ex}}-F\|_{\infty,S}}{\varepsilon_0}
 \le\frac{3}{4}\sigma^\nu
 \le\frac{3}{4}\sigma_0^\nu=1,
 \qquad
 \frac{\|DW^{\mathrm{ex}}-DF\|_{\infty,S}}{\varepsilon_1}
 \le\frac{3}{4}\sigma^{\nu-1}
 \le\frac{3}{4}\sigma_0^{\nu-1}\le1.
\]
The last inequality uses $\sigma_0>1$ and $\nu-1<\nu$.
This case uses $\binom{d+p}{p}$ evaluations and includes
$L_p=0$.
Its reconstruction is the interpolation operator of
Proposition~\ref{prop:local-reconstruction}; its coefficient
functions are the corresponding polynomial Lagrange basis.

Suppose henceforth that $\sigma>\sigma_0$.
We construct a model at a scale $0<h\le\rho$, then choose
$h$ to meet the two approximation budgets.

\noindent\textbf{Covering and polynomial models.}
Choose a maximal set
$\{\boldsymbol c_1=\boldsymbol c,\ldots,\boldsymbol c_n\}
\subset\operatorname{int}(S)$
whose distinct points have distance at least $h$.
The open balls of radius $\frac{h}{2}$ about these centers
are disjoint and lie in
$B(\boldsymbol c,\rho+\frac{h}{2})$.
Comparing their volumes gives
$n\le(1+\frac{2\rho}{h})^d$.
This finite bound also ensures that successively adding
admissible centers terminates.

By maximality, every point of $\operatorname{int}(S)$
is within distance less than $h$ of some center.
Since $S$ is convex with nonempty interior,
$S=\overline{\operatorname{int}(S)}$.
Taking closures therefore shows that the closed $h$-balls
about the centers cover $S$.

For each $i$, set
$S_i:=S\cap\overline B(\boldsymbol c_i,2h)$.
This set is compact and convex,
$\boldsymbol c_i\in\operatorname{int}(S_i)$,
and its radius about $\boldsymbol c_i$ is at most $2h$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:local-reconstruction}, with exact data
and $\frac{3}{2}$ weakened to $2$, provides a polynomial map
$P_i$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-patch-accuracy}
\begin{aligned}
 \|P_i-F\|_{\infty,S_i}
 &\le A_h:=2^{\nu+1}a_{p,\beta}L_ph^\nu,\\
 \|DP_i-DF\|_{\infty,S_i}
 &\le B_h:=2^\nu a_{p-1,\beta}L_ph^{\nu-1}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Let $V_i$ be its interpolation nodes and let $V$ be their
union, with any repeated nodes included only once.
Then $|V|\le n\binom{d+p}{p}$ and $\boldsymbol c\in V$.

\noindent\textbf{Smooth weights.}
Choose a smooth function $\psi:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$
equal to $1$ on $(-\infty,1]$ and $0$ on $[4,\infty)$,
with $\|\psi'\|_\infty\le\frac{1}{2}$.
One construction smooths the linear transition on
$[\frac{3}{2},\frac{7}{2}]$ with a nonnegative unit-mass
kernel supported in $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$.
Define
$b_i(\boldsymbol y)
:=\psi(\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol c_i\|_2^2/h^2)$,
$Z:=\sum\limits_i b_i^d$, and $\theta_i:=b_i^d/Z$.
At every point of $S$, the covering supplies an index with
$b_i=1$, so $Z\ge1$ on $S$.
Consequently, the $\theta_i$ are smooth on the open
neighborhood $\{Z>0\}$ of $S$, are nonnegative, and sum
to one.
Whenever $\theta_i$ or its gradient is nonzero at a point
of $S$, that point belongs to $S_i$.

At any point $\boldsymbol y$, at most $5^d$ of the
$b_i(\boldsymbol y)$ are positive.
Indeed, positivity requires
$\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol c_i\|_2<2h$.
The corresponding disjoint balls of radius $\frac{h}{2}$
therefore lie in $B(\boldsymbol y,\frac{5h}{2})$,
and volume comparison gives the bound.

The chain rule and the support of $\psi'$ give
$\|\nabla b_i\|_2\le\frac{2}{h}$.
For $d\ge2$, H\"older's inequality yields
$\sum\limits_{b_i>0}b_i^{d-1}
\le(5^d)^{\frac{1}{d}}
(\sum\limits_i b_i^d)^{\frac{d-1}{d}}
=5Z^{1-\frac{1}{d}}$.
For $d=1$, the same bound follows from the number of
positive terms.
Since $b_i=0$ implies $\nabla b_i=0$, the quotient rule
gives, for $\boldsymbol y\in S$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-partition-derivatives}
\begin{aligned}
 \sum\limits_i\|\nabla\theta_i\|_2
 &\le
 \frac{1}{Z}\sum\limits_i\|\nabla(b_i^d)\|_2
 +\frac{\|\nabla Z\|_2}{Z^2}\sum\limits_i b_i^d\\
 &\le
 \frac{2}{Z}\sum\limits_i\|\nabla(b_i^d)\|_2\\
 &\le
 \frac{4d}{hZ}\sum\limits_{b_i>0}b_i^{d-1}\\
 &\le\frac{20d}{h}Z^{-\frac{1}{d}}
 \le\frac{20d}{h}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The second inequality uses
$\|\nabla Z\|_2\le\sum\limits_i\|\nabla(b_i^d)\|_2$,
and the last uses $Z\ge1$.

\noindent\textbf{Errors for exact data.}
Set $\widetilde W^{\mathrm{ex}}
:=\sum\limits_i\theta_iP_i$ and $E_i:=P_i-F$.
Since the weights sum to one,
$\widetilde W^{\mathrm{ex}}-F
=\sum\limits_i\theta_iE_i$.
Every nonzero term uses an error bound on its own set $S_i$,
so $\|\widetilde W^{\mathrm{ex}}-F\|_{\infty,S}\le A_h$.
Differentiating gives
\[
 D\widetilde W^{\mathrm{ex}}-DF
 =\sum\limits_i\theta_iDE_i
 +\sum\limits_i E_i(\nabla\theta_i)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
The first sum has norm at most $B_h$.
For the second, the rank-one norm identity and
\eqref{eq:apx-partition-derivatives} give
$\|\sum\limits_i E_i(\nabla\theta_i)^{\mathsf T}\|
\le A_h\sum\limits_i\|\nabla\theta_i\|_2
\le\frac{20dA_h}{h}$.

Define
$W^{\mathrm{ex}}:=\widetilde W^{\mathrm{ex}}
+F(\boldsymbol c)-\widetilde W^{\mathrm{ex}}(\boldsymbol c)$.
The value $F(\boldsymbol c)$ is among the sampled values.
This correction enforces
$W^{\mathrm{ex}}(\boldsymbol c)=F(\boldsymbol c)$
and leaves derivatives unchanged.
Since
$\|F(\boldsymbol c)-\widetilde W^{\mathrm{ex}}(\boldsymbol c)\|
\le A_h$, it increases the value error by at most $A_h$.
Using $a_{p-1,\beta}=\nu a_{p,\beta}$ gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-global-scale-bounds}
\begin{aligned}
 \|W^{\mathrm{ex}}-F\|_{\infty,S}
 &\le2A_h
 =2^{\nu+2}a_{p,\beta}L_ph^\nu,\\
 \|DW^{\mathrm{ex}}-DF\|_{\infty,S}
 &\le B_h+\frac{20dA_h}{h}
 =2^\nu a_{p,\beta}(\nu+40d)L_ph^{\nu-1}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

\noindent\textbf{Scale and node count.}
Set
\[
 H_d:=\max\left\{
 2^{1+\frac{1}{\nu}},\,
 2\left(1+\frac{40d}{\nu}\right)^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
 \right\},
 \qquad h:=\frac{\rho}{H_d\sigma}.
\]
Then $0<h<\rho$ because $\sigma>\sigma_0>1$.
The definition of $\sigma$ implies
$a_{p,\beta}L_p\rho^\nu
\le\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\sigma^\nu$
and
$a_{p-1,\beta}L_p\rho^{\nu-1}
\le\frac{\varepsilon_1}{2}\sigma^{\nu-1}$.
Substitution into \eqref{eq:apx-global-scale-bounds} yields
\[
 \frac{\|W^{\mathrm{ex}}-F\|_{\infty,S}}{\varepsilon_0}
 \le\frac{2^{\nu+1}}{H_d^\nu}\le1,
 \qquad
 \frac{\|DW^{\mathrm{ex}}-DF\|_{\infty,S}}{\varepsilon_1}
 \le
 \frac{2^{\nu-1}(1+\frac{40d}{\nu})}{H_d^{\nu-1}}
 \le1.
\]

The node count is at most
$\binom{d+p}{p}(1+2H_d\sigma)^d$.
Since $d\ge1$ and
$1+\frac{40d}{\nu}\le d(1+\frac{40}{\nu})$,
we have $H_d\le H_1d^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}$.
Moreover, $\sigma>\sigma_0$ implies
$\sigma-1\ge(1-\sigma_0^{-1})\sigma$.
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
 1+2H_d\sigma
 &\le(1+2H_1)d^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}\sigma\\
 &\le
 \frac{1+2H_1}{1-\sigma_0^{-1}}
 d^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}(\sigma-1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking $C_{p,\beta}:=\frac{1+2H_1}{1-\sigma_0^{-1}}$
and combining the two cases proves
\eqref{eq:apx-two-accuracy-queries}.

\noindent\textbf{Perturbing the supplied values.}
Each local polynomial is linear in its nodal values.
Write
$P_i=\sum\limits_{\boldsymbol v\in V_i}
F(\boldsymbol v)\ell_{i,\boldsymbol v}$
for its Lagrange representation, and extend the index set
by setting $\ell_{i,\boldsymbol v}=0$ when
$\boldsymbol v\notin V_i$.
Define
$\widetilde L_{\boldsymbol v}
:=\sum\limits_i\theta_i\ell_{i,\boldsymbol v}$ and
$L_{\boldsymbol v}(\boldsymbol y)
:=\widetilde L_{\boldsymbol v}(\boldsymbol y)
-\widetilde L_{\boldsymbol v}(\boldsymbol c)
+\mathbf 1_{\{\boldsymbol v=\boldsymbol c\}}$.
Expanding the blend and its center correction shows that
$W^{\mathrm{ex}}=\sum\limits_{\boldsymbol v\in V}
F(\boldsymbol v)L_{\boldsymbol v}$.
All coefficient functions are $C^\infty$ on $\{Z>0\}$
and satisfy
$L_{\boldsymbol v}(\boldsymbol c)
=\mathbf 1_{\{\boldsymbol v=\boldsymbol c\}}$.
In the single-polynomial case, take its Lagrange basis as
$L_{\boldsymbol v}$; these properties hold there as well.
Since $V$ is finite and $S$ is compact, both
$\Lambda_0$ and $\Lambda_1$
are finite.

Applying the same coefficients to the supplied values gives
$W:=\sum\limits_{\boldsymbol v\in V}
\widetilde F_{\boldsymbol v}L_{\boldsymbol v}$ and
$W(\boldsymbol c)=\widetilde F_{\boldsymbol c}$.
For $j=0,1$, the data error bound and the triangle inequality
give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|D^j(W-W^{\mathrm{ex}})\|_{\infty,S}
 &\le
 \sup\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in S}
 \sum\limits_{\boldsymbol v\in V}
 \|\widetilde F_{\boldsymbol v}-F(\boldsymbol v)\|
 \|D^jL_{\boldsymbol v}(\boldsymbol y)\|\\
 &\le\tau\Lambda_j.
\end{aligned}
\]
For $j=1$, the summands are rank-one derivatives, whose
operator norms are the displayed products.
Adding the corresponding exact-data error proves
\eqref{eq:apx-vector-value-bounds}.
Every covering center, interpolation node, and coefficient
function is fixed by the prescribed parameters and the
geometry of $S$, before any values are observed.
Thus all queries form one nonadaptive batch.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:radial-scalar-reconstruction}
Let $\boldsymbol x\in S$ and
$\rho_{\boldsymbol x}
:=\max\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in S}
\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2$.
Suppose that $f$ is $C^1$ on a neighborhood of $S$
and $W\in(\Pi_{p-1}^d)^d$.
Define
\[
 P(\boldsymbol x+\boldsymbol v)
 :=
 \int\limits_0^1
 \langle W(\boldsymbol x+t\boldsymbol v),
 \boldsymbol v\rangle\,dt.
\]
Then $P\in\Pi_p^d$, $P(\boldsymbol x)=0$, and
$\nabla P(\boldsymbol x)=W(\boldsymbol x)$.
If $\|W-\nabla f\|_{\infty,S}\le\eta_0$, then
$\|P-f+f(\boldsymbol x)\|_{\infty,S}
\le\rho_{\boldsymbol x}\eta_0$.

If additionally $f$ is $C^2$ on a neighborhood of $S$
and $\|DW-\nabla^2f\|_{\infty,S}\le\eta_1$, then
$\|\nabla P-\nabla f\|_{\infty,S}
\le\eta_0+\frac{1}{2}\rho_{\boldsymbol x}\eta_1$.
The construction uses only the coefficients of $W$
and requires no additional queries.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The integrand is a polynomial in $\boldsymbol v$
of degree at most $p$.
Integrating its coefficients in $t$ therefore gives
$P\in\Pi_p^d$.
Its constant term is zero, and its linear term is
$\langle W(\boldsymbol x),\boldsymbol v\rangle$.
Thus $P(\boldsymbol x)=0$ and
$\nabla P(\boldsymbol x)=W(\boldsymbol x)$.

Write $E:=W-\nabla f$ for the vector-field error and
$e:=P-f+f(\boldsymbol x)$ for the scalar error.
For $\boldsymbol x+\boldsymbol v\in S$, convexity
keeps the segment
$[\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol x+\boldsymbol v]$ in $S$.
The fundamental theorem of calculus gives
$f(\boldsymbol x+\boldsymbol v)-f(\boldsymbol x)
=\int\limits_0^1
\langle\nabla f(\boldsymbol x+t\boldsymbol v),
\boldsymbol v\rangle\,dt$.
Subtracting this identity from the definition of $P$
yields
$e(\boldsymbol x+\boldsymbol v)
=\int\limits_0^1
\langle E(\boldsymbol x+t\boldsymbol v),
\boldsymbol v\rangle\,dt$.
Consequently,
$|e(\boldsymbol x+\boldsymbol v)|
\le\int\limits_0^1
\|E(\boldsymbol x+t\boldsymbol v)\|_2
\|\boldsymbol v\|_2\,dt
\le\eta_0\|\boldsymbol v\|_2
\le\rho_{\boldsymbol x}\eta_0$.

Under the additional differentiability assumptions,
differentiating with respect to $\boldsymbol v$ yields
\[
 \nabla e(\boldsymbol x+\boldsymbol v)
 =
 \int\limits_0^1
 \left[
 E(\boldsymbol x+t\boldsymbol v)
 +t\,DE(\boldsymbol x+t\boldsymbol v)^{\mathsf T}
 \boldsymbol v
 \right]dt.
\]
This differentiation is valid also when
$\boldsymbol x+\boldsymbol v$ lies on the boundary of $S$:
the segment is compact and lies in the open neighborhood
where $f$ is defined, so sufficiently small perturbations
of $\boldsymbol v$ keep the whole segment in that
neighborhood.
The integrand has norm at most
$\eta_0+t\eta_1\|\boldsymbol v\|_2$.
Integration therefore gives
$\|\nabla e(\boldsymbol x+\boldsymbol v)\|_2
\le\eta_0+\eta_1\|\boldsymbol v\|_2
\int\limits_0^1t\,dt
=\eta_0+\frac{1}{2}\eta_1\|\boldsymbol v\|_2
\le\eta_0+\frac{1}{2}\rho_{\boldsymbol x}\eta_1$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:gradient-only-scalar-reconstruction}
Suppose that $f\in C^{p,\beta}(L_p)$ on a neighborhood of $S$.
There is a nonadaptively chosen set of
$\binom{d+p-1}{p-1}$ nodes in $S$, including
$\boldsymbol c$, such that supplied gradients satisfying
$\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol g}_i
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol z_i)\|_2\le\tau$
determine $P\in\Pi_p^d$ with
$P(\boldsymbol c)=0$,
$\nabla P(\boldsymbol c)
=\widetilde{\boldsymbol g}_{\boldsymbol c}$, and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-gradient-only-bounds}
 \|P-f+f(\boldsymbol c)\|_{\infty,S}\le B_0,
 \qquad
 \|\nabla P-\nabla f\|_{\infty,S}\le B_1.
\end{equation}
Here $\widetilde{\boldsymbol g}_{\boldsymbol c}$ is the
supplied gradient at $\boldsymbol c$, and $\Lambda_0,\Lambda_1$
are the stability constants of the degree-$(p-1)$
interpolation at these nodes.
For $p\ge2$, the bounds are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 B_0
 &:=2a_{p-1,\beta}L_p\rho^\nu
 +\rho\Lambda_0\tau,\\
 B_1
 &:=(2a_{p-1,\beta}+a_{p-2,\beta})L_p\rho^{\nu-1}
 +\left(\Lambda_0+\frac{\rho}{2}\Lambda_1\right)\tau.
\end{aligned}
\]
For $p=1$, they are
$B_0:=a_{1,\beta}L_1\rho^{1+\beta}+\rho\tau$
and $B_1:=L_1\rho^\beta+\tau$, with
$\Lambda_0=1$ and $\Lambda_1=0$.

Moreover, for all $\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y\in S$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-gradient-only-increments}
 \left|
 P(\boldsymbol y)-P(\boldsymbol x)
 -f(\boldsymbol y)+f(\boldsymbol x)
 \right|
 \le
 \min\left\{
 2B_0,\,
 B_1\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2
 \right\}.
\end{equation}
The term $2B_0$ can be replaced by $B_0$ when
$\boldsymbol x=\boldsymbol c$.
No function values are required.
For $\tau=0$, these are the exact-gradient bounds;
if also $L_p=0$, then $P=f-f(\boldsymbol c)$ on $S$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Suppose first that $p\ge2$.
Pairing the vector output of $D^{p-1}\nabla f$
with a unit vector supplies the last argument of
the scalar $p$-linear form $D^pf$.
Taking the supremum over this unit vector and the other
$p-1$ unit arguments gives
$\|D^{p-1}\nabla f(\boldsymbol y)
-D^{p-1}\nabla f(\boldsymbol z)\|
=\|D^pf(\boldsymbol y)-D^pf(\boldsymbol z)\|$.
Hence $\nabla f\in C^{p-1,\beta}(L_p)$.

Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:local-reconstruction}
to $F=\nabla f$ at degree $p-1$ with the supplied
gradient vectors as its input values.
The resulting vector polynomial
$W\in(\Pi_{p-1}^d)^d$ uses
$\binom{d+p-1}{p-1}$ supplied gradients and satisfies
$W(\boldsymbol c)=\widetilde{\boldsymbol g}_{\boldsymbol c}$.
Weakening the factor $\frac{3}{2}$ to $2$, its errors obey
$\|W-\nabla f\|_{\infty,S}
\le2a_{p-1,\beta}L_p\rho^{p-1+\beta}+\Lambda_0\tau$
and
$\|DW-\nabla^2f\|_{\infty,S}
\le2a_{p-2,\beta}L_p\rho^{p-2+\beta}+\Lambda_1\tau$.

Use Lemma~\ref{lem:radial-scalar-reconstruction}
with $\boldsymbol x=\boldsymbol c$ to construct $P$.
It gives $P(\boldsymbol c)=0$ and
$\nabla P(\boldsymbol c)=W(\boldsymbol c)
=\widetilde{\boldsymbol g}_{\boldsymbol c}$.
Its error bounds yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|P-f+f(\boldsymbol c)\|_{\infty,S}
 &\le
 \rho\left(
 2a_{p-1,\beta}L_p\rho^{p-1+\beta}
 +\Lambda_0\tau\right)
 =B_0,\\
 \|\nabla P-\nabla f\|_{\infty,S}
 &\le
 2a_{p-1,\beta}L_p\rho^{p-1+\beta}
 +\Lambda_0\tau\\
 &\quad+
 \frac{\rho}{2}\left(
 2a_{p-2,\beta}L_p\rho^{p-2+\beta}
 +\Lambda_1\tau\right)
 =B_1.
\end{aligned}
\]

For $p=1$, use only the supplied gradient
$\widetilde{\boldsymbol g}_{\boldsymbol c}$ and set
$P(\boldsymbol c+\boldsymbol v)
:=\langle\widetilde{\boldsymbol g}_{\boldsymbol c},
\boldsymbol v\rangle$.
Then $P(\boldsymbol c)=0$ and
$\nabla P=\widetilde{\boldsymbol g}_{\boldsymbol c}$.
The triangle inequality and H\"older continuity give
$\|\nabla P(\boldsymbol c+\boldsymbol v)
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol c+\boldsymbol v)\|_2
\le\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol g}_{\boldsymbol c}
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol c)\|_2
+\|\nabla f(\boldsymbol c)
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol c+\boldsymbol v)\|_2
\le\tau+L_1\|\boldsymbol v\|_2^\beta\le B_1$.
For the value error, integrate along the segment to obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\left|
 P(\boldsymbol c+\boldsymbol v)
 -f(\boldsymbol c+\boldsymbol v)+f(\boldsymbol c)
 \right|\\
 &\quad=
 \left|
 \int\limits_0^1
 \left\langle
 \widetilde{\boldsymbol g}_{\boldsymbol c}
 -\nabla f(\boldsymbol c+t\boldsymbol v),
 \boldsymbol v
 \right\rangle\,dt
 \right|\\
 &\quad\le
 \int\limits_0^1
 \left(\tau+L_1t^\beta\|\boldsymbol v\|_2^\beta\right)
 \|\boldsymbol v\|_2\,dt\\
 &\quad=
 \tau\|\boldsymbol v\|_2
 +a_{1,\beta}L_1\|\boldsymbol v\|_2^{1+\beta}
 \le B_0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The constant vector interpolant has the single basis
function $1$, so $\Lambda_0=1$ and $\Lambda_1=0$.

Finally, set $e:=P-f+f(\boldsymbol c)$.
The established bounds give
$\|e\|_{\infty,S}\le B_0$ and
$\|\nabla e\|_{\infty,S}\le B_1$.
Applying \eqref{eq:apx-increment-control} to $e$
proves \eqref{eq:apx-gradient-only-increments}.
Since $P(\boldsymbol c)=0$, we have $e(\boldsymbol c)=0$
even for inexact gradient data, so the centered bound
replaces $2B_0$ by $B_0$.
Setting $\tau=0$ recovers all exact-gradient conclusions,
including $\nabla P(\boldsymbol c)=\nabla f(\boldsymbol c)$.
If $L_p=\tau=0$, then $B_0=0$, which gives
$P=f-f(\boldsymbol c)$ throughout $S$.
The interpolation nodes are chosen nonadaptively, and
integration of the known vector polynomial requires
no further queries.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:approximation-minimization-transfer}
Let $Y$ be nonempty and compact, let
$f,\widehat f,q\in C(Y)$, and let $\zeta\ge0$.
If $\widehat{\boldsymbol y}\in Y$ satisfies
$(\widehat f+q)(\widehat{\boldsymbol y})
\le\min\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in Y}
(\widehat f+q)(\boldsymbol y)+\zeta$, then
\[
 (f+q)(\widehat{\boldsymbol y})
 -\min\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in Y}(f+q)(\boldsymbol y)
 \le
 \operatorname{osc}_Y(\widehat f-f)+\zeta
 \le
 2\|\widehat f-f\|_{\infty,Y}+\zeta.
\]
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Continuity and compactness give a minimizer
$\boldsymbol y^\star\in
\operatorname*{arg\,min}\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in Y}
(f+q)(\boldsymbol y)$.
Write $E:=\widehat f-f$.
Since
$\min\limits_Y(\widehat f+q)
\le(\widehat f+q)(\boldsymbol y^\star)$,
the assumed model suboptimality implies
$(\widehat f+q)(\widehat{\boldsymbol y})
-(\widehat f+q)(\boldsymbol y^\star)\le\zeta$.
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &(f+q)(\widehat{\boldsymbol y})
 -(f+q)(\boldsymbol y^\star)\\
 &\quad=
 (\widehat f+q)(\widehat{\boldsymbol y})
 -(\widehat f+q)(\boldsymbol y^\star)
 +E(\boldsymbol y^\star)-E(\widehat{\boldsymbol y})\\
 &\quad\le
 \zeta+\max\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in Y}E(\boldsymbol y)
 -\min\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in Y}E(\boldsymbol y)\\
 &\quad=
 \zeta+\operatorname{osc}_Y(E)
 \le\zeta+2\|E\|_{\infty,Y}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last inequality follows from
$\max\limits_Y E\le\|E\|_{\infty,Y}$ and
$\min\limits_Y E\ge-\|E\|_{\infty,Y}$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:global-minimization-known-term}
Let $Y:=\prod\limits_{i=1}^k[a_i,b_i]$, where
$a_i<b_i$, and suppose that $\operatorname{diam}(Y)\le D$.
Let $f\in C^{p,\beta}(L_p)$ on a neighborhood of $Y$,
where $p\ge1$, and let $q\in C(Y)$ be known.
Write $\nu:=p+\beta$.

For every $\delta>0$, there is a nonadaptively chosen
node set $V\subset Y$ with
\[
 |V|\le C_{k,p,\beta}
 \max\left\{
 1,\,
 D^k\left(\frac{L_p}{\delta}\right)^{\frac{k}{\nu}}
 \right\},
\]
where $C_{k,p,\beta}$ depends only on $k,p,\beta$.
There are explicit coefficient functions
$L_{\boldsymbol v}$, smooth on a neighborhood of $Y$,
with value stability constant
$\Lambda_0:=
\sup\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in Y}
\sum\limits_{\boldsymbol v\in V}
|L_{\boldsymbol v}(\boldsymbol y)|<\infty$,
such that supplied values satisfying
\[
 \max\limits_{\boldsymbol v\in V}
 |\widetilde f(\boldsymbol v)-f(\boldsymbol v)|
 \le\tau\le\frac{\delta}{8\Lambda_0}
\]
determine the model
$\widehat f:=
\sum\limits_{\boldsymbol v\in V}
\widetilde f(\boldsymbol v)L_{\boldsymbol v}$
with
$\|\widehat f-f\|_{\infty,Y}\le\frac{\delta}{4}$.

Consequently, any $\frac{\delta}{2}$-approximate
minimizer $\widehat{\boldsymbol y}\in Y$ of
$\widehat f+q$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-global-minimum-accuracy}
 (f+q)(\widehat{\boldsymbol y})
 -\min\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in Y}(f+q)(\boldsymbol y)
 \le\delta.
\end{equation}
The model, its optimization, and the evaluation of
$\widehat f(\widehat{\boldsymbol y})$ require no further
queries to $f$.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Take $\boldsymbol c$ to be the center of $Y$ and set
$\rho:=\max\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in Y}
\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol c\|_2\le D$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:polynomial-reconstruction} with
value budget $\varepsilon_0:=\frac{\delta}{8}$.
Since no derivative accuracy is required here, choose
any $\varepsilon_1>0$ satisfying
$\varepsilon_1\ge
2a_{p-1,\beta}L_p\rho^{\nu-1}$.
The refinement parameter then satisfies
$\sigma\le
\max\{1,
(\frac{16a_{p,\beta}L_p\rho^\nu}{\delta})^{\frac1\nu}\}$.
The node bound in that lemma therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |V|
 &\le C_{k,p,\beta}\max\{1,\sigma\}^k\\
 &\le C_{k,p,\beta}
 \max\left\{
 1,\,
 D^k\left(\frac{L_p}{\delta}\right)^{\frac{k}{\nu}}
 \right\},
\end{aligned}
\]
after enlarging $C_{k,p,\beta}$.
This also covers $L_p=0$.

The same lemma supplies the coefficient functions and
their finite stability constant $\Lambda_0$.
Under the assumed data accuracy, its value estimate gives
$\|\widehat f-f\|_{\infty,Y}
\le\frac{\delta}{8}+\Lambda_0\tau
\le\frac{\delta}{4}$.

Since $\widehat f+q$ is continuous on compact $Y$,
a $\frac{\delta}{2}$-approximate minimizer exists.
For any such point $\widehat{\boldsymbol y}$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:approximation-minimization-transfer} yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
 (f+q)(\widehat{\boldsymbol y})
 -\min\limits_{\boldsymbol y\in Y}(f+q)(\boldsymbol y)
 &\le
 2\|\widehat f-f\|_{\infty,Y}+\frac{\delta}{2}\\
 &\le
 2\cdot\frac{\delta}{4}+\frac{\delta}{2}
 =\delta.
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient functions are predetermined, and
$\widehat f$ is completely determined by the supplied
values. All subsequent operations use only
$\widehat f$ and the known function $q$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- fact-1: body_md -->
$\boldsymbol x^{t+1}\in R_{t+1}$ and
$\operatorname{dist}(\boldsymbol x^{t+1},F_t)\ge r^t/6$.
<!-- end fact-1 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The updated pivot $\boldsymbol x^{t+1}$ is either
$\boldsymbol x^t$ or $\boldsymbol z^\star\in\mathcal E^t$,
and hence belongs to $R_t$.
If $[\boldsymbol x^{t+1}]_j\ge a_j^t+r^t/2$, the algorithm retains
$[a_j^t+r^t/3,b_j^t]$ and $F_t=E_1^t$.
The updated pivot lies in this interval, at distance
$[\boldsymbol x^{t+1}]_j-a_j^t-r^t/3\ge r^t/6$ from $F_t$.
If $[\boldsymbol x^{t+1}]_j<a_j^t+r^t/2$, the retained interval is
$[a_j^t,b_j^t-r^t/3]$ and $F_t=E_2^t$.
The updated pivot again lies in the retained interval, now at
distance $a_j^t+2r^t/3-[\boldsymbol x^{t+1}]_j>r^t/6$ from $F_t$.
These are the Euclidean distances to the corresponding separators:
orthogonal projection leaves the other coordinates unchanged and
within their original intervals.
Consequently, $\boldsymbol x^{t+1}\in R_{t+1}$ and
$\operatorname{dist}(\boldsymbol x^{t+1},F_t)\ge r^t/6$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The case $\ell=0$ is immediate. Otherwise, condition on
$\mathcal F$, fixing the endpoints and accuracy parameters,
and write $M:=L_p\ell^\nu$ for the remainder of the proof.

\noindent\textbf{Reduction to scalar integration.}
Write $w:=v-u$ and $g(t):=\langle\nabla f(u+tw),w\rangle$,
$t\in[0,1]$. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives
$\int_0^1g(t)\,dt=f(v)-f(u)$, and one gradient query evaluates
$g$ at any prescribed point. For $0\le r\le p-1$, the chain
rule gives $g^{(r)}(t)=D^{r+1}f(u+tw)[w^{\otimes(r+1)}]$.
Consequently,
\[
 |g^{(p-1)}(t)-g^{(p-1)}(s)|
 \le L_p\|(t-s)w\|_2^{\beta_p}\|w\|_2^p
 =M|t-s|^{\beta_p}.
\]

\noindent\textbf{Local polynomial models.}
Fix an integer $n\ge1$, set $h:=1/n$, and partition $[0,1]$
into $J_j:=[a_j,a_j+h]$, where $a_j:=(j-1)h$.
Let interpolant polynomial as 
\[P_j :=
\begin{cases}
\text{the degree-$(p-1)$ interpolant of $g$ at }
\left\{a_j+\frac{hi}{p-1}\right\}_{i=0}^{p-1},
& p\ge2,\\
g(a_j),
& p=1.
\end{cases}\]
Write $R_j:=g-P_j$ and
$C_p:=1+\lambda_{p-1}$. 
 
For $p\geq 2$, applying Lemma~\ref{lem:interpolation-error-decomposition}
with polynomial degree $p-1$ and
$\operatorname{diam}(J_j)=h$ gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-line-local-residual}
 \|R_j\|_{\infty,J_j} =  \|g-P_j\|_{\infty,J_j}
 \le C_pa_{p-1,\beta_p}Mh^{\nu-1}
 \le C_pMh^{\nu-1},
\end{equation}
where $a_{r,\beta_p}=\prod_{i=1}^r(\beta_p+i)^{-1}\le1$.
For $p=1$, the H\"older condition gives
$|R_j(t)|\le M|t-a_j|^{\beta_p}$, which also implies
\eqref{eq:apx-line-local-residual}.

\noindent\textbf{Deterministic rule.}
Define $I_n^{\mathrm{det}}:=\sum_{j=1}^n\int_{J_j}P_j(t)\,dt$.
For $p\ge2$, integration of
\eqref{eq:apx-line-local-residual} yields
\[
 |I_n^{\mathrm{det}}-(f(v)-f(u))|
 \le\sum_{j=1}^n\int_{J_j}|R_j(t)|\,dt
 \le nh\,C_pa_{p-1,\beta_p}Mh^{\nu-1}
 =C_pa_{p-1,\beta_p}Mn^{-(\nu-1)}.
\]
For $p=1$, the rule is $I_n^{\mathrm{det}}=h\sum_jg(a_j)$.
Integrating the sharper residual bound gives error 
         
                                    
                                    
\begin{align*}
\bigl|I_n^{\mathrm{det}}-(f(v)-f(u))\bigr|
&=\left|
\sum_{j=1}^n\int_{a_j}^{a_j+h}
\bigl(g(a_j)-g(t)\bigr)\,dt
\right|\\
&\le\sum_{j=1}^n\int_{a_j}^{a_j+h}
|g(t)-g(a_j)|\,dt\\
&\le M\sum_{j=1}^n\int_{a_j}^{a_j+h}
(t-a_j)^{\beta_p}\,dt\\
&=M\sum_{j=1}^n
\left[\frac{(t-a_j)^{1+\beta_p}}{1+\beta_p}
\right]_{a_j}^{a_j+h}\\
&=\frac{nMh^{1+\beta_p}}{1+\beta_p}\\
&=\frac{M}{1+\beta_p}\,
n\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^{1+\beta_p}
=\frac{Mn^{-\beta_p}}{1+\beta_p}.
\end{align*}
Thus, with
$K_{1,\beta_p}:=\frac{1}{1+\beta_p}$ and
$K_{p,\beta_p}:=C_pa_{p-1,\beta_p}$ for $p\ge2$, both cases
satisfy
\[|I_n^{\mathrm{det}}-(f(v)-f(u))|
\le K_{p,\beta_p}Mn^{-(\nu-1)}.\]
Choosing
$n=n_{\mathrm{det}}:=\max\left\{1,
\left\lceil
\left(\frac{K_{p,\beta_p}M}{\varepsilon_0}\right)^{
\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
\right\rceil\right\}$
proves the claimed deterministic accuracy.

\noindent\textbf{Randomized rule.}
Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be independent uniform random variables on
$[0,1]$, independent of $\mathcal F$, and set
$U_j:=a_j+hZ_j$. Define random estimation as 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-line-integration-estimator}
 \widehat I_n
 :=\sum_{j=1}^n
 \left[\int_{J_j}P_j(t)\,dt+hR_j(U_j)\right].
\end{equation}
Conditionally on $\mathcal F$, the objective and interpolation
nodes, and hence $P_j$, are fixed. Since $U_j$ is uniform on
$J_j$, we have $\mathbb E[hR_j(U_j)\mid\mathcal F]
=\int_{J_j}R_j(t)\,dt$. Substituting this identity in
\eqref{eq:apx-line-integration-estimator} proves conditional
unbiasedness.

Set $Y_j:=hR_j(U_j)$. These variables are conditionally
independent, with range lengths at most $2C_pMh^\nu$ by
\eqref{eq:apx-line-local-residual}. Since $|R_j(t)|\le C_pMh^{\nu-1}$, the random variable
$hR_j(U_j)$ takes values in
$[-C_pMh^\nu,C_pMh^\nu]$.
Centering does not change its range length.
Therefore, using $h=1/n$,
\begin{align*}
\sum_{j=1}^n
\left[
h\left(\sup_{t\in J_j}R_j(t)-\inf_{t\in J_j}R_j(t)\right)
\right]^2
&\le \sum_{j=1}^n(2C_pMh^\nu)^2\\
&=4C_p^2M^2nh^{2\nu}\\
&=4C_p^2M^2n\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^{2\nu}\\
&=4C_p^2M^2n^{1-2\nu}.
\end{align*}
Moreover, 
\[\widehat I_n-(f(v)-f(u))
=\sum_j(Y_j-\mathbb E[Y_j\mid\mathcal F]).\]
For $M>0$ and every positive $\mathcal F$-measurable threshold
$\xi$, conditional Hoeffding's inequality gives
\begin{equation}
