\label{eq:apx-line-integration-tail}
 \mathbb P\!\left(
 |\widehat I_n-(f(v)-f(u))|>\xi\mid\mathcal F\right)
 \le2\exp\!\left(
 -\frac{\xi^2n^{2\nu-1}}{2C_p^2M^2}\right).
\end{equation}
Choose
\[
 n=n_{\mathrm{rand}}
 :=\max\left\{1,\left\lceil
 \left[2C_p^2\left(\frac{M}{\varepsilon_0}\right)^2
 \log\frac{2}{\vartheta}\right]^{1/(2\nu-1)}
 \right\rceil\right\}.
\]
At $\xi=\varepsilon_0$, the exponent in
\eqref{eq:apx-line-integration-tail} is at least
$\log(2/\vartheta)$, proving
\eqref{eq:apx-line-integration-accuracy}. If $M=0$, the residual
bound gives $R_j\equiv0$, so both rules are exact.

\noindent\textbf{Queries.}
For $p\ge2$, sharing interpolation endpoints gives
$n(p-1)+1$ deterministic queries and at most $pn+1$
randomized queries.
For $p=1$, both rules use $n$ queries, since the randomized
estimator simplifies to $h\sum_{j=1}^n g(U_j)$.
Polynomial integration requires no additional queries.
Substituting $n_{\mathrm{det}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{rand}}$
yields the claimed bounds, with constants depending only on $p$.

\noindent\textbf{Nonadaptivity.}
Conditional on $\mathcal F$, the sample counts are fixed,
and all query points are selected before observing any new
oracle answer. Each rule thus uses one nonadaptive batch.
Taking $\mathcal F$ to be trivial recovers the guarantees
for deterministic inputs.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- fact-2: body_md -->
\label{fact:gradient-only-edge-accuracy}
In deterministic mode, $\mathcal G_t$ always holds.
In randomized mode,
$\mathbb P(\mathcal G_t\mid\mathcal H_t)\ge1-\rho_t$.
<!-- end fact-2 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
The deterministic quadrature guarantee implies $\mathcal G_t$.
In randomized mode,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb P(\mathcal G_t^c\mid\mathcal H_t)
 &\le
 \sum_{\ell=0}^{J_t}
 \sum_{e=(\boldsymbol u,\boldsymbol v)\in\mathcal A_{t,\ell}}
 \mathbb P\!\left(
 \left|\widehat I_e-f(\boldsymbol v)+f(\boldsymbol u)\right|
 >\xi_{t,\ell}
 \,\middle|\,\mathcal H_t
 \right)\\
 &\le
 \sum_{\ell=0}^{J_t}
 |\mathcal A_{t,\ell}|
 \frac{\rho_t}{|\mathcal A_t|}
 =\rho_t,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality is the conditional union bound,
and the second uses the edgewise failure guarantees.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- fact-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:uniform-gradient-reconstruction}
\label{lem:gradient-only-update-certificate}
On $\mathcal G_t$, $ \|\widehat F_t-F_t\|_{\infty,\mathcal E^t}
 =
 \|\widehat\phi_t-\phi_t\|_{\infty,\mathcal E^t}
 \le\frac{\delta_t}{4},$
    
                                             
    
                                                  
                         
    
and $\widehat{\boldsymbol z}^t$ is a
$\delta_t$-approximate minimizer of $\phi_t$ on $\mathcal E^t$.
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-only-update-certificates}
\begin{aligned}
 \phi_t(\boldsymbol x^{t+1})&\le0,\\
 \phi_t(\boldsymbol y)-\phi_t(\boldsymbol x^{t+1})
 &\ge-\delta_t,
 \qquad\forall \boldsymbol y\in\mathcal E^t.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
<!-- end fact-3 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Assume $\mathcal G_t$ holds.
For a finest-grid node $\boldsymbol z$, let
$\mathcal P_t(\boldsymbol z)$ denote its root path.
Writing $e=(\boldsymbol u_e,\boldsymbol v_e)$, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \left|\widehat F_t(\boldsymbol z)-F_t(\boldsymbol z)\right|
 &=
 \left|
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal P_t(\boldsymbol z)}
 \bigl(\widehat I_e-f(\boldsymbol v_e)+f(\boldsymbol u_e)\bigr)
 \right|\\
 &\le
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal P_t(\boldsymbol z)}
 \left|\widehat I_e-f(\boldsymbol v_e)+f(\boldsymbol u_e)\right|\\
 &\le\sum_{\ell=0}^{J_t}\xi_{t,\ell}
 =\frac{\delta_t}{8\Lambda_{d-1,p}},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the equality follows by telescoping, and the last
inequality uses $\mathcal G_t$ and the fact that each root path
contains at most one edge from each creation level.
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|\widehat\phi_t-\phi_t\|_{\infty,\mathcal E^t}
 &=
 \|\widehat F_t-F_t\|_{\infty,\mathcal E^t}\\
 &\le
 A_{d-1,p,\beta_p}L_p
 \left(\frac{\sqrt{d-1}\,r^t}{2^{J_t}}\right)^\nu
 +\Lambda_{d-1,p}
  \frac{\delta_t}{8\Lambda_{d-1,p}}\\
 &\le\frac{\delta_t}{8}+\frac{\delta_t}{8}
 =\frac{\delta_t}{4},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality follows from the approximation lemma
with cell diameter at most
$\frac{\sqrt{d-1}\,r^t}{2^{J_t}}$
and nodal error at most
$\frac{\delta_t}{8\Lambda_{d-1,p}}$,
and the second uses Eq.~
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-refinement-level}, which gives
$A_{d-1,p,\beta_p}L_p
\left(\frac{\sqrt{d-1}\,r^t}{2^{J_t}}\right)^\nu
\le\frac{\varepsilon_0^t}{8}
=\frac{\delta_t}{8}$.

For every $\boldsymbol y\in\mathcal E^t$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-only-separator-suboptimality}
\begin{aligned}
 \phi_t(\widehat{\boldsymbol z}^t)
 &\le
 \widehat\phi_t(\widehat{\boldsymbol z}^t)
 +\frac{\delta_t}{4}\\
 &\le
 \min_{\mathcal E^t}\widehat\phi_t
 +\frac{\delta_t}{2}+\frac{\delta_t}{4}\\
 &\le
 \widehat\phi_t(\boldsymbol y)+\frac{3\delta_t}{4}\\
 &\le\phi_t(\boldsymbol y)+\delta_t,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the first and fourth inequalities use the uniform error
bound, and the second uses the surrogate minimization tolerance.
This proves the claimed approximate optimality.

If $\widehat\phi_t(\widehat{\boldsymbol z}^t)
\le-\frac{\delta_t}{4}$, then
$\boldsymbol x^{t+1}=\widehat{\boldsymbol z}^t$, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \phi_t(\boldsymbol x^{t+1})
 &\le
 \widehat\phi_t(\widehat{\boldsymbol z}^t)
 +\frac{\delta_t}{4}
 \le0,\\
 \phi_t(\boldsymbol y)-\phi_t(\boldsymbol x^{t+1})
 &=\phi_t(\boldsymbol y)
   -\phi_t(\widehat{\boldsymbol z}^t)
 \ge-\delta_t
 \qquad(\boldsymbol y\in\mathcal E^t),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first line uses the acceptance condition,
and the second uses
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-separator-suboptimality}.

Otherwise, $\boldsymbol x^{t+1}=\boldsymbol x^t$, so
$\phi_t(\boldsymbol x^{t+1})=0$, and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-only-retention-certificate}
\begin{aligned}
 \phi_t(\boldsymbol y)-\phi_t(\boldsymbol x^{t+1})
 &=\phi_t(\boldsymbol y)\\
 &\ge\widehat\phi_t(\boldsymbol y)-\frac{\delta_t}{4}\\
 &\ge
 \widehat\phi_t(\widehat{\boldsymbol z}^t)
 -\frac{\delta_t}{2}-\frac{\delta_t}{4}\\
 &>-\delta_t,
 \qquad \boldsymbol y\in\mathcal E^t,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the inequalities use the uniform error bound,
the surrogate minimization tolerance, and the rejection
condition, respectively.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:gradient-only-terminal-output}
Suppose that the trapping invariant holds at termination.
Then the terminal procedure terminates after finitely many
offline operations and returns a point
$\boldsymbol z^T\in R_T$ satisfying
\[
\begin{cases}
 \|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z^T)\|_2\le\varepsilon,
 &\text{in the unconstrained case},\\
 \|G_\gamma(\boldsymbol z^T)\|_2\le\varepsilon
 \quad\text{for every }\gamma>0,
 &\text{in the cube-constrained case}.
\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Write $R:=R_T$, $\boldsymbol x:=\boldsymbol x^T$,
$P:=P_T$, $\Psi:=\Psi_T$, and
$\zeta:=\zeta_T=\frac{\varepsilon r^T}{16}>0$.

\noindent\textbf{Finite termination of the terminal procedure.}
The coefficients of $P$ give computable constants
\[
 K\ge
 \max\left\{1,\sup_R\|\nabla P\|_2+\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}\right\},
 \qquad
 H\ge
 \max\left\{1,\sup_R\|\nabla^2P\|_{\mathrm{op}}\right\}.
\]
Choose a finite grid $\mathcal Q\subset R$ with covering radius
at most $\frac{\zeta}{K}$, and set
$\boldsymbol y_0\in
\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathcal Q\cup\{\boldsymbol x\}}\Psi$.
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Psi(\boldsymbol y_0)&\le\Psi(\boldsymbol x)=0,\\
 \Psi(\boldsymbol y_0)-\min_R\Psi
 &\le\min_{\mathcal Q}\Psi-\min_R\Psi
 \le K\frac{\zeta}{K}
 =\zeta,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the second line uses the $K$-Lipschitz continuity of
$\Psi$ and the covering radius of $\mathcal Q$.

Starting from $\boldsymbol y_0$, define
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-only-offline-proximal-step}
 \boldsymbol y_{k+1}:=
 \operatorname*{argmin}_{\boldsymbol y\in R}
 \left\{
 \langle\nabla P(\boldsymbol y_k),
          \boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol y_k\rangle
 +H\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol y_k\|_2^2
 +\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}
       \|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2
 \right\}.
\end{equation}
Each auxiliary problem has a unique minimizer, computable
by finite algebraic computation in the exact-real model. 
\footnote{
Completing the square reduces the problem to minimizing
$H\|\boldsymbol w-\boldsymbol c\|_2^2+a\|\boldsymbol w\|_2$
over $B:=R-\boldsymbol x$, where
$a:=\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$ and
$\boldsymbol c:=\boldsymbol y_k-\boldsymbol x
-\frac{\nabla P(\boldsymbol y_k)}{2H}$.
For a nonzero minimizer, convex optimality gives
$\boldsymbol w=\operatorname{proj}_B(\tau\boldsymbol c)$,
where
$\tau=\frac{2H\|\boldsymbol w\|_2}
{2H\|\boldsymbol w\|_2+a}\in(0,1)$.
For each clipping pattern,
$\|\boldsymbol w\|_2^2=D+C\tau^2$
with known $C,D\ge0$, so
$a^2\tau^2=4H^2(1-\tau)^2(D+C\tau^2)$.
Enumerate the finitely many clipping patterns and real roots
of these polynomial equations, retaining those satisfying
the unsquared equation, $0<\tau<1$, and the clipping inequalities.
Test $\boldsymbol w=0$ separately using
$\operatorname{dist}(2H\boldsymbol c,N_B(\boldsymbol0))\le a$.
These tests identify the unique minimizer.
}
Set $\boldsymbol d_k:=\boldsymbol y_{k+1}-\boldsymbol y_k$.
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Psi(\boldsymbol y_{k+1})-\Psi(\boldsymbol y_k)
 &\le
 \langle\nabla P(\boldsymbol y_k),\boldsymbol d_k\rangle
 +\frac{H}{2}\|\boldsymbol d_k\|_2^2\\
 &\qquad
 +\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}
 \bigl(
 \|\boldsymbol y_{k+1}-\boldsymbol x\|_2
 -\|\boldsymbol y_k-\boldsymbol x\|_2
 \bigr)\\
 &\le-\frac{H}{2}\|\boldsymbol d_k\|_2^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality uses the $H$-Lipschitz continuity
of $\nabla P$, and the second compares the auxiliary minimizer
with $\boldsymbol y_k$.
Consequently,
\[
 \Psi(\boldsymbol y_k)\le0,
 \qquad
 \Psi(\boldsymbol y_k)-\min_R\Psi\le\zeta
 \qquad(k\ge0).
\]

Convex optimality supplies
$\boldsymbol v_k\in
\partial\|\cdot-\boldsymbol x\|_2(\boldsymbol y_{k+1})$
and $\boldsymbol n_k\in N_R(\boldsymbol y_{k+1})$ such that
\[
 \nabla P(\boldsymbol y_k)+2H\boldsymbol d_k
 +\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}\boldsymbol v_k+\boldsymbol n_k
 =\boldsymbol0.
\]
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\left\|
 \nabla P(\boldsymbol y_{k+1})
 +\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}\boldsymbol v_k+\boldsymbol n_k
 \right\|_2\\
 &\quad=
 \|\nabla P(\boldsymbol y_{k+1})
   -\nabla P(\boldsymbol y_k)-2H\boldsymbol d_k\|_2\\
 &\quad\le
 \|\nabla P(\boldsymbol y_{k+1})
   -\nabla P(\boldsymbol y_k)\|_2
 +2H\|\boldsymbol d_k\|_2\\
 &\quad\le3H\|\boldsymbol d_k\|_2,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last inequality uses the Hessian bound for $P$.

Stop at the first step with
$\|\boldsymbol d_k\|_2\le\frac{\varepsilon}{24H}$.
If the first $N\ge1$ steps were all nonterminating, then
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac{N\varepsilon^2}{1152H}
 &<
 \frac{H}{2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\|\boldsymbol d_k\|_2^2\\
 &\le
 \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}
 \bigl(\Psi(\boldsymbol y_k)-\Psi(\boldsymbol y_{k+1})\bigr)\\
 &=\Psi(\boldsymbol y_0)-\Psi(\boldsymbol y_N)\\
 &\le\Psi(\boldsymbol y_0)-\min_R\Psi
 \le\zeta,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality uses
$\|\boldsymbol d_k\|_2>\frac{\varepsilon}{24H}$,
and the second is the descent bound.
Thus termination occurs within
$\left\lfloor\frac{1152H\zeta}{\varepsilon^2}\right\rfloor+1$
steps.

At the terminating step, return
$\boldsymbol z^T:=\boldsymbol y_{k+1}$ and set
$\boldsymbol v:=\boldsymbol v_k$,
$\boldsymbol n:=\boldsymbol n_k$.
The preceding estimates give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Psi(\boldsymbol z^T)&\le0,\\
 \Psi(\boldsymbol z^T)-\min_R\Psi&\le\zeta,\\
 \left\|
 \nabla P(\boldsymbol z^T)
 +\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}\boldsymbol v+\boldsymbol n
 \right\|_2
 &\le3H\|\boldsymbol d_k\|_2
 \le\frac{\varepsilon}{8}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This implements the prescribed terminal step using finitely
many offline operations and no additional oracle queries
after constructing $P$.

\noindent\textbf{Correctness of the output.}
The terminal reconstruction satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|\nabla P-\nabla f\|_{\infty,R}
 &\le
 c_{p,\beta_p}L_p
 \left(\max_{\boldsymbol y\in R}
       \|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol c_T\|_2\right)^{\nu-1}\\
 &\le
 c_{p,\beta_p}L_p
 \left(\frac{\sqrt d\,r^T}{2}\right)^{\nu-1}\\
 &\le\frac{\varepsilon}{8},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the inequalities follow from
Corollary~\ref{lem:gradient-only-scalar-reconstruction},
the geometry of $R$, and
Eq.~\eqref{eq:gradient-only-terminal-radius}, respectively.
                                                 

For every $\boldsymbol y\in R$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\left|P(\boldsymbol y)-P(\boldsymbol x)
       -f(\boldsymbol y)+f(\boldsymbol x)\right|\\
 &\quad=
 \left|
 \int_0^1
 \left\langle
 (\nabla P-\nabla f)
   (\boldsymbol x+u(\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x)),
 \boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x
 \right\rangle\,du
 \right|\\
 &\quad\le
 \|\nabla P-\nabla f\|_{\infty,R}
 \|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2\\
 &\quad\le
 \frac{\varepsilon}{8}\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the segment lies in $R$ by convexity.
For $\boldsymbol y\in\Gamma_T$, this gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-only-terminal-barrier}
\begin{aligned}
 \Psi(\boldsymbol y)
 &=P(\boldsymbol y)-P(\boldsymbol x)
   +\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}
      \|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2\\
 &\ge
 f(\boldsymbol y)-f(\boldsymbol x)
 +\frac{5\varepsilon}{8}
      \|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2\\
 &=\phi_T(\boldsymbol y)
   +\left(\frac{5\varepsilon}{8}-\varepsilon_T\right)
      \|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2\\
 &\ge
 \phi_T(\boldsymbol y)
 +\frac{\varepsilon}{8}\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2
 >0,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the last line uses
$\varepsilon_T\le\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and the trapping
invariant.
Since $\Psi(\boldsymbol z^T)\le0$, we obtain
$\boldsymbol z^T\notin\Gamma_T$.

Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-only-terminal-stationarity}
\begin{aligned}
 \|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z^T)+\boldsymbol n\|_2
 &\le
 \|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z^T)-\nabla P(\boldsymbol z^T)\|_2\\
 &\qquad+
 \left\|\nabla P(\boldsymbol z^T)
       +\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}\boldsymbol v
       +\boldsymbol n\right\|_2
 +\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}\|\boldsymbol v\|_2\\
 &\le
 \frac{\varepsilon}{8}
 +\frac{\varepsilon}{8}
 +\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}
 =\varepsilon,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the second inequality uses the model error,
the terminal residual bound, and
$\|\boldsymbol v\|_2\le1$.

In the unconstrained case,
$\boldsymbol z^T\notin\partial R$ implies
$\boldsymbol z^T\in\operatorname{int}R$.
Hence $\boldsymbol n=\boldsymbol0$, and
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-terminal-stationarity} gives
$\|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z^T)\|_2\le\varepsilon$.

In the cube-constrained case,
$\boldsymbol z^T\notin\Gamma_T$ implies
$\boldsymbol z^T\in\operatorname{int}_{[0,1]^d}R$.
Therefore
$N_R(\boldsymbol z^T)=N_{[0,1]^d}(\boldsymbol z^T)$,
as established in Section~\ref{sec:3}.
For every $\gamma>0$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|G_\gamma(\boldsymbol z^T)\|_2
 &=
 \frac{1}{\gamma}
 \left\|
 \boldsymbol z^T-
 \operatorname{proj}_{[0,1]^d}
       (\boldsymbol z^T-\gamma\nabla f(\boldsymbol z^T))
 \right\|_2\\
 &=
 \frac{1}{\gamma}
 \left\|
 \operatorname{proj}_{[0,1]^d}
       (\boldsymbol z^T+\gamma\boldsymbol n)
 -
 \operatorname{proj}_{[0,1]^d}
       (\boldsymbol z^T-\gamma\nabla f(\boldsymbol z^T))
 \right\|_2\\
 &\le\|\nabla f(\boldsymbol z^T)+\boldsymbol n\|_2\\
 &\le\varepsilon,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the second equality follows from
$\boldsymbol n\in N_{[0,1]^d}(\boldsymbol z^T)$,
and the first inequality is nonexpansiveness of projection.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- fact-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:shared-root-tree-geometry}
The edge counts satisfy
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |\mathcal A_{t,0}|
 &=2(p+1)^{d-1},\\
 |\mathcal A_{t,\ell}|
 &=2\bigl[
 (p2^\ell+1)^{d-1}-(p2^{\ell-1}+1)^{d-1}
 \bigr],
 \qquad 1\le\ell\le J_t,\\
 |\mathcal A_t|
 &=2(p2^{J_t}+1)^{d-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For every $0\le\ell\le J_t$ and
$e=(\boldsymbol u,\boldsymbol v)\in\mathcal A_{t,\ell}$,
the edge length satisfies $ h_e:=\|\boldsymbol v-\boldsymbol u\|_2
 \le\frac{C_{d,p}r^t}{2^\ell}.$
Moreover, for every exponent $a>0$,
\[
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal A_{t,\ell}}h_e^a
 \le C_{d,p,a}(r^t)^a2^{(d-1-a)\ell}.
\]
<!-- end fact-4 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
At level $\ell$, each free coordinate of a separator has
$p2^\ell+1$ grid points. Since each separator has $d-1$
free coordinates, its grid contains $(p2^\ell+1)^{d-1}$ nodes.
Each newly introduced node contributes exactly one parent edge,
including a zero-length edge if it coincides with the root.
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |\mathcal A_{t,0}|
 &=2(p+1)^{d-1},\\
 |\mathcal A_{t,\ell}|
 &=2\bigl[
 (p2^\ell+1)^{d-1}-(p2^{\ell-1}+1)^{d-1}
 \bigr],
 \qquad 1\le\ell\le J_t,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the factor $2$ accounts for the two separators,
and the difference counts newly introduced nodes because
the grids are nested.
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |\mathcal A_t|=\sum_{\ell=0}^{J_t}|\mathcal A_{t,\ell}|=2(p+1)^{d-1}
 +2\sum_{\ell=1}^{J_t}
 \bigl[
 (p2^\ell+1)^{d-1}-(p2^{\ell-1}+1)^{d-1}
 \bigr]=2(p2^{J_t}+1)^{d-1},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first equality uses the disjointness of the
levelwise edge sets, and the last equality follows by telescoping.

For a level-zero edge $e=(\boldsymbol x^t,\boldsymbol v)$,
both endpoints lie in
$R_t=\prod_{i=1}^d[a_i^t,b_i^t]$, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
 h_e
 &=\|\boldsymbol v-\boldsymbol x^t\|_2\le
 \left(\sum_{i=1}^d(b_i^t-a_i^t)^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\le\sqrt d\,r^t,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality bounds each coordinate difference
by the corresponding side length, and the second uses
$b_i^t-a_i^t\le r^t$.

Now let $\ell\ge1$ and
$e=(\boldsymbol u,\boldsymbol v)\in\mathcal A_{t,\ell}$.
Let $j$ be the fixed coordinate of the separator.
For each $i\ne j$, write the child coordinate as
\[
 [\boldsymbol v]_i
 =a_i^t+\frac{k_i(b_i^t-a_i^t)}{p2^\ell}.
\]
The parent rule assigns index
$\left\lfloor\frac{k_i}{2}\right\rfloor$ at level $\ell-1$.
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |[\boldsymbol v]_i-[\boldsymbol u]_i|
 &=
 \left|
 \frac{k_i}{p2^\ell}
 -
 \frac{\left\lfloor\frac{k_i}{2}\right\rfloor}
      {p2^{\ell-1}}
 \right|(b_i^t-a_i^t)=
 \frac{k_i-2\left\lfloor\frac{k_i}{2}\right\rfloor}
      {p2^\ell}(b_i^t-a_i^t)\le\frac{b_i^t-a_i^t}{p2^\ell}\le\frac{r^t}{p2^\ell},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the numerator in the second line belongs to $\{0,1\}$,
and the last inequality uses the definition of $r^t$.
Since the parent and child lie on the same separator,
$[\boldsymbol u]_j=[\boldsymbol v]_j$, and therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
 h_e
 &=
 \left(
 \sum_{i\ne j}|[\boldsymbol v]_i-[\boldsymbol u]_i|^2
 \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\le
 \left(
 (d-1)\left(\frac{r^t}{p2^\ell}\right)^2
 \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{d-1}\,r^t}{p2^\ell}\le\frac{\sqrt d\,r^t}{2^\ell},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality uses the coordinate bounds,
and the last uses $p\ge1$.
Together with the level-zero estimate, this proves the
edge-length bound with $C_{d,p}=\sqrt d$.

For every $0\le\ell\le J_t$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |\mathcal A_{t,\ell}|
 &\le2(p2^\ell+1)^{d-1}\le2(p+1)^{d-1}2^{(d-1)\ell},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality counts all level-$\ell$ grid nodes,
and the second uses
$p2^\ell+1\le(p+1)2^\ell$.
Thus, for every $a>0$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal A_{t,\ell}}h_e^a
 &\le
 |\mathcal A_{t,\ell}|
 \left(\frac{\sqrt d\,r^t}{2^\ell}\right)^a\\
 &\le
 2(p+1)^{d-1}2^{(d-1)\ell}
 \frac{d^{\frac{a}{2}}(r^t)^a}{2^{a\ell}}\\
 &=
 2(p+1)^{d-1}d^{\frac{a}{2}}
 (r^t)^a2^{(d-1-a)\ell},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality uses the edge-length bound
and the monotonicity of $u\mapsto u^a$ on $[0,\infty)$,
and the second uses the edge-count bound.
The claimed estimate follows with
$C_{d,p,a}=2(p+1)^{d-1}d^{\frac{a}{2}}$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:gradient-queries-one-iteration}
For $C=C_{d,p,\beta_p}\ge2$, the issued query counts satisfy
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-only-one-iteration-cost}
\begin{aligned}
 Q_t^{\mathrm{det}}
 &\le C\mathcal D(B_t),\\
 Q_t^{\mathrm{rand}}
 &\le
 C(1+B_t^{\chi_{\mathrm{rand}}})
 \left[
 \log\frac{C(1+B_t)^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}}}{\rho_t}
 \right]^{\frac{1}{2\nu-1}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
These bounds hold irrespective of reconstruction success.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
We first bound the refinement level $J_t$ and the number of edges $|\mathcal A_t|$.
If $B_t=0$, the refinement condition already holds at level
zero, so $J_t=0$.
If $J_t\ge1$, its minimality gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac{\delta_t}{8}
 &<
 A_{d-1,p,\beta_p}L_p
 \left(\frac{\sqrt{d-1}\,r^t}{2^{J_t-1}}\right)^\nu\\
 &=
 \frac{
 A_{d-1,p,\beta_p}(d-1)^{\frac{\nu}{2}}
 \delta_t B_t}
 {2^{\nu(J_t-1)}},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the inequality says that level $J_t-1$ fails
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-refinement-level}, and the equality
uses $L_p(r^t)^\nu=\delta_t B_t$.
Since $\delta_t>0$, rearranging yields
\[
 2^{J_t}
 <
 2\left(
 8A_{d-1,p,\beta_p}(d-1)^{\frac{\nu}{2}}B_t
 \right)^{\frac{1}{\nu}}.
\]
Including the case $J_t=0$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-only-refinement-cost-bounds}
\begin{aligned}
 2^{J_t}
 &\le C\max\left\{1,B_t^{\frac{1}{\nu}}\right\},\\
 J_t+1
 &\le
 1+\frac{\log C}{\log2}
 +\frac{\log\max\{1,B_t\}}{\nu\log2}\le C[1+\log(1+B_t)],\\
 |\mathcal A_t|
 &=2(p2^{J_t}+1)^{d-1}\le2(p+1)^{d-1}2^{(d-1)J_t}\le C(1+B_t^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}}).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here the bound on $J_t+1$ follows by taking logarithms
and using $\max\{1,B_t\}\le1+B_t$.
The edge-count identity is
Fact~\ref{lem:shared-root-tree-geometry} and
the following inequalities use
$p2^{J_t}+1\le(p+1)2^{J_t}$ and the bound on $2^{J_t}$.

Fix a mode and write $\kappa:=\kappa_{\mathsf m}$.
Set $ \mathcal L_t:=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&\mathsf m=\mathrm{det},\\
 \left[
 \log\frac{2|\mathcal A_t|}{\rho_t}
 \right]^{\frac{1}{2\nu-1}},
 &\mathsf m=\mathrm{rand}.
 \end{cases}$
In both modes, $\mathcal L_t\ge1$ while
in randomized mode this follows from
$|\mathcal A_t|\ge4$ and $0<\rho_t<1$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:randomized-line-integration} bounds the cost
of an edge $e\in\mathcal A_{t,\ell}$ by
\[
 C_p\left[
 1+\mathcal L_t
 \left(\frac{L_ph_e^\nu}{\xi_{t,\ell}}\right)^\kappa
 \right].
\]
Recall from Eq.~\eqref{eq:edge-error-budget} that
\[
 S_t=
 \sum_{\ell=0}^{J_t}
 2^{\frac{(d-1-\nu\kappa)\ell}{1+\kappa}},
 \qquad
 w_{t,\ell}
 =
 \frac{2^{\frac{(d-1-\nu\kappa)\ell}{1+\kappa}}}{S_t},
 \qquad
 \xi_{t,\ell}
 =
 \frac{\delta_t w_{t,\ell}}{8\Lambda_{d-1,p}}.
\]
Summing the edge costs gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-only-weighted-level-sum}
\begin{aligned}
 Q_t
 &\le
 C|\mathcal A_t|
 +C\mathcal L_t
 \left(\frac{L_p}{\delta_t}\right)^\kappa
 \sum_{\ell=0}^{J_t}w_{t,\ell}^{-\kappa}
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal A_{t,\ell}}h_e^{\nu\kappa}\\
 &\le
 C|\mathcal A_t|
 +C\mathcal L_t B_t^\kappa
 \sum_{\ell=0}^{J_t}
 2^{(d-1-\nu\kappa)\ell}w_{t,\ell}^{-\kappa}\\
 &=
 C|\mathcal A_t|
 +C\mathcal L_t B_t^\kappa S_t^\kappa
 \sum_{\ell=0}^{J_t}
 2^{\frac{(d-1-\nu\kappa)\ell}{1+\kappa}}\\
 &=
 C|\mathcal A_t|
 +C\mathcal L_t B_t^\kappa S_t^{1+\kappa}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The first inequality substitutes the edge tolerances into
the quadrature bound.
The second uses
Fact~\ref{lem:shared-root-tree-geometry} with $a=\nu\kappa$
and
$\left(\frac{L_p}{\delta_t}\right)^\kappa
(r^t)^{\nu\kappa}=B_t^\kappa$.
The equalities substitute $w_{t,\ell}$ and then use the
definition of $S_t$.

If $d-1<\nu\kappa$, then
\[
\begin{aligned}
 S_t
 &\le
 \sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}
 2^{\frac{(d-1-\nu\kappa)\ell}{1+\kappa}}=
 \frac{1}{
 1-2^{\frac{d-1-\nu\kappa}{1+\kappa}}},\\
 B_t^\kappa S_t^{1+\kappa}
 &\le CB_t^\kappa,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the infinite series converges because
$2^{\frac{d-1-\nu\kappa}{1+\kappa}}\in(0,1)$.

If $d-1>\nu\kappa$, the finite geometric sum satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
 S_t
 &=
 \frac{
 2^{\frac{(d-1-\nu\kappa)(J_t+1)}{1+\kappa}}-1}
 {2^{\frac{d-1-\nu\kappa}{1+\kappa}}-1}\le
 \frac{
 2^{\frac{d-1-\nu\kappa}{1+\kappa}}}
 {2^{\frac{d-1-\nu\kappa}{1+\kappa}}-1}
 2^{\frac{(d-1-\nu\kappa)J_t}{1+\kappa}}\le C2^{\frac{(d-1-\nu\kappa)J_t}{1+\kappa}},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the denominator is positive and depends only on the
fixed parameters.
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 B_t^\kappa S_t^{1+\kappa}
 &\le
 CB_t^\kappa2^{(d-1-\nu\kappa)J_t}\\
 &\le
 CB_t^\kappa
 \max\left\{1,B_t^{\frac{d-1-\nu\kappa}{\nu}}\right\}\\
 &=C\max\left\{
 B_t^\kappa,B_t^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}}
 \right\}\\
 &\le C(1+B_t^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}}),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the second inequality uses
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-refinement-cost-bounds}.
The equality uses
$\kappa+\frac{d-1-\nu\kappa}{\nu}=\frac{d-1}{\nu}$.
For the last inequality, use $B_t^\kappa\le1$ when
$B_t\le1$, and
$B_t^\kappa\le B_t^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}}$ when $B_t\ge1$.

If $d-1=\nu\kappa$, every summand defining $S_t$ equals one.
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
 S_t&=J_t+1,\\
 B_t^\kappa S_t^{1+\kappa}
 &=B_t^\kappa(J_t+1)^{1+\kappa}\\
 &\le
 CB_t^\kappa[1+\log(1+B_t)]^{1+\kappa},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the inequality uses
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-refinement-cost-bounds}.

Combining these estimates with
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-weighted-level-sum} gives
\[
 Q_t\le C\mathcal L_t
 \begin{cases}
 1+B_t^{\chi_{\mathsf m}},
 &d-1\ne\nu\kappa,\\
 1+B_t^\kappa[1+\log(1+B_t)]^{1+\kappa},
 &d-1=\nu\kappa.
 \end{cases}
\]
Here the edge-count term is absorbed using
$\mathcal L_t\ge1$ and
$B_t^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}}\le1+B_t^{\chi_{\mathsf m}}$
in the noncritical cases.
In the critical case,
$\frac{d-1}{\nu}=\kappa$ and
$[1+\log(1+B_t)]^{1+\kappa}\ge1$.

For deterministic integration,
\[
 \mathcal L_t=1,
 \qquad
 \nu\kappa_{\mathrm{det}}
 =1+\kappa_{\mathrm{det}}
 =\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}.
\]
Substitution into the preceding bound gives
$Q_t^{\mathrm{det}}\le C\mathcal D(B_t)$.

For randomized integration,
$\nu\kappa_{\mathrm{rand}}
=\frac{2\nu}{2\nu-1}\in(1,2)$.
Since $d-1$ is a positive integer, the critical case cannot occur.
Therefore,
\[
 Q_t^{\mathrm{rand}}
 \le C\mathcal L_t(1+B_t^{\chi_{\mathrm{rand}}}).
\]
Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal L_t
 &=
 \left[
 \log\frac{2|\mathcal A_t|}{\rho_t}
 \right]^{\frac{1}{2\nu-1}}\le
 \left[
 \log\frac{C(1+B_t^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}})}{\rho_t}
 \right]^{\frac{1}{2\nu-1}}\le
 \left[
 \log\frac{C(1+B_t)^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}}}{\rho_t}
 \right]^{\frac{1}{2\nu-1}},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality uses the edge-count bound,
and the second uses
$1+B_t^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}}
\le2(1+B_t)^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}}$,
absorbing the factor $2$ into $C$.
This proves \eqref{eq:gradient-only-one-iteration-cost}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:total-gradient-query-complexity}
For $C=C_{d,p,\beta_p}\ge2$, the total query counts,
including the terminal reconstruction, satisfy
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-only-total-explicit}
\begin{aligned}
 Q^{\mathrm{det}}
 &\le N_{d,p}^\nabla+C\mathcal D(B_0),\\
 Q^{\mathrm{rand}}
 &\le N_{d,p}^\nabla+
 C(1+B_0^{\chi_{\mathrm{rand}}})
 \left[
 \log\frac{C(1+B_0)}{\rho}
 \right]^{\frac{1}{2\nu-1}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
These bounds hold for every run.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The radius and error schedules give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 B_t
 &=
 \frac{12L_p(r^t)^{\nu-1}}{\Delta_t}\\
 &=
 \frac{48dL_p(r^0)^{\nu-1}}{(1-\alpha)\varepsilon}
 \left(
 \frac{\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{\nu-1}}{\alpha}
 \right)^{\left\lfloor\frac{t}{d}\right\rfloor}\\
 &=B_0\theta^{\left\lfloor\frac{t}{d}\right\rfloor},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the second equality substitutes
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-side-schedule} and
$\Delta_t=
\frac{\varepsilon(1-\alpha)}{4d}
\alpha^{\left\lfloor\frac{t}{d}\right\rfloor}$.

For every fixed exponent $a>0$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-only-geometric-sum}
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}B_t^a
 &=
 B_0^a\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}
 \theta^{a\left\lfloor\frac{t}{d}\right\rfloor}\\
 &\le
 dB_0^a\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\theta^{am}\\
 &=\frac{dB_0^a}{1-\theta^a},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the inequality uses the fact that each value of
$\left\lfloor\frac{t}{d}\right\rfloor$ occurs at most $d$ times,
and the last equality uses $0<\theta^a<1$.

We also have
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gradient-only-constant-cost-absorption}
 T\le C_a(1+B_0^a),
\end{equation}
where $C_a$ may additionally depend on $a$.
For $B_0\le1$, this follows directly from
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-iteration-bound}.
For $B_0>1$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \log(1+B_0)
 &\le\log2+\log B_0\\
 &=\log2+\int_1^{B_0}\frac{1}{u}\,du\\
 &\le\log2+\int_1^{B_0}u^{a-1}\,du\\
 &=\log2+\frac{B_0^a-1}{a}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the first inequality uses $1+B_0\le2B_0$,
and the second uses $u^a\ge1$ for $u\ge1$.
Substituting this estimate into
$T\le C[1+\log(1+B_0)]$
proves \eqref{eq:gradient-only-constant-cost-absorption}.

\noindent\textbf{Deterministic integration.}
If $d-1\ne\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}$, then
\[
\begin{aligned}
 Q^{\mathrm{det}}
 &\le
 N_{d,p}^\nabla+
 C\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}(1+B_t^{\chi_{\mathrm{det}}})\\
 &\le
 N_{d,p}^\nabla+C(T+B_0^{\chi_{\mathrm{det}}})\\
 &\le
 N_{d,p}^\nabla+C(1+B_0^{\chi_{\mathrm{det}}})\\
 &=N_{d,p}^\nabla+C\mathcal D(B_0),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality sums
Lemma~\ref{lem:gradient-queries-one-iteration}
and adds the terminal batch.
The second uses
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-geometric-sum}
with $a=\chi_{\mathrm{det}}$;
the third uses
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-constant-cost-absorption}
with the same exponent.

If $d-1=\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}$, then
\[
\begin{aligned}
 Q^{\mathrm{det}}
 &\le
 N_{d,p}^\nabla+
 C\left[
 T+\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}
 B_t^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
 [1+\log(1+B_t)]^{\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
 \right]\\
 &\le
 N_{d,p}^\nabla+
 C\left[
 T+
 [1+\log(1+B_0)]^{\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
 \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}B_t^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
 \right]\\
 &\le
 N_{d,p}^\nabla+
 C\left[
 T+B_0^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
 [1+\log(1+B_0)]^{\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
 \right]\\
 &\le N_{d,p}^\nabla+C\mathcal D(B_0),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality uses the critical case of
Lemma~\ref{lem:gradient-queries-one-iteration}.
The second uses $B_t\le B_0$.
The third uses
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-geometric-sum}
with $a=\frac{1}{\nu-1}$.
The last uses
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-constant-cost-absorption}
with the same exponent and
$[1+\log(1+B_0)]^{\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}\ge1$.

\noindent\textbf{Randomized integration.}
For every $t<T$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \log\frac{C(1+B_t)^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}}}{\rho_t}
 &\le
 \log\frac{C(1+B_0)^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}}(t+1)^2}{\rho}\\
 &\le
 \log\frac{
 C(1+B_0)^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}}
 [1+\log(1+B_0)]^2}{\rho}\\
 &\le
 \log\frac{C(1+B_0)^{\frac{d-1}{\nu}+2}}{\rho}\\
 &=
 \log\frac{C}{\rho}
 +\left(\frac{d-1}{\nu}+2\right)\log(1+B_0)\\
 &\le
 \left(\frac{d-1}{\nu}+2\right)
 \log\frac{C(1+B_0)}{\rho}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first inequality uses $B_t\le B_0$ and
$\rho_t=\frac{6\rho}{\pi^2(t+1)^2}$.
The second uses
$t+1\le T\le C[1+\log(1+B_0)]$.
The third uses $\log(1+B_0)\le B_0$.
The last uses
$\frac{d-1}{\nu}+2\ge1$ and
$\log\frac{C}{\rho}>0$.

Absorbing the fixed prefactor into $C$, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 Q^{\mathrm{rand}}
 &\le
 N_{d,p}^\nabla+
 C\left[
 \log\frac{C(1+B_0)}{\rho}
 \right]^{\frac{1}{2\nu-1}}
 \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}(1+B_t^{\chi_{\mathrm{rand}}})\\
 &\le
 N_{d,p}^\nabla+
 C\left[
 \log\frac{C(1+B_0)}{\rho}
 \right]^{\frac{1}{2\nu-1}}
 (T+B_0^{\chi_{\mathrm{rand}}})\\
 &\le
 N_{d,p}^\nabla+
 C(1+B_0^{\chi_{\mathrm{rand}}})
 \left[
 \log\frac{C(1+B_0)}{\rho}
 \right]^{\frac{1}{2\nu-1}},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality sums the single-iteration bound
and uses the uniform logarithmic estimate.
The second uses
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-geometric-sum}
with $a=\chi_{\mathrm{rand}}$,
and the third uses
\eqref{eq:gradient-only-constant-cost-absorption}
with the same exponent.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Substituting $r^0=\frac{16\Delta}{\varepsilon}$
in the unconstrained case and $r^0=1$ in the
cube-constrained case gives
\[
 B_0=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle
 \frac{48d\,16^{\nu-1}}{1-\alpha}
 L_p\Delta^{\nu-1}\varepsilon^{-\nu},
 &\text{unconstrained},\\[2mm]
 \displaystyle
 \frac{48d}{1-\alpha}\frac{L_p}{\varepsilon},
 &\text{cube-constrained}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Thus $B_0$ is a fixed multiple of $\mathcal B$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:total-gradient-query-complexity}
gives the parameter-dependent query bounds, including the
critical deterministic logarithmic factor.

For fixed problem parameters, $B_0$ scales as
$\varepsilon^{-\nu}$ in the unconstrained case.
Hence the accuracy exponents are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu\chi_{\mathrm{det}}
 &=
 \nu\max\left\{
 \frac{d-1}{\nu},\frac{1}{\nu-1}
 \right\}
 =
 \max\left\{d-1,\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}\right\},\\
 \nu\chi_{\mathrm{rand}}
 &=
 \nu\max\left\{
 \frac{d-1}{\nu},\frac{2}{2\nu-1}
 \right\}
 =
 \max\left\{d-1,\frac{2\nu}{2\nu-1}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In the cube-constrained case, $B_0$ scales as
$\varepsilon^{-1}$, giving exponents
\[
 \chi_{\mathrm{det}}
 =\max\left\{
 \frac{d-1}{\nu},\frac{1}{\nu-1}
 \right\},
 \qquad
 \chi_{\mathrm{rand}}
 =\max\left\{
 \frac{d-1}{\nu},\frac{2}{2\nu-1}
 \right\}.
\]
The terminal cost $N_{d,p}^\nabla$ is constant for fixed $d,p$.

Finally, the same substitutions into
$T+1\le C[1+\log(1+B_0)]$
give $O(1+\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ adaptive rounds
for fixed parameters and $0<\varepsilon\le1$.
Deterministic correctness and randomized success probability
at least $1-\rho$ follow from
Subsection~\ref{subsec:gradient-only-analysis}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
Suppose that $\Gamma\ne\varnothing$ and that a continuous
surrogate $\widehat\phi_x$ on $\Gamma$ satisfies
$\|\widehat\phi_x-\phi_{x,\frac{\varepsilon}{4}}\|_{\infty,\Gamma}
\le\frac{\varepsilon r}{16}$.
Let $\widehat y\in\Gamma$ satisfy
$\widehat\phi_x(\widehat y)
\le\min_\Gamma\widehat\phi_x+\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}$.
Then the following alternatives are exhaustive and disjoint.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\widehat\phi_x(\widehat y)>\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}$, then
every point of $\partial_XQ$ is $\frac{3\varepsilon}{8}$-unreachable
from $x$.
\item If $\widehat\phi_x(\widehat y)\le\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}$, then
$f(\widehat y)\le f(x)-\frac{5\varepsilon r}{32}
\le f(x)-\frac{\varepsilon}{8}$.
\end{enumerate}
If $\Gamma=\varnothing$, the trapping certificate in the first
alternative holds vacuously.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
If $\Gamma=\varnothing$, then $\partial_XQ=\varnothing$,
so the trapping claim holds vacuously. Assume $\Gamma\ne\varnothing$.

If $\widehat\phi_x(\widehat y)>\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}$,
then, for every $y\in\Gamma$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \phi_{x,\frac{3\varepsilon}{8}}(y)
 &=\phi_{x,\frac{\varepsilon}{4}}(y)
   +\frac{\varepsilon r}{8}\ge\widehat\phi_x(y)+\frac{\varepsilon r}{16}\ge\widehat\phi_x(\widehat y)+\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}>\frac{\varepsilon r}{16}>0,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the equality uses $\|y-x\|_2=r$, and the inequalities
use the surrogate error, approximate minimality, and the
threshold condition, respectively.
Since $\partial_XQ\subseteq\Gamma$, the first alternative follows.

Otherwise, $\widehat y\in\Gamma\subseteq X$ satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
 f(\widehat y)-f(x)
 &=\phi_{x,\frac{\varepsilon}{4}}(\widehat y)
   -\frac{\varepsilon r}{4}\le\widehat\phi_x(\widehat y)-\frac{3\varepsilon r}{16}\le-\frac{5\varepsilon r}{32}
 \le-\frac{\varepsilon r}{8},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the equality uses $\|\widehat y-x\|_2=r$,
and the first two inequalities use the surrogate error and
$\widehat\phi_x(\widehat y)\le\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}$.
This proves the second alternative.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
Let $Q:=Q_x(r)$.
Suppose that $\phi_{x,\frac{3\varepsilon}{8}}>0$ on
$\partial_XQ$, and that the known scalar polynomial $P_x$
satisfies
$\|\nabla P_x-\nabla f\|_{\infty,Q}
\le\frac{\varepsilon}{16}$.
Then Algorithm~\ref{alg:trap-localize} terminates after
finitely many offline operations, without further oracle queries,
and returns a point $z\in Q$ satisfying
\[
\begin{cases}
 \|\nabla f(z)\|_2\le\varepsilon,
 &X=\mathbb R^d,\\
 \|G_\gamma(z)\|_2\le\varepsilon
 \quad\text{for every }\gamma>0,
 &X=[0,1]^d.
\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Write $P:=P_x$, $\Psi(y):=P(y)-P(x)
+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\|y-x\|_2$, and
$\zeta:=\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}$.

\noindent\textbf{Finite termination.}
Termwise bounds on the derivatives of the known polynomial
over $x+[-r,r]^d$ give computable constants
\[
 M_P\ge\sup_{y\in Q}\|\nabla P(y)\|_2+\frac{\varepsilon}{2},
 \qquad
 L_P\ge\sup_{y\in Q}\|\nabla^2P(y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}.
\]
Thus $M_P>0$, $\Psi$ is $M_P$-Lipschitz on $Q$, and
$\nabla P$ is $L_P$-Lipschitz on $Q$.
Set $\tau:=\frac{1}{L_P+1}$, as in
Algorithm~\ref{alg:trap-localize}.

A finite $\frac{\zeta}{M_P}$-net $\mathcal V\subseteq Q$
containing $x$ can be constructed by projecting a Cartesian
grid in $x+[-r,r]^d$ onto $Q$ and adding $x$.
Indeed, choose coordinate spacing at most
$\frac{\zeta}{M_P\sqrt d}$.
For every $y\in Q$, some grid point $a$ then satisfies
\[
 \|\Pi_Q(a)-y\|_2
 =\|\Pi_Q(a)-\Pi_Q(y)\|_2
 \le\|a-y\|_2
 \le\frac{\zeta}{M_P},
\]
where the inequality uses nonexpansiveness of projection.
Let $z^0\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathcal V}\Psi$.
If $y^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_Q\Psi$, choose
$a^\star\in\mathcal V$ within distance
$\frac{\zeta}{M_P}$ of $y^\star$. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Psi(z^0)&\le\Psi(x)=0,\\
 \Psi(z^0)
 &\le\Psi(a^\star)
 \le\Psi(y^\star)+M_P\|a^\star-y^\star\|_2
 \le\min_Q\Psi+\zeta,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first line uses $x\in\mathcal V$, and the second
uses the choice of $z^0$ and Lipschitz continuity.

The algorithm subsequently computes
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-trapping-proximal-refinement}
 z^{k+1}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Q}
 \left\{
 \langle\nabla P(z^k),y-z^k\rangle
 +\frac{\|y-z^k\|_2^2}{2\tau}
 +\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\|y-x\|_2
 \right\}.
\end{equation}
Each minimizer exists and is unique because $Q$ is nonempty,
compact, and convex, and the objective is continuous and
strongly convex.

Both these minimizers and the grid projections admit finite
real-algebraic computation in the exact-real query model.
The cap is described by $\|y-x\|_2^2\le r^2$ and, in the
constrained case, $0\le y_i\le1$.
The norm term can be represented by an auxiliary variable
$u\ge0$ with $u^2\ge\|y-x\|_2^2$ and its positive coefficient
forces equality at a minimizer.
Thus the optimization problems have polynomial objectives
and constraints with known coefficients, and finite
real-algebraic elimination and root selection determine their
unique minimizers.

Put $s_k:=z^{k+1}-z^k$.
The update satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-trapping-proximal-decrease}
\begin{aligned}
 \Psi(z^{k+1})-\Psi(z^k)
 &\le
 \langle\nabla P(z^k),s_k\rangle
 +\frac{L_P}{2}\|s_k\|_2^2
 +\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
 \bigl(\|z^{k+1}-x\|_2-\|z^k-x\|_2\bigr)\\
 &\le
 -\left(\frac{1}{2\tau}-\frac{L_P}{2}\right)
 \|s_k\|_2^2\\
 &=-\frac{1}{2}\|s_k\|_2^2,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the first inequality uses the Hessian bound,
the second compares the proximal objective at $z^{k+1}$
and $z^k$, and the equality uses
$\frac{1}{\tau}=L_P+1$.
Consequently, every iterate satisfies
$\Psi(z^k)\le0$ and $\Psi(z^k)\le\min_Q\Psi+\zeta$.

Convex optimality gives
$v^{k+1}\in\partial\|\cdot-x\|_2(z^{k+1})$ and
$n^{k+1}\in N_Q(z^{k+1})$ such that
\[
 \nabla P(z^k)+\frac{s_k}{\tau}
 +\frac{\varepsilon}{2}v^{k+1}+n^{k+1}=0.
\]
The subdifferential sum rule applies because the norm is
continuous everywhere.
Hence the residual monitored by the algorithm satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
 e^{k+1}
 &:=\nabla P(z^{k+1})-\nabla P(z^k)-\frac{s_k}{\tau}\\
 &=\nabla P(z^{k+1})
   +\frac{\varepsilon}{2}v^{k+1}+n^{k+1},\\
 \|e^{k+1}\|_2
 &\le\left(L_P+\frac{1}{\tau}\right)\|s_k\|_2
 =(2L_P+1)\|s_k\|_2,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the inequality uses Lipschitz continuity of $\nabla P$.

At every step at which the algorithm does not return,
$\|e^{k+1}\|_2>\frac{\varepsilon}{16}$, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Psi(z^k)-\Psi(z^{k+1})
 &\ge\frac{1}{2}\|s_k\|_2^2\\
 &>\frac{1}{2}
 \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{16(2L_P+1)}\right)^2
 =\frac{\varepsilon^2}{512(2L_P+1)^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $\Psi(z^0)-\min_Q\Psi\le\zeta$, the algorithm terminates
after at most
$\left\lfloor
\frac{512(2L_P+1)^2\zeta}{\varepsilon^2}
\right\rfloor+1$
proximal solves.
Its output $z$ therefore satisfies Eq.~\eqref{eq:trapping-terminal-certificates} and
$\Psi(z)\le\min_Q\Psi+\zeta$.
All computations use the known polynomial and require
no additional oracle queries.

\noindent\textbf{Correctness of the output.}
For every $y\in Q$, convexity of $Q$ and the model accuracy give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |P(y)-P(x)-f(y)+f(x)|&=
 \left|
 \int_0^1
 \left\langle
 (\nabla P-\nabla f)(x+t(y-x)),y-x
 \right\rangle\,dt
 \right|\\
 &\le
 \|\nabla P-\nabla f\|_{\infty,Q}\|y-x\|_2\\
 &\le\frac{\varepsilon}{16}\|y-x\|_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, for every $y\in\partial_XQ$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Psi(y)
 &\ge f(y)-f(x)+\frac{7\varepsilon}{16}\|y-x\|_2\\
 &=\phi_{x,\frac{3\varepsilon}{8}}(y)
   +\frac{\varepsilon}{16}\|y-x\|_2\\
 &>\frac{\varepsilon r}{16}>0,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last inequality uses the trapping hypothesis and
$\partial_XQ\subseteq\Gamma$.
Since $\Psi(z)\le0$, we obtain $z\in\operatorname{int}_XQ$.

It follows that $N_Q(z)=N_X(z)$.
Indeed, $Q\subseteq X$ gives $N_X(z)\subseteq N_Q(z)$.
Conversely, for $n\in N_Q(z)$ and $y\in X$, relative interior
and convexity of $X$ imply $z+t(y-z)\in Q$ for sufficiently
small $t>0$. Hence
$0\ge\langle n,z+t(y-z)-z\rangle=t\langle n,y-z\rangle$,
which proves $n\in N_X(z)$.

For the vectors $v,n$ supplied by the terminal certificate,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|\nabla f(z)+n\|_2
 &\le
 \|\nabla f(z)-\nabla P(z)\|_2
 +\left\|\nabla P(z)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}v+n\right\|_2
 +\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\|v\|_2\\
 &\le
 \frac{\varepsilon}{16}
 +\frac{\varepsilon}{16}
 +\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
 =\frac{5\varepsilon}{8}<\varepsilon,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the second inequality uses the model accuracy,
the residual stopping condition, and $\|v\|_2\le1$.

When $X=\mathbb R^d$, we have $n=0$, giving the required
gradient bound.
When $X=[0,1]^d$, the inclusion $n\in N_X(z)$ implies
$\Pi_X(z+\gamma n)=z$ for every $\gamma>0$. Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|G_\gamma(z)\|_2
 &=
 \frac{1}{\gamma}
 \left\|
 \Pi_X(z+\gamma n)
 -\Pi_X(z-\gamma\nabla f(z))
 \right\|_2\\
 &\le\|\nabla f(z)+n\|_2
 \le\frac{5\varepsilon}{8}<\varepsilon,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality uses nonexpansiveness of projection.
The same output $z$ satisfies this bound for every $\gamma>0$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:unconstrained-trapping-outer}
\label{prop:box-constrained-guarantee}
                                                 
                                               
                                                          
                      
                                             
       
Under the above assumptions,
Algorithm~\ref{alg:unconstrained-boundary-lazy}
terminates and returns $z\in X$ satisfying
$\|\nabla f(z)\|_2\le\varepsilon$ when $X=\mathbb R^d$,
or $\|G_\gamma(z)\|_2\le\varepsilon$ for every $\gamma>0$
when $X=[0,1]^d$.
The number of accepted moves satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:outer-move-count}
 N_{\mathrm{mov}}
 \le\left\lfloor\frac{8\Delta}{\varepsilon r}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
The algorithm makes exactly $N_{\mathrm{mov}}+1$ calls to
construct $(P_{\boldsymbol x},\widehat\phi_{\boldsymbol x})$
using the selected fresh or lazy procedure, and one call to
$\mathsf{TrapLocalize}$ (Algorithm~\ref{alg:trap-localize}).
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Every accepted move remains in $X$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-trapping-or-descent},
after $N$ accepted moves,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 N\frac{\varepsilon r}{8}
 &\le\sum_{t=0}^{N-1}\bigl(f(x^t)-f(x^{t+1})\bigr)\\
 &=f(x^0)-f(x^N)\\
 &\le f(x^0)-\inf_Xf
 \le\Delta,
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:outer-move-count}.
Each boundary minimization concerns a known polynomial on
a compact semialgebraic set and admits finite real-algebraic
computation. Hence the algorithm reaches a trapping branch
after finitely many iterations.

At the terminal center,
$\phi_{x,\frac{3\varepsilon}{8}}>0$ on $\partial_XQ$
by Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-trapping-or-descent}.
When $\Gamma=\varnothing$, this condition holds vacuously.
Lemma~\ref{lem:trapped-ball-localization} therefore guarantees
finite termination of localization and correctness of the output.

There is one model call at the initial center and after each
accepted move, giving exactly $N_{\mathrm{mov}}+1$ calls.
Terminal localization is invoked exactly once.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:function-value-query-complexity}
\label{prop:gradient-only-query-complexity}
Under the standing assumptions, use the radius
$r=\frac{1}{2}
\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{48L_p}\right)^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}$
from Eq.~\eqref{eq:function-value-radius}.
The fresh implementations of
Algorithm~\ref{alg:unconstrained-boundary-lazy}
satisfy the output guarantees of
Proposition~\ref{prop:unconstrained-trapping-outer}.
Their deterministic query complexities are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 Q_{\mathrm{val}}
 &=\mathcal O_{p,\beta_p}\!\left(
 d^p\left[
 1+L_p^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
 \Delta\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
 \right]\right),\\
 Q_{\mathrm{grad}}
 &=\mathcal O_{p,\beta_p}\!\left(
 d^{p-1}\left[
 1+L_p^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
 \Delta\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
 \right]\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
All queries lie in $X$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
At a pivot $\boldsymbol x$, let $Q:=Q_{\boldsymbol x}(r)$
and choose $\boldsymbol c\in\operatorname{int}(Q)$.
For $X=\mathbb R^d$, take $\boldsymbol c=\boldsymbol x$;
for the cube, a sufficiently small move from $\boldsymbol x$
toward $(\frac{1}{2},\ldots,\frac{1}{2})$ gives such a point.
Then
$\rho:=\max_{\boldsymbol y\in Q}
\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol c\|_2\le2r$.

Write $N_{d,q}:=\binom{d+q}{q}$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:local-reconstruction} and
Corollary~\ref{lem:gradient-only-scalar-reconstruction}
construct $P_{\boldsymbol x}$ using one nonadaptive batch of
$N_{d,p}$ function-value queries or $N_{d,p-1}$ gradient queries,
respectively, all in $Q$.
In both cases,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|\nabla P_{\boldsymbol x}-\nabla f\|_{\infty,Q}
 &\le3L_p\rho^{\nu-1}\le3L_p(2r)^{\nu-1}
 =\frac{\varepsilon}{16},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first inequality uses $a_{j,\beta_p}\le1$,
and the equality follows from the choice of $r$.
For every $\boldsymbol y\in Q$, integrating this error
along $[\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y]\subseteq Q$ gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &|P_{\boldsymbol x}(\boldsymbol y)
   -P_{\boldsymbol x}(\boldsymbol x)
   -f(\boldsymbol y)+f(\boldsymbol x)|\le
 \frac{\varepsilon}{16}\|\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x\|_2
 \le\frac{\varepsilon r}{16}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:boundary-approximation} and
\eqref{eq:terminal-ball-gradient-accuracy} hold,
and the same polynomial serves at termination.

Proposition~\ref{prop:unconstrained-trapping-outer}
therefore gives correctness and at most
$1+\left\lfloor\frac{8\Delta}{\varepsilon r}\right\rfloor$
model calls.
Since terminal localization requires no additional queries,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 Q_{\mathrm{val}}
 &\le N_{d,p}
 \left(1+\left\lfloor\frac{8\Delta}{\varepsilon r}\right\rfloor\right),\\
 Q_{\mathrm{grad}}
 &\le N_{d,p-1}
 \left(1+\left\lfloor\frac{8\Delta}{\varepsilon r}\right\rfloor\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally,
\[
 \frac{1}{\varepsilon r}
 =
 2\,48^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
 L_p^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
 \varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}.
\]
Substituting this identity and
$N_{d,q}=\mathcal O_q(d^q)$ with $q=p,p-1$
proves the stated bounds.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:lazy-function-value-accuracy}
\label{lem:lazy-gradient-accuracy}
With the fixed interpolation operators above, every call to
Algorithm~\ref{alg:lazy-approx-boundary} returns
$P_{\boldsymbol x}\in\Pi_p^d$ and
$\widehat\phi_{\boldsymbol x}$ satisfying
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \left\|
 \widehat\phi_{\boldsymbol x}
 -\phi_{\boldsymbol x,\frac{\varepsilon}{4}}
 \right\|_{\infty,\Gamma_{\boldsymbol x}(r)}
 &\le\frac{\varepsilon r}{16},\\
 \left\|\nabla P_{\boldsymbol x}-\nabla f\right\|
 _{\infty,Q_{\boldsymbol x}(r)}
 &\le\frac{\varepsilon}{16}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The same polynomial can be used for terminal localization
without further oracle queries.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
\noindent\textbf{Phase identities.}
Let $\boldsymbol x_0=\boldsymbol a,\ldots,
\boldsymbol x_k=\boldsymbol x$ be the centers visited
within the current phase, where $k\le m-1$.
Since each accepted move has length $r$,
$\|\boldsymbol x-\boldsymbol a\|_2\le kr\le(m-1)r$.
The update rules and linearity give
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-lazy-scalar-phase-identity}
\begin{aligned}
 \widehat A_{\boldsymbol x}
 &=I_pA_{\boldsymbol a}
   +\sum_{j=1}^k
    I_{p-1}(A_{\boldsymbol x_j}-A_{\boldsymbol x_{j-1}})\\
 &=I_pA_{\boldsymbol a}
   +I_{p-1}(A_{\boldsymbol x}-A_{\boldsymbol a}),\\
 V_{\boldsymbol x}
 &=I_{p-1}B_{\boldsymbol a}
   +\sum_{j=1}^k
    I_{p-2}(B_{\boldsymbol x_j}-B_{\boldsymbol x_{j-1}})\\
 &=I_{p-1}B_{\boldsymbol a}
   +I_{p-2}(B_{\boldsymbol x}-B_{\boldsymbol a}),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the second equality in each pair follows by telescoping.

\noindent\textbf{Model error.}
The chain rule gives
$A_{\boldsymbol a}\in C^{p,\beta_p}(L_pr^\nu)$ and
$B_{\boldsymbol a}\in C^{p-1,\beta_p}(L_pr^\nu)$.
Moreover, for every $\boldsymbol u\in\mathbb B$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-lazy-aggregate-derivative}
\begin{aligned}
 \|D^p(A_{\boldsymbol x}-A_{\boldsymbol a})
       (\boldsymbol u)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 &=
 \|D^{p-1}(B_{\boldsymbol x}-B_{\boldsymbol a})
       (\boldsymbol u)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\\
 &=r^p
 \|D^pf(\boldsymbol x+r\boldsymbol u)
   -D^pf(\boldsymbol a+r\boldsymbol u)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\\
 &\le L_pr^p
       \|\boldsymbol x-\boldsymbol a\|_2^{\beta_p},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the first equality uses
$B_{\boldsymbol x}=\nabla A_{\boldsymbol x}$ and
Euclidean duality, and the inequality uses H\"older continuity.

Integrating these derivatives along segments in $\mathbb B$
shows that $A_{\boldsymbol x}-A_{\boldsymbol a}$ and
$B_{\boldsymbol x}-B_{\boldsymbol a}$ have Lipschitz
derivatives of orders $p-1$ and $p-2$, respectively, with
constant $L_pr^p\|\boldsymbol x-\boldsymbol a\|_2^{\beta_p}$.
For $p=2$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:apx-lazy-aggregate-derivative}
also supplies the derivative bound required for $I_0$.

Subtracting $A_{\boldsymbol x}$ and $B_{\boldsymbol x}$
from the phase identities and applying the interpolation
bounds therefore gives, for $i=0,1$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-lazy-joint-invariants}
\begin{aligned}
 &\max\left\{
 \|D^i(\widehat A_{\boldsymbol x}-A_{\boldsymbol x})
       \|_{\infty,\mathbb B},
 \|D^i(V_{\boldsymbol x}-B_{\boldsymbol x})
       \|_{\infty,\mathbb B}
 \right\}\\
 &\quad\le
 \frac{3}{2}L_pr^\nu
 +\frac{3}{2}L_pr^p
       \|\boldsymbol x-\boldsymbol a\|_2^{\beta_p}\\
 &\quad\le
 \frac{3}{2}L_pr^\nu
 \left[1+(m-1)^{\beta_p}\right]\\
 &\quad\le3m^{\beta_p}L_pr^\nu
 =\frac{\varepsilon r}{32},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the second inequality uses the displacement bound,
the third uses $1+(m-1)^{\beta_p}\le2m^{\beta_p}$,
and the equality follows from the choice of $r$.

\noindent\textbf{Boundary and terminal guarantees.}
In function-value mode, set
$P_{\boldsymbol x}(\boldsymbol y)
:=\widehat A_{\boldsymbol x}
(\frac{\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x}{r})$.
Since every $I_j$ interpolates at $\boldsymbol0$,
$\widehat A_{\boldsymbol x}(\boldsymbol0)=0$.
The preceding error bounds and the chain rule give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|P_{\boldsymbol x}-f+f(\boldsymbol x)\|
       _{\infty,Q_{\boldsymbol x}(r)}
 &\le\frac{\varepsilon r}{32},\\
 \|\nabla P_{\boldsymbol x}-\nabla f\|
       _{\infty,Q_{\boldsymbol x}(r)}
 &\le\frac{1}{r}\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}
 =\frac{\varepsilon}{32}.
\end{aligned}
\]

In gradient-only mode, define
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-lazy-radial-potential}
 S_{\boldsymbol x}(\boldsymbol u)
 :=\int_0^1
 \langle V_{\boldsymbol x}(t\boldsymbol u),
         \boldsymbol u\rangle\,dt,
 \qquad
 P_{\boldsymbol x}(\boldsymbol y)
 :=S_{\boldsymbol x}
   \left(\frac{\boldsymbol y-\boldsymbol x}{r}\right).
\end{equation}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:radial-scalar-reconstruction} to
$A_{\boldsymbol x}$ and $V_{\boldsymbol x}$ on $\mathbb B$,
using Eq.~\eqref{eq:apx-lazy-joint-invariants}.
It gives $S_{\boldsymbol x}\in\Pi_p^d$,
$S_{\boldsymbol x}(\boldsymbol0)=0$, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|P_{\boldsymbol x}-f+f(\boldsymbol x)\|
       _{\infty,Q_{\boldsymbol x}(r)}
 &\le\frac{\varepsilon r}{32},\\
 \|\nabla P_{\boldsymbol x}-\nabla f\|
       _{\infty,Q_{\boldsymbol x}(r)}
 &\le
 \frac{1}{r}
 \left(\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}
       +\frac{1}{2}\frac{\varepsilon r}{32}\right)\\
 &=\frac{3\varepsilon}{64}
 \le\frac{\varepsilon}{16}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In both modes, $P_{\boldsymbol x}(\boldsymbol x)=0$,
so the value bounds imply
Eq.~\eqref{eq:boundary-approximation}, while the gradient bounds
give Eq.~\eqref{eq:terminal-ball-gradient-accuracy}.
Both scalar polynomials are computed from the retained models
without further oracle queries.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:lazy-boundary-reuse-complexity}
Under the standing assumptions, take $m=d$ and use
$r=r_m$ from Eq.~\eqref{eq:lazy-radius}.
Both lazy implementations deterministically return an
$\varepsilon$-stationary point, with query complexities
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:optimized-lazy-complexities}
\begin{aligned}
 Q_{\mathrm{val}}
 &=\mathcal O_{p,\beta_p}\!\left(
 d^p+d^{p-1+\frac{\beta_p}{\nu-1}}
 L_p^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
 \Delta\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
 \right),\\
 Q_{\mathrm{grad}}
 &=\mathcal O_{p,\beta_p}\!\left(
 d^{p-1}+d^{p-2+\frac{\beta_p}{\nu-1}}
 L_p^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
 \Delta\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
 \right).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Each model call uses one nonadaptive batch, and terminal
localization requires no additional queries.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
We first keep $m\ge1$ arbitrary.
Lemma~\ref{lem:lazy-function-value-accuracy} verifies the
model requirements of
Proposition~\ref{prop:unconstrained-trapping-outer}.
Hence correctness follows, and the number $K$ of model calls
satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-lazy-number-of-calls}
\begin{aligned}
 K
 &\le1+\left\lfloor\frac{8\Delta}{\varepsilon r}\right\rfloor\\
 &\le1+C_{p,\beta_p}
 m^{\frac{\beta_p}{\nu-1}}
 L_p^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
 \Delta\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the second inequality substitutes Eq.~\eqref{eq:lazy-radius}.

For function values, put $q=p$; for gradients, put $q=p-1$.
A refresh queries the nodes in
$\boldsymbol x+rU_q$ and retains the data on
$\boldsymbol x+rU_{q-1}$.
A rolling update queries only
$\boldsymbol x+rU_{q-1}$, since the corresponding data at
the preceding center are already cached.
Thus refreshes and rolling updates use $N_{d,q}$ and
$N_{d,q-1}$ queries, respectively.

Among $K$ calls, exactly
$\left\lceil\frac{K}{m}\right\rceil$ are refreshes.
Counting the prescribed stencil queries, the total is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-lazy-exact-query-count}
\begin{aligned}
 Q
 &=
 \left\lceil\frac{K}{m}\right\rceil N_{d,q}
 +\left(K-\left\lceil\frac{K}{m}\right\rceil\right)
   N_{d,q-1}\\
 &\le
 N_{d,q}
 +K\left(\frac{N_{d,q}}{m}+N_{d,q-1}\right),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the inequality uses
$\left\lceil\frac{K}{m}\right\rceil\le1+\frac{K}{m}$.
Combining this with Eq.~\eqref{eq:apx-lazy-number-of-calls}
and $N_{d,q}=\mathcal O_q(d^q)$ gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:apx-lazy-general-complexity}
 Q\le C_{p,\beta_p}\left[
 d^q+
 \left(
 d^q m^{-\frac{p-1}{\nu-1}}
 +d^{q-1}m^{\frac{\beta_p}{\nu-1}}
 \right)
 L_p^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
 \Delta\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}
 \right].
\end{equation}
Here the terms independent of $\Delta$ are at most
$3N_{d,q}$ because $m\ge1$ and $N_{d,q-1}\le N_{d,q}$,
and we used
$\frac{\beta_p}{\nu-1}-1=-\frac{p-1}{\nu-1}$.

For $m=d$, both dimension powers in parentheses equal
$q-1+\frac{\beta_p}{\nu-1}$.
Taking $q=p$ and $q=p-1$ proves
Eq.~\eqref{eq:optimized-lazy-complexities}.
Each translated node set is fixed before its answers are
observed, so every model call uses one nonadaptive batch.
The terminal polynomial is already supplied by
Lemma~\ref{lem:lazy-function-value-accuracy}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:drhs-spectrum}
There are numerical constants \(c_0>0\) and \(\kappa_0\ge4\) such that the
following holds.  Suppose \(\kappa\ge\kappa_0\), set
\(t:=\lfloor c_0\sqrt\kappa\rfloor\ge1\) and \(K:=t+2\), and let
\(M\ge2\kappa\) be an integer.  Then there are distinct numbers
\(\mu\le\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_K\le\bar L\) and positive integers
\(n_1,\ldots,n_K\), with \(\sum_{i=1}^K n_i=M\), such that, for every
real polynomial \(q\) of degree at most \(t\),
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-flat-spectrum}
 n_i\ge\frac{M}{2\kappa}\quad(i\in[K]),
 \qquad
 \sum_{i=1}^K\frac{n_i}{M}
 \left|\frac1{\lambda_i}-q(\lambda_i)\right|^2
 \ge\frac{3}{512\mu^2}.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\(D:=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1I_{n_1},\ldots,\lambda_KI_{n_K})\)
satisfies \(\mu I\preceq D\preceq\bar L I\).
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
The uniform approximation of \(x\mapsto x^{-1}\) on a positive interval is classical.  Exact minimax errors are given in \cite[Theorem~2.1 and Corollary~2.2]{kraus2012bestinverse} and \cite[Theorem~3.4]{plonka2026reciprocal}; in particular, for every fixed \(C>0\), degree \(m\leq C\sqrt\kappa\) entails uniform error \(\Omega_C(\mu^{-1})\) on \([\mu,\bar L]\).  Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-spectrum} converts this uniform obstruction into a weighted-\(L_2\) certificate on exactly \(t+2\) spectral points and rounds its weights to integer multiplicities bounded below by \(M/(2\kappa)\).  Related discretization and replication arguments appear in \cite[Appendix~A.4--A.5]{derezinski2026matrixvector}, which constructs two moment-matching spectral measures on a common finite support and rounds both to integer multiplicities; this paired-measure construction does not directly yield the single-measure weighted-\(L_2\) bound in \eqref{eq:drhs-flat-spectrum}.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:drhs-delayed-krylov}
Let \(q_0,q_1\in\mathbb N_{+}\), \(j_\star:=q_0+1\), and
\(m:=q_0+q_1+2\), and suppose \(m^2<M\).
Every deterministic two-stage algorithm above admits a
joint-law-preserving orthogonal coupling with
\(\widehat A=\widehat U^\top D\widehat U\), where
\(\widehat U\sim\operatorname{Haar}(O(M))\), and with
\(h_1,\ldots,h_m\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,I_M)\), independent of
\(\widehat U\).

Write \(\widetilde\xi,\widetilde y\) for the coupled input and output, and
set
\(\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}
 :=\operatorname{span}\{\widehat A^a h_j:
 1\leq j\leq q_0,\ a\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0},\
 a+j\leq q_0+1\}\).
Then, almost surely,
\begin{align}
 \widetilde\xi
 &=
 P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}}\widetilde\xi
 +\beta
 \frac{(I-P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}})h_{j_\star}}
      {\|(I-P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}})h_{j_\star}\|_2},
 \qquad
 \beta:=\|(I-P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}})\widetilde\xi\|_2>0,
 \label{eq:drhs-flat-fresh-input}\\
 \widetilde y
 &\in
 \operatorname{span}
 \{\widehat A^a h_j:
 1\leq j\leq m,\ a\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0},\ a+j\leq m\},
 \label{eq:drhs-flat-output-span}\\
 \widehat A^a h_{j_\star}
 \text{ appearing in \eqref{eq:drhs-flat-output-span}}
 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 a\leq m-j_\star=q_1+1.
 \label{eq:drhs-flat-degree}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
The adaptive block-Krylov lifting of
\cite[Lemma~6.3 and Appendix~A]{bakshi2023krylov} represents an adaptive
matrix–vector products transcript in a triangular block-Krylov space.  It does not directly
specify where a vector disclosed only after preprocessing enters this
representation.  Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-delayed-krylov} supplies this
time-respecting extension by assigning the fresh component of the delayed
input to its disclosure slot, while preserving the full disclosed vector
and allowing an unqueried terminal output.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:drhs-fresh-mass}
In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-delayed-krylov}, let \(\mathcal S\)
be the analyst-only augmented span immediately before \(\xi\) is disclosed,
and let \(\beta=\|(I-P_{\mathcal S})\xi\|_2\).  If the procedure makes
\(q_0\) pre-disclosure products, then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-preprocessing-span-dimension}
 \dim(\mathcal S)
 \le\frac{q_0(q_0+3)}2
 \le(q_0+1)^2.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if \(M\ge8(q_0+1)^2\), then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-flat-beta-tail}
 \Pr(\beta<1/2)\le2e^{-M/32}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
In the analyst-only augmentation, preprocessing slot \(j\) contributes at
most the vectors
\(v_j,Av_j,\ldots,A^{q_0+1-j}v_j\), and hence at most
\(q_0+2-j\) dimensions.  Summing over the preprocessing slots gives
\[
 \dim(\mathcal S)
 \le
 \sum_{j=1}^{q_0}(q_0+2-j)
 =\frac{q_0(q_0+3)}2
 \le(q_0+1)^2,
\]
which proves the first part (Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-preprocessing-span-dimension}).

Let \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{pre}}\) be the sigma-field generated by the
augmented preprocessing transcript.  Conditional on
\(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{pre}}\), the subspace \(\mathcal S\) is fixed, while
\(\xi\) remains an independent uniform unit vector.  Write
\(\xi=g/\|g\|_2\) with \(g\sim N(0,I_M)\), put
\(r:=\dim(\mathcal S)\), and define
\[
 X:=\|P_{\mathcal S}g\|_2^2,
 \qquad
 Y:=\|(I-P_{\mathcal S})g\|_2^2.
\]
Conditionally on \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{pre}}\), the variables \(X\) and
\(Y\) are independent with \(X\sim\chi_r^2\) and
\(Y\sim\chi_{M-r}^2\), and \(\beta^2=Y/(X+Y)\).  Hence
\(\beta<1/2\) implies \(X>3Y\), so
\[
 \Pr(\beta<1/2\mid\mathcal F_{\mathrm{pre}})
 \le
 \Pr\left(Y<\frac{M-r}{2}\right)
 +
 \Pr\left(X>\frac{3(M-r)}2\right).
\]
The chi-square moment-generating function gives
\[
 \Pr\left(Y<\frac{M-r}{2}\right)
 \le e^{-(M-r)/16},
 \qquad
 \Pr\left(X>\frac{3(M-r)}2\right)
 \le e^{-3(M-r)/8}2^{r/2}.
\]
If \(M\ge8(q_0+1)^2\), then
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-preprocessing-span-dimension} gives \(r\le M/8\).  The two
terms in the last display are then at most \(e^{-M/32}\).  Thus
\(\Pr(\beta<1/2\mid\mathcal F_{\mathrm{pre}})\le2e^{-M/32}\), and
averaging over \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{pre}}\) proves the second part 
(Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-flat-beta-tail}).
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:drhs-fixed-time}
Assume the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-one-phase},
with $C_0$ in \eqref{eq:drhs-one-phase-dimension}
sufficiently large.
Fix $r\in\{0,\ldots,Q\}$.
Consider any deterministic algorithm that makes exactly $r$
queries to $v\mapsto Av$ before receiving $b$, then makes at
most $t-1$ further queries and returns $y\in\mathbb R^M$.
                                                            
                                          
Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-flat-fixed-time-exclusion}
 \Pr_{(A,b)\sim\mathsf P_0}
 \left(\|y-A^{-1}b\|_2<3\rho\right)
 \le\delta_\star.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
\noindent\textbf{Step 1: Obtain the Krylov representation.}
Store the output $y$ and pad the execution with zero-vector
queries until exactly $t-1$ post-disclosure queries have been
made. The stored output is unchanged.
Since $b=B_0\varepsilon\xi$ and $B_0\varepsilon$ is known,
the algorithm can recover $\xi=\frac{b}{B_0\varepsilon}$.
Thus the padded algorithm has
$q_0=r$ and $q_1=t-1$.

Set $m:=r+t+1$ and $j_\star:=r+1$.
Since $r,t\le Q$ and $Q\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-flat-dimension-consequences}
 m^2\le(2Q+1)^2\le9Q^2<M,
\end{equation}
where the last inequality follows from the $Q^2$ term in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-one-phase-dimension}, for sufficiently large $C_0$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-delayed-krylov} therefore applies.

Use its coupled matrix $\widehat A$, input $\widetilde\xi$,
output $\widetilde y$, and Gaussian vectors $h_1,\ldots,h_m$.
Writing
$\sigma_\star:=
\|(I-P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}})h_{j_\star}\|_2$,
the input and output satisfy, almost surely,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \widetilde\xi
 &=
 P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}}\widetilde\xi
 +\frac{\beta}{\sigma_\star}
  (I-P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}})h_{j_\star},\\
 \widetilde y
 &=\sum_{j=1}^m p_j(\widehat A)h_j,
 \qquad \deg p_j\le m-j,
\end{aligned}
\]
for some real polynomials $p_j$, where $\beta>0$ and
$\sigma_\star>0$.
In particular,
$q_y:=p_{j_\star}$ has degree at most
$m-j_\star=t$.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 2: Isolate the fresh direction.}
For each $i\in[K]$, let $E_i$ be the
$\lambda_i$-eigenspace of $\widehat A$, and let $P_i$ be
its orthogonal projector.
Define $R_i$ as the orthogonal projector onto
\[
 E_i\cap
 \operatorname{span}
 \{P_i h_j:1\le j\le m,\ j\ne j_\star\}^{\perp}.
\]
For every $j\ne j_\star$ and $a\ge0$,
$R_i\widehat A^a h_j=\lambda_i^aR_i h_j=0$.
Thus $R_i$ annihilates all output terms except the one
generated by $h_{j_\star}$.
It also annihilates $\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}$, whose
generators have indices $j\le r<j_\star$.
Applying $R_i$ to the representations from Step~1 gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-flat-projected-representation}
 R_i\widetilde\xi
 =\frac{\beta}{\sigma_\star}R_i h_{j_\star},
 \qquad
 R_i\widetilde y
 =q_y(\lambda_i)R_i h_{j_\star}.
\end{equation}
The same polynomial $q_y=p_{j_\star}$ occurs for every $i$;
only its evaluation point $\lambda_i$ changes.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 3: Reduce the error to polynomial approximation.}
Define
$q(\lambda):=
\frac{\sigma_\star}{B_0\varepsilon\beta}q_y(\lambda)$,
so that $\deg q\le t$.
Since $R_i\widehat A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\lambda_i}R_i$,
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-flat-projected-representation} yields
\[
 R_i\left(
 \widetilde y-B_0\varepsilon\widehat A^{-1}\widetilde\xi
 \right)
 =
 \frac{B_0\varepsilon\beta}{\sigma_\star}
 \left(q(\lambda_i)-\frac{1}{\lambda_i}\right)
 R_i h_{j_\star}.
\]
The ranges of the $R_i$ lie in mutually orthogonal eigenspaces.
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-flat-error-reduction}
\begin{aligned}
 &\|\widetilde y-
 B_0\varepsilon\widehat A^{-1}\widetilde\xi\|_2^2\ge
 \sum_{i=1}^K
 \left\|R_i\left(
 \widetilde y-B_0\varepsilon\widehat A^{-1}\widetilde\xi
 \right)\right\|_2^2=
 B_0^2\varepsilon^2
 \frac{\beta^2}{\sigma_\star^2}
 \sum_{i=1}^K
 \|R_i h_{j_\star}\|_2^2
 \left|\frac{1}{\lambda_i}-q(\lambda_i)\right|^2.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
It remains to lower-bound the random prefactor and weights
in this expression.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 4: Control the random prefactor and weights.}
Let $\mathcal G_\star$ be the event
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-flat-good-event}
 \beta\ge\frac{1}{2},
 \qquad
 \|h_{j_\star}\|_2^2\le2M,
 \qquad
 \|R_i h_{j_\star}\|_2^2\ge\frac{n_i}{4}
 \quad(i\in[K]).
\end{equation}
We bound the failure probability of each condition.

First, the $Q^2$ term in the dimension assumption ensures
$M\ge8(Q+1)^2\ge8(r+1)^2$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-fresh-mass} therefore gives
$\Pr(\beta<\frac{1}{2})\le2e^{-\frac{M}{32}}$.

Second, $\|h_{j_\star}\|_2^2\sim\chi_M^2$.
Markov's inequality and the chi-square moment-generating
function give
$\Pr(\|h_{j_\star}\|_2^2>2M)
\le e^{-\frac{M}{2}}2^{\frac{M}{2}}
\le e^{-\frac{M}{8}}$,
where the last inequality uses $\log2\le\frac{3}{4}$.

Third, the $\kappa Q$ term in the dimension assumption
ensures $M\ge8\kappa Q$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-spectrum},
$n_i\ge\frac{M}{2\kappa}\ge4Q\ge2(m-1)$.
The definition of $R_i$ removes at most $m-1$ dimensions
from $E_i$, so
$\operatorname{rank}(R_i)\ge n_i-(m-1)\ge\frac{n_i}{2}$.
Conditional on $\widehat A$ and $\{h_j:j\ne j_\star\}$,
the projector $R_i$ is fixed and $h_{j_\star}$ remains
standard Gaussian.
Hence $\|R_i h_{j_\star}\|_2^2$ is chi-square with
$\operatorname{rank}(R_i)$ degrees of freedom.
The chi-square lower-tail bound used in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-fresh-mass}, followed by averaging over
the conditioning variables, gives
\[
 \Pr\left(
 \|R_i h_{j_\star}\|_2^2<\frac{n_i}{4}
 \right)
 \le e^{-\frac{n_i}{32}}
 \le e^{-\frac{M}{64\kappa}}.
\]

Combining these bounds by a union bound, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-flat-tail-budget}
\begin{aligned}
 \Pr(\mathcal G_\star^c)
 &\le
 2e^{-\frac{M}{32}}
 +e^{-\frac{M}{8}}
 +K e^{-\frac{M}{64\kappa}}\\
 &\le
 (K+3)e^{-\frac{M}{64\kappa}}
 \le\delta_\star.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The second inequality uses $\kappa\ge1$.
For the last inequality, recall that $K=t+2\le Q+2$ and
$\delta_\star=\frac{\delta}{2(Q+1)\mathsf L}$.
Since $K+3\le2(Q+2)$ and $\log(Q+1)\le Q$,
\[
 \log\frac{K+3}{\delta_\star}
 =
 \log\frac{2(K+3)(Q+1)\mathsf L}{\delta}
 \le
 Q+\log\frac{4(Q+2)\mathsf L}{\delta}.
\]
The $\kappa Q$ and logarithmic terms in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-one-phase-dimension} therefore ensure
$\frac{M}{64\kappa}\ge
\log\frac{K+3}{\delta_\star}$ for sufficiently large $C_0$.
Thus $\mathcal G_\star$ has probability at least
$1-\delta_\star$.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 5: Apply the spectral lower bound.}
On $\mathcal G_\star$,
$\sigma_\star^2\le\|h_{j_\star}\|_2^2\le2M$ and
$\beta^2\ge\frac{1}{4}$, so
$\frac{\beta^2}{\sigma_\star^2}\ge\frac{1}{8M}$.
Substituting this and
$\|R_i h_{j_\star}\|_2^2\ge\frac{n_i}{4}$
into Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-flat-error-reduction} gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|\widetilde y-
 B_0\varepsilon\widehat A^{-1}\widetilde\xi\|_2^2
 &\ge
 \frac{B_0^2\varepsilon^2}{32}
 \sum_{i=1}^K\frac{n_i}{M}
 \left|\frac{1}{\lambda_i}-q(\lambda_i)\right|^2\\
 &\ge
 \frac{3B_0^2\varepsilon^2}{16384\mu^2}\\
 &=48\rho^2>9\rho^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The second inequality is Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-spectrum},
applicable because $\deg q\le t$.
Its bound holds for every such polynomial, including the
polynomial determined by the coupled realization.
The equality uses $B_0=512$ and
$\rho=\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}$.

The orthogonal coupling preserves the distance:
$\|y-A^{-1}b\|_2
=\|\widetilde y-
B_0\varepsilon\widehat A^{-1}\widetilde\xi\|_2$.
Thus $\|y-A^{-1}b\|_2<3\rho$ implies
$\mathcal G_\star^c$.
Taking probabilities and using
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-flat-tail-budget} proves the lemma with
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-flat-fixed-time-exclusion}.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
\noindent\textbf{Adaptive disclosure and multiple candidates.}
Let $\tau\in\{0,\ldots,Q\}$ be the disclosure index.
If the procedure terminates without disclosure, append
zero-vector queries up to index $Q$, disclose $b$, and terminate
without naming further candidates.
Enumerate the candidates as $y_1,\ldots,y_{\mathsf L}$,
padding missing entries with zeros.

For each $(r,\ell)\in\{0,\ldots,Q\}\times[\mathsf L]$,
construct a procedure $\mathsf S_{r,\ell}$ that receives $b$
after exactly $r$ responses.
It simulates the original procedure, recording its $\ell$th
candidate whenever named, including before disclosure.
If the original rule requests disclosure before $r$, or
does not request it at $r$, the simulation switches to
zero-vector queries and a zero output.
Otherwise, it continues the original simulation and returns
the recorded candidate, or zero if none is named.
Pad every post-disclosure stage to $t-1$ queries.

These decisions use only available information.
Writing $y^{r,\ell}$ for the resulting output, we have
$y^{r,\ell}=y_\ell$ on $\{\tau=r\}$, and hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-flat-dummy-inclusion}
 \{\tau=r,\ \|y_\ell-A^{-1}b\|_2<3\rho\}
 \subseteq
 \{\|y^{r,\ell}-A^{-1}b\|_2<3\rho\}.
\end{equation}
Let $H$ be the event that some named vector lies within
$3\rho$ of $A^{-1}b$.
By Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-flat-dummy-inclusion} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-fixed-time},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-flat-unconditioned-exclusion}
\begin{aligned}
 \Pr_{\mathsf P_0}(H)
 &\le
 \sum_{r=0}^Q\sum_{\ell=1}^{\mathsf L}
 \Pr_{\mathsf P_0}
 \bigl(\tau=r,\ \|y_\ell-A^{-1}b\|_2<3\rho\bigr)\\
 &\le
 \sum_{r=0}^Q\sum_{\ell=1}^{\mathsf L}
 \Pr_{\mathsf P_0}
 \bigl(\|y^{r,\ell}-A^{-1}b\|_2<3\rho\bigr)\\
 &\le (Q+1)\mathsf L\delta_\star
 =\frac{\delta}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Conditioning on admissibility.}
Write $\xi=\frac{g}{\|g\|_2}$, where $g\sim N(0,I_M)$
is independent of $A$, and let $P_i$ project onto the
$\lambda_i$-eigenspace of $A$.
Define
\[
 \mathcal E:=
 \left\{
 \|g\|_2^2\le2M,\quad
 \|P_i g\|_2^2\ge\frac{n_i}{2}
 \text{ for every }i\in[K]
 \right\}.
\]
The chi-square tail bounds, $n_i\ge\frac{M}{2\kappa}$,
and Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-one-phase-dimension} give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Pr_{\mathsf P_0}(\mathcal E^c)
 &\le e^{-\frac{M}{8}}
      +\sum_{i=1}^K e^{-\frac{n_i}{16}}\le e^{-\frac{M}{8}}
      +K e^{-\frac{M}{32\kappa}}
 \le\frac{1}{8}.
\end{aligned}
\]
On $\mathcal E$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|A^{-1}b\|_2^2
 &=
 B_0^2\varepsilon^2
 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^K
       \lambda_i^{-2}\|P_i g\|_2^2}
      {\|g\|_2^2}\ge
 \frac{B_0^2\varepsilon^2}{4}
 \sum_{i=1}^K\frac{n_i}{M}\lambda_i^{-2}\ge
 \frac{3B_0^2\varepsilon^2}{2048\mu^2}
 \ge(16\rho)^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the second inequality uses
Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-spectrum} with $q\equiv0$,
and the last uses $B_0=512$ and
$\rho=\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}$.
Moreover,
$\|A^{-1}b\|_2
\le\|A^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|b\|_2
\le B_0\rho$ deterministically, as do
$\mu I\preceq A\preceq\bar L I$ and
$\|b\|_2=B_0\varepsilon$.
Thus the admissibility event $\mathcal G$ in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-phase-conditioning-event}
contains $\mathcal E$, so
$\mathsf P_0(\mathcal G)\ge\frac{7}{8}$.

The law $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{ph}}
=\mathsf P_0(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal G)$ therefore has the
required support. By
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-flat-unconditioned-exclusion},
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Pr_{\mathsf P_{\mathrm{ph}}}(H)
 &=
 \frac{\Pr_{\mathsf P_0}(H\cap\mathcal G)}
      {\mathsf P_0(\mathcal G)}\le
 \frac{\Pr_{\mathsf P_0}(H)}
      {\mathsf P_0(\mathcal G)}
 \le
 \frac{\frac{\delta}{2}}{\frac{7}{8}}
 =\frac{4\delta}{7}<\delta.
\end{aligned}
\]
The construction of $D$, $\mathsf P_0$, and $\mathcal G$
is independent of the procedure.
A procedure designed for $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{ph}}$ remains
a fixed family of Borel maps, to which the bound under
$\mathsf P_0$ applies.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:drhs-phasewise-reduction}
Fix \(s\in[N]\) and condition on
\(\mathcal F_{-s}:=\sigma((A_r,b_r):r\neq s)\).  For almost every
realization of \(\mathcal F_{-s}\), there is a deterministic Borel
delayed-input procedure \(\mathsf S_s\) for \((A_s,b_s)\) that uses at
most \(T-1\) products with \(A_s\) before \(b_s\) is disclosed, fewer
than \(t\) products afterward, and names at most \(T\) vectors.  Under a
coupling with the conditioned chain execution,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-seq-fast-reduction}
 \{\tau_s<\tau_{s-1}+t\}
 \subseteq
 \left\{
  \min\limits_{y\ {\rm named\ by}\ \mathsf S_s}
  \|y-A_s^{-1}b_s\|_2<3\rho
 \right\},
 \qquad s\in[N],
\end{equation}
where \(+\infty+t:=+\infty\).
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
\noindent\textbf{Step 1: Construct the simulator.}
Fix $s$ and a realization of $\mathcal F_{-s}$.
The other phase data are available to the simulator for reconstructing
responses, but are not supplied to the original algorithm.
Whenever the simulated algorithm selects a candidate
$\widehat z^{(j)}$, the simulator freezes it and records its
$s$th block $\widehat z_s^{(j)}$.

For $s=1$, disclose $b_1$ before selecting the first candidate and
set $\sigma_1:=0$.
For $s\ge2$, let $\sigma_s$ be the first candidate index satisfying
$\|\widehat z_{s-1}^{(j)}-x_{s-1}^\star\|_2<3\rho$.
At this index, disclose $b_s$ after the candidate has been frozen
and recorded, but before returning any response.
If no such index occurs, set $\sigma_s:=T$ and disclose $b_s$
after the terminal candidate.
In every case, stop after recording candidate
\[
 \ell_s:=\min\{\sigma_s+t-1,T-1\},
\]
without requesting its response.

At each earlier candidate, request
$v^{(j)}:=A_s\widehat z_s^{(j)}$.
This supplies the current quadratic gradient and value,
respectively,
$v^{(j)}$ and
$\frac{1}{2}\langle\widehat z_s^{(j)},v^{(j)}\rangle$.
All terms involving only other phases are directly computable.

For $s\ge2$, the incoming link $-G_{s-1}\Phi_s$ contributes zero
before disclosure, since both $G_{s-1}$ and $\nabla G_{s-1}$
vanish there. After disclosure, $\Phi_s$ and its derivatives
are computable from $b_s$.
For $s=1$, $b_1$ is available from the start.
For $s<N$, delete the entire outgoing link $-G_s\Phi_{s+1}$,
including its value and both gradient contributions, and suppress
the corresponding disclosure of $b_{s+1}$.
All other disclosures follow the original protocol.
Thus no response computation requires the unknown center
$x_s^\star=A_s^{-1}b_s$.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 2: Verify validity and query budgets.}
For $s\ge2$, the disclosure test uses only the current frozen
candidate and the known center $x_{s-1}^\star$.
It can therefore be performed before returning the current
response, using only information already available.
All decisions and response computations are Borel measurable.

If $\sigma_s<T$, the pre-disclosure products have indices
$0,\ldots,\sigma_s-1$, while the post-disclosure products have
indices $\sigma_s,\ldots,\ell_s-1$.
Their numbers are therefore $\sigma_s\le T-1$ and
$\ell_s-\sigma_s\le t-1$, respectively.
This includes $s=1$, for which $\sigma_1=0$ and $\ell_1=t-1$.
If $\sigma_s=T$, there are $T-1$ pre-disclosure products and
none afterward.
In every case, at most $T$ candidates are recorded.
In particular, if the disclosure candidate is also the stopping
candidate, no product is requested at that index.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 3: Establish agreement up to the first hit.}
Couple the simulated and true executions using the same phase data.
We claim that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-seq-coupling}
 \widehat z^{(j)}=z^{(j)}
 \qquad
 \bigl(0\le j\le\min\{\tau_s,\ell_s\}\bigr).
\end{equation}

We induct on the complete information returned to the algorithm,
including both oracle responses and right-hand-side disclosures.
If the preceding records agree, determinism gives the same
current candidate in both executions.
For $j<\tau_s$, the true candidate satisfies
$G_s(z_s^{(j)})=0$ and $\nabla G_s(z_s^{(j)})=0$.
Hence the deleted outgoing link contributes zero to the true
value and gradient, and $b_{s+1}$ has not yet been disclosed.
The incoming link is either zero before disclosure or exactly
reconstructed afterward; all remaining terms and disclosures
also agree.
Thus, whenever a response is returned at such an index, the
complete records remain identical.

This proves Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-seq-coupling}.
At the first phase-$s$ hit, only agreement of the frozen
candidate is needed: its $s$th block has already been recorded,
regardless of whether the subsequent responses agree.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 4: Capture every fast transition.}
Suppose that $\tau_s<\tau_{s-1}+t$.
Then $\tau_s$ is finite and $\tau_s\le T-1$.
It suffices to show $\tau_s\le\ell_s$, since
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-seq-coupling} then guarantees that the
successful vector $z_s^{(\tau_s)}$ is recorded.

For $s=1$, the fast-transition condition gives
$\tau_1\le t-1=\ell_1$.

Now let $s\ge2$.
If $\tau_s<\tau_{s-1}$, then $\sigma_s>\tau_s$.
Indeed, otherwise $\sigma_s\le\tau_s$ and
$\sigma_s\le\ell_s$, so Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-seq-coupling}
would give a true predecessor hit at index
$\sigma_s\le\tau_s<\tau_{s-1}$, a contradiction.
The definition of $\ell_s$ therefore gives
$\tau_s\le\ell_s$, and the successful vector is recorded
before disclosure.

Otherwise, put $r:=\tau_{s-1}\le\tau_s$.
Here $r$ is finite.
The same argument excludes $\sigma_s<r$, so
$\sigma_s\ge r$ and consequently $\ell_s\ge r$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:drhs-seq-coupling} then applies at index $r$,
where the true predecessor is first hit, and forces
$\sigma_s=r$.
By integrality and the fast-transition condition,
\[
 \tau_s
 \le\min\{r+t-1,T-1\}
 =\ell_s.
\]
Thus the successful vector is again recorded within the
allowed query budget.
This includes $\tau_s=\tau_{s-1}$, when the common candidate
is recorded before $b_s$ is disclosed.
