The required inclusion
Eq.~\eqref{eq:drhs-seq-fast-reduction} follows.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Fix \(s\in[N]\) and condition on \(\mathcal F_{-s}\).  Independence of
the phases gives
\(\mathcal L((A_s,b_s)\mid\mathcal F_{-s})=\mathsf P_{\mathrm{ph}}\).
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-one-phase} to the procedure supplied by
Proposition~\ref{prop:drhs-phasewise-reduction}, with
\(Q=\mathsf L=T\) and \(\delta=1/(12N)\).  Here \(Q=T=Nt\geq t\),
\(\mathsf L=T\geq1\), and \(\delta\leq1/12<1/4\).  Moreover,
\[
 \log\frac{(Q+2)\mathsf L}{\delta}
 =
 \log\bigl(12NT(T+2)\bigr),
\]
so the assumed lower bound on \(M\) is exactly the dimension hypothesis
of the one-phase lemma.  Proposition~\ref{prop:drhs-phasewise-reduction}
and that lemma therefore give, almost surely,
\[
 \Pr\bigl(\tau_s<\tau_{s-1}+t\mid\mathcal F_{-s}\bigr)
 \leq
 \Pr\left(
  \min_{y\ {\rm named\ by}\ \mathsf S_s}
  \|y-A_s^{-1}b_s\|_2<3\rho
  \,\middle|\,\mathcal F_{-s}
 \right)
 \leq\frac1{12N}.
\]
Taking expectations over \(\mathcal F_{-s}\) yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-seq-phasewise-delay}
 \Pr(\tau_s<\tau_{s-1}+t)
 \leq\frac1{12N},
 \qquad s\in[N].
\end{equation}

Let
\(\mathcal B:=\bigcup_{s=1}^N
\{\tau_s<\tau_{s-1}+t\}\).  By
\eqref{eq:drhs-seq-phasewise-delay} and the union bound,
\(\Pr(\mathcal B)\leq1/12\).  On \(\mathcal B^c\), we have
\(\tau_s\geq\tau_{s-1}+t\) for every \(s\in[N]\).  Since
\(\tau_0=0\), induction gives \(\tau_s\geq st\), and in particular
\(\tau_N\geq Nt=T\).

If the terminal output lies within \(3\rho\) of every phase center, then
its \(N\)th block gives \(\tau_N\leq T-1\).  Hence
\[
 \left\{
  \|z_s^{\mathrm{out}}-x_s^\star\|_2<3\rho
  \text{ for every }s\in[N]
 \right\}
 \subseteq\mathcal B,
 \qquad
 \Pr\left(
  \|z_s^{\mathrm{out}}-x_s^\star\|_2<3\rho
  \text{ for every }s\in[N]
 \right)
 \leq\frac1{12}.
\]
The ambient term \(\mu\|u\|_2^2/2\) is independent of the phase data, and
its value and gradient can be reconstructed without any product with
\(A_s\).  It therefore does not affect the simulator or the argument.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:drhs-active-phase-gradient}
Fix an admissible phase realization, \(z\in(\mathbb R^M)^N\), and
\(s\in[N]\).  If \(\alpha_s(z)=1\) and
\(\|z_s-x_s^\star\|_2\geq2\rho\), then
\[
 \|\nabla_sF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}(z)\|_2>\varepsilon.
\]
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
The construction gives \(\Phi_s>0\) in
\eqref{eq:drhs-forcing-positive} and
\(\|x_s^\star\|_2+3\rho<R\) in
\eqref{eq:drhs-clipping-separation}.  We shall also use
\[
 \sup_w\|\nabla\Phi_s(w)\|_2
 \leq a_\chi\|b_s\|_2
 =a_\chi B_0\varepsilon,
\]
which follows from
\(\nabla\Phi_s=(D\pi_R)^\top b_s\) and the previously established bound
\(\sup_w\|D\pi_R(w)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq a_\chi\).

Put \(e_s:=z_s-x_s^\star\).  We distinguish whether clipping is active.
Suppose first that \(\|z_s\|_2\leq R\).  Then \(\pi_R\) is the identity
at \(z_s\), and hence
\(\nabla\Phi_s(z_s)=b_s=A_sx_s^\star\).  Using
\(\alpha_s(z)=1\) in \eqref{eq:drhs-cert-block-gradient}, we obtain
\[
 \nabla_sF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}(z)=A_se_s-\beta_s(z).
\]
The gate derivative is
\(\nabla G_s(z_s)=2\rho^{-2}
\eta'(\|e_s\|_2^2/\rho^2)e_s\).  Therefore, when \(s<N\),
\[
 \left\langle e_s,
 -\Phi_{s+1}(z_{s+1})\nabla G_s(z_s)\right\rangle
 =
 -\frac{2\Phi_{s+1}(z_{s+1})}{\rho^2}
 \eta'\!\left(\frac{\|e_s\|_2^2}{\rho^2}\right)
 \|e_s\|_2^2
 \geq0,
\]
where we used \eqref{eq:drhs-forcing-positive} and \(\eta'\leq0\).
For \(s=N\), this term is absent.  Thus
\[
 \|e_s\|_2\,
 \|\nabla_sF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}(z)\|_2
 \geq
 \langle e_s,\nabla_sF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}(z)\rangle
 \geq e_s^\top A_se_s
 \geq\mu\|e_s\|_2^2.
\]
Because \(\|e_s\|_2\geq2\rho>0\), division by \(\|e_s\|_2\) yields
\[
 \|\nabla_sF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}(z)\|_2
 \geq\mu\|e_s\|_2
 \geq2\mu\rho
 =2\varepsilon.
\]

Suppose now that \(\|z_s\|_2>R\).  Admissibility and
\(R=C_R\rho\) imply
\[
 \|z_s-x_s^\star\|_2
 \geq\|z_s\|_2-\|x_s^\star\|_2
 >R-B_0\rho
 =(C_R-B_0)\rho
 >3\rho.
\]
The outgoing gate is therefore in its exact dead zone, so
\(\beta_s(z)=0\).  Equation~\eqref{eq:drhs-cert-block-gradient}
reduces to
\(\nabla_sF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}(z)
=A_sz_s-\nabla\Phi_s(z_s)\).  Using
\(A_s\succeq\mu I\), the uniform forcing-gradient bound above, and
\(\mu R=C_R\varepsilon\), we obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|\nabla_sF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}(z)\|_2
 &\geq\|A_sz_s\|_2-\|\nabla\Phi_s(z_s)\|_2\\
 &\geq\mu\|z_s\|_2-a_\chi B_0\varepsilon\\
 &>(C_R-a_\chi B_0)\varepsilon\\
 &=(B_0+4)\varepsilon
 >\varepsilon.
 \end{aligned}
\]
This proves the proposition in both regimes.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Suppose, toward the contrapositive, that at least one phase is not
inner-complete, and let
\[
 s:=\min\{r\in[N]:
 \|z_r-x_r^\star\|_2\geq2\rho\}.
\]
If \(s=1\), then \(\alpha_s(z)=1\) by definition.  If \(s\geq2\),
minimality gives
\(\|z_{s-1}-x_{s-1}^\star\|_2<2\rho\), so
\(G_{s-1}(z_{s-1})=1\) and again \(\alpha_s(z)=1\).
Proposition~\ref{prop:drhs-active-phase-gradient} therefore gives
\(\|\nabla_sF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}(z)\|_2>\varepsilon\).

For the ambient extension,
\[
 \|\nabla F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}(z,u)\|_2^2
 =
 \sum_{r=1}^N
 \|\nabla_rF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}(z)\|_2^2
 +\mu^2\|u\|_2^2
 >\varepsilon^2.
\]
Thus failure of inner completion implies
\(\|\nabla F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}(z,u)\|_2>\varepsilon\).
Taking the contrapositive proves the lemma.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:drhs-local-derivatives}
For every integer \(j\geq1\), there are constants
\(a_j,b_j<\infty\), depending only on \(j\) and the fixed cutoff
profile, such that, for every phase \(s\),
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-reg-local-derivatives}
 \sup_w\|D^jG_s(w)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq a_j\rho^{-j},
 \qquad
 \sup_w\|D^j\Phi_s(w)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq b_j\varepsilon\rho^{1-j}.
\end{equation}
The corresponding zero-order bounds are
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-reg-forcing-range}
 0\leq G_s(w)\leq1,
 \qquad
 2B_0\varepsilon R
 \leq\Phi_s(w)\leq6B_0\varepsilon R,
 \qquad w\in\mathbb R^M.
\end{equation}
All constants are independent of \(M\), \(s\), and the phase
realization.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Define the unscaled maps
\(\Gamma(y):=\eta(\|y\|_2^2)\) and
\(\Pi(y):=\chi(\|y\|_2)y\).  Then
\[
 G_s(w)=\Gamma\!\left(\frac{w-x_s^\star}{\rho}\right),
 \qquad
 \pi_R(w)=R\Pi\!\left(\frac{w}{R}\right).
\]

Let \(r_2(y):=\|y\|_2^2\).  Its only nonzero derivatives are
\[
 Dr_2(y)[h]=2\langle y,h\rangle,
 \qquad
 D^2r_2(y)[h_1,h_2]=2\langle h_1,h_2\rangle.
\]
Thus the multilinear chain rule gives
\[
 D^j\Gamma(y)[h_1,\ldots,h_j]
 =
 \sum_{\mathcal P}
 \eta^{(|\mathcal P|)}(r_2(y))
 \prod_{B\in\mathcal P}
 D^{|B|}r_2(y)[h_i:i\in B],
\]
where the sum is over the set partitions of \([j]\) whose blocks have
size one or two.  Every summand is zero unless \(\|y\|_2\leq3\).
Consequently, when \(\|h_i\|_2\leq1\), every factor is bounded by a
constant depending only on \(j\), and the number of summands also depends
only on \(j\).  Hence
\[
 \sup_y\|D^j\Gamma(y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq a_j,
\]
uniformly in \(M\).  Scaling by \(\rho\) proves the gate bound in
\eqref{eq:drhs-reg-local-derivatives}.

For the clipping map, \(\Pi(y)=y\) on \(\|y\|_2\leq1\) and
\(\Pi(y)=0\) on \(\|y\|_2\geq2\).  It remains to control the annulus
\(1<\|y\|_2<2\).  Write
\(r(y):=\|y\|_2\) and \(e(y):=y/r(y)\).  Then
\[
 Dr(y)[h]=\langle e(y),h\rangle,
 \qquad
 De(y)[h]
 =r(y)^{-1}(I-e(y)e(y)^\top)h.
\]
Repeated differentiation shows that \(D^kr(y)\) is a finite sum of
contractions among \(e(y),h_1,\ldots,h_k\), multiplied by powers of
\(r(y)^{-1}\).  Since \(1<r(y)<2\), for every fixed \(k\geq1\),
\[
 \sup_{1<\|y\|_2<2}
 \|D^kr(y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty,
\]
with a bound independent of \(M\).  The product and chain rules now imply
\(\sup_y\|D^j\Pi(y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq d_j\).  Smoothness across the
radii one and two follows because \(\chi\) agrees with a constant on
both sides and all positive-order derivatives match there.

The scaling identity
\(D^j\pi_R(w)=R^{1-j}D^j\Pi(w/R)\) therefore gives
\[
 \sup_w\|D^j\pi_R(w)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq d_jR^{1-j}.
\]
For \(j\geq1\), contracting with \(b_s\) and using
\(\|b_s\|_2=B_0\varepsilon\), we obtain
\[
 \sup_w\|D^j\Phi_s(w)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq B_0d_j\varepsilon R^{1-j}
 =B_0d_jC_R^{1-j}\varepsilon\rho^{1-j}.
\]
For the zero-order estimate,
\(\|\pi_R(w)\|_2\leq2R\) gives
\[
 |\langle b_s,\pi_R(w)\rangle|
 \leq2B_0\varepsilon R.
\]
Together with \(H=4B_0\varepsilon R\), this proves
\eqref{eq:drhs-reg-forcing-range}; the gate bound follows directly from
\(0\leq\eta\leq1\).
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:drhs-link-aggregation}
Let
\[
 \mathcal P(z):=
 \Phi_1(z_1)
 +\sum_{s=2}^N
 G_{s-1}(z_{s-1})\Phi_s(z_s).
\]
For every integer \(r\geq2\), there is a constant \(K_r<\infty\),
depending only on \(r\) and the fixed cutoff profile, such that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-reg-global-derivative}
 \sup_z\|D^r\mathcal P(z)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq K_r\varepsilon\rho^{1-r}.
\end{equation}
The constant \(K_r\) is independent of \(M\), \(N\), and the phase
realization.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Fix directions
\(v^{(1)},\ldots,v^{(r)}\in(\mathbb R^M)^N\), where
\(v^{(i)}=(v_1^{(i)},\ldots,v_N^{(i)})\).  For one link, the
multilinear Leibniz rule gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &D^r\!\left[
   G_{s-1}(z_{s-1})\Phi_s(z_s)
 \right][v^{(1)},\ldots,v^{(r)}]=
 \sum_{I\subseteq[r]}
 D^{|I|}G_{s-1}(z_{s-1})
 [v_{s-1}^{(i)}:i\in I]\,
 D^{r-|I|}\Phi_s(z_s)
 [v_s^{(i)}:i\notin I].
 \end{aligned}
\]
By the derivative and zero-order bounds of
Proposition~\ref{prop:drhs-local-derivatives}, the summand indexed by
\(I\) has absolute value at most
\[
 K_r'\varepsilon\rho^{1-r}
 \prod_{i\in I}\|v_{s-1}^{(i)}\|_2
 \prod_{i\notin I}\|v_s^{(i)}\|_2.
\]
Indeed, the gate contributes \(\rho^{-|I|}\), while the forcing
contributes
\(\varepsilon\rho^{1-r+|I|}\), so their product is always
\(\varepsilon\rho^{1-r}\), independently of \(I\).

For a fixed \(I\), generalized H\"older's inequality and
\(\|a\|_{\ell_r}\leq\|a\|_{\ell_2}\) for \(r\geq2\) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{s=2}^N
 \prod_{i\in I}\|v_{s-1}^{(i)}\|_2
 \prod_{i\notin I}\|v_s^{(i)}\|_2&\quad\leq
 \prod_{i\in I}
 \left(
  \sum_{s=2}^N\|v_{s-1}^{(i)}\|_2^r
 \right)^{1/r}
 \prod_{i\notin I}
 \left(
  \sum_{s=2}^N\|v_s^{(i)}\|_2^r
 \right)^{1/r}\\
 &\quad\leq
 \prod_{i=1}^r\|v^{(i)}\|_2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Summing over the links and the \(2^r\) subsets \(I\) therefore costs
only an \(r\)-dependent factor.  The initial term satisfies
\[
 \left|
 D^r\Phi_1(z_1)
 [v_1^{(1)},\ldots,v_1^{(r)}]
 \right|
 \leq
 b_r\varepsilon\rho^{1-r}
 \prod_{i=1}^r\|v^{(i)}\|_2.
\]
Taking the supremum over unit directions proves
\eqref{eq:drhs-reg-global-derivative}.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Write
\[
 \mathcal Q(z,u):=
 \frac12\sum_{s=1}^Nz_s^\top A_sz_s
 +\frac{\mu}{2}\|u\|_2^2,
 \qquad
 F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}
 =\mathcal Q-\mathcal P,
\]
with the \(u\)-term omitted when \(d=NM\).  The first proposition shows
that all local components, and hence \(F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}\),
are \(C^\infty\).  We regard \(\mathcal P\) as independent of \(u\);
the ambient operator norm of each derivative is then the same as its
operator norm on the hard coordinates.

The Hessian of \(\mathcal Q\) is
\(\operatorname{diag}(A_1,\ldots,A_N,\mu I)\), whose operator norm is at
most \(\bar L\).  Proposition~\ref{prop:drhs-link-aggregation} with
\(r=2\), together with \(\varepsilon/\rho=\mu\), gives
\[
 \sup_x
 \|D^2F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq\bar L+K_2\mu.
\]
For arbitrary \(x,y\in\mathbb R^d\),
\[
 \nabla F(x)-\nabla F(y)
 =
 \int_0^1
 D^2F(y+\theta(x-y))[x-y]\,d\theta.
\]
Taking norms proves
\[
 \operatorname{Lip}
 \bigl(\nabla F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}\bigr)
 \leq\bar L+C_{\mathrm{sm}}\mu,
 \qquad
 C_{\mathrm{sm}}:=K_2.
\]

Now fix \(q\geq2\).  Since \(D^{q+1}\mathcal Q=0\), the second
proposition with \(r=q+1\) gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-reg-qplusone}
 \sup_x
 \|D^{q+1}F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq
 K_{q+1}\varepsilon\rho^{-q}
 =
 K_{q+1}\frac{\mu^q}{\varepsilon^{q-1}}.
\end{equation}
Applying the line-segment identity to \(D^qF\) and using
\eqref{eq:drhs-reg-qplusone},
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|D^qF(x)-D^qF(y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 &\leq
 \int_0^1
 \|D^{q+1}F(y+\theta(x-y))\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \|x-y\|_2\,d\theta\\
 &\leq
 K_{q+1}\frac{\mu^q}{\varepsilon^{q-1}}
 \|x-y\|_2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
 \operatorname{Lip}
 \bigl(D^qF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}\bigr)
 \leq
 C_q\frac{\mu^q}{\varepsilon^{q-1}},
 \qquad
 C_q:=K_{q+1}.
\]

It remains to prove coercivity and the gap estimate.  By
\eqref{eq:drhs-reg-forcing-range},
\(0\leq\mathcal P(z)\leq6NB_0\varepsilon R\).  Since
\(A_s\succeq\mu I\),
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:drhs-reg-coercive-lower}
 F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}(z,u)
 \geq
 \frac{\mu}{2}
 \left(
  \sum_{s=1}^N\|z_s\|_2^2+\|u\|_2^2
 \right)
 -6NB_0\varepsilon R.
\end{equation}
The right-hand side tends to \(+\infty\) with \(\|(z,u)\|_2\), so the
function is coercive.

At the origin, admissibility gives
\(\|x_s^\star\|_2\geq16\rho>3\rho\), and hence \(G_s(0)=0\).
Also \(\pi_R(0)=0\), so
\[
 F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}(0)
 =-\Phi_1(0)
 =-H
 =-4B_0\varepsilon R.
\]
Equation~\eqref{eq:drhs-reg-coercive-lower} gives
\(\inf_xF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}(x)
\geq-6NB_0\varepsilon R\).  Therefore
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 F_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}(0)
 -\inf_xF_{\mathbf A,\mathbf b}^{(d)}(x)
 &\leq(6N-4)B_0\varepsilon R\\
 &\leq
 6B_0C_RN\frac{\varepsilon^2}{\mu},
 \end{aligned}
\]
where \(R=C_R\rho=C_R\varepsilon/\mu\).  Hence the gap bound holds with
\(C_{\mathrm{gap}}:=6B_0C_R\).  All constants above depend only on the
relevant derivative order and the fixed cutoff profile, and not on
\(M,N,d,\mu,\bar L,\varepsilon\), or the phase realization.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
There are numerical constants \(c_0>0\) and \(\kappa_0\ge4\) such that the
following holds.  Suppose \(\kappa\ge\kappa_0\), set
\(t:=\lfloor c_0\sqrt\kappa\rfloor\ge1\) and \(K:=t+2\), and let
\(M\ge2\kappa\) be an integer.  Then there are distinct numbers
\(\mu\le\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_K\le\bar L\) and positive integers
\(n_1,\ldots,n_K\), with \(\sum_{i=1}^K n_i=M\), such that, for every
real polynomial \(q\) of degree at most \(t\),
\begin{equation}
 n_i\ge\frac{M}{2\kappa}\quad(i\in[K]),
 \qquad
 \sum_{i=1}^K\frac{n_i}{M}
 \left|\frac1{\lambda_i}-q(\lambda_i)\right|^2
 \ge\frac{3}{512\mu^2}.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\(D:=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1I_{n_1},\ldots,\lambda_KI_{n_K})\)
satisfies \(\mu I\preceq D\preceq\bar L I\).
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Let $\Pi_t$ denote the space of real polynomials of degree at most $t$,
and write
\[
 E_t
 :=
 \inf_{q\in\Pi_t}
 \sup_{\lambda\in[\mu,\bar L]}
 \left|\frac{1}{\lambda}-q(\lambda)\right|.
\]

\begin{fact}[\bf Uniform approximation lower bound]
\label{fact:drhs-uniform-approximation}
Suppose that $\kappa=\bar L/\mu\geq4$ and
$t\leq c_0\sqrt{\kappa}$, where $c_0>0$ is a sufficiently small
numerical constant. Then $E_t\geq\frac{1}{8\mu}$.
\end{fact}

\begin{proof}
Suppose, toward a contradiction, that there exists $q\in\Pi_t$
such that
$\|\lambda^{-1}-q(\lambda)\|_{\infty,[\mu,\bar L]}
<\frac{1}{8\mu}$.
Since $\kappa\geq4$, both $\mu$ and $4\mu$ belong to
$[\mu,\bar L]$. Evaluating the approximation bound at these points gives
$q(\mu)>\frac{7}{8\mu}$ and
$q(4\mu)<\frac{3}{8\mu}$.
Thus $q(\mu)-q(4\mu)>\frac{1}{2\mu}$, and the mean-value theorem yields
$\|q'\|_{\infty,[\mu,\bar L]}>\frac{1}{6\mu^2}$.

On the other hand, the same approximation bound implies
$\|q\|_{\infty,[\mu,\bar L]}\leq\frac{9}{8\mu}$.
Markov's inequality for polynomials, rescaled from $[-1,1]$
to $[\mu,\bar L]$, therefore gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|q'\|_{\infty,[\mu,\bar L]}
 &\leq
 \frac{2t^2}{\bar L-\mu}
 \|q\|_{\infty,[\mu,\bar L]}\\
 &\leq
 \frac{9t^2}{4(\kappa-1)\mu^2}
 \leq
 \frac{9c_0^2\kappa}{4(\kappa-1)\mu^2}
 \leq
 \frac{3c_0^2}{\mu^2},
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the last inequality uses
$\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-1}\leq\frac{4}{3}$.
Choosing $c_0$ so that $3c_0^2<\frac{1}{6}$ contradicts
the preceding derivative lower bound.
Hence $E_t\geq\frac{1}{8\mu}$.
\end{proof}


The uniform approximation bound does not yet specify a fixed spectral
measure. We next construct positive weights for which a best uniform
approximant is also a best weighted least-squares approximant.

\begin{fact}[\bf Discrete weighted approximation lower bound]
\label{fact:drhs-weighted-approximation}
Let $K:=t+2$. There exist distinct points
$\mu\leq\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_K\leq\bar L$
and positive weights $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_K$, with
$\sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i=1$, such that
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i
 \left|\frac{1}{\lambda_i}-q(\lambda_i)\right|^2
 \geq E_t^2
 \qquad\text{for every }q\in\Pi_t.
\]
\end{fact}

\begin{proof}
Let $q^\star\in\Pi_t$ be a best uniform approximant to
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{-1}$ on $[\mu,\bar L]$.
By the Chebyshev alternation theorem, there exist
$K=t+2$ ordered points $\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_K$ such that
the residuals
$e_i:=\lambda_i^{-1}-q^\star(\lambda_i)$
satisfy $|e_i|=E_t$ and alternate in sign.

For each $i\in[K]$, define
$c_i:=\prod_{j\neq i}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)^{-1}$.
We first observe that
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^K c_i s(\lambda_i)=0
 \qquad\text{for every }s\in\Pi_t.
\]
Indeed, the $i$th Lagrange basis polynomial
$\ell_i(x):=\prod_{j\neq i}\frac{x-\lambda_j}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j}$
has leading coefficient $c_i$.
Comparing the coefficients of $x^{K-1}$ in the interpolation identity
$s(x)=\sum_{i=1}^K s(\lambda_i)\ell_i(x)$
gives the claim, since $\deg(s)\leq t=K-2$.

Set $C:=\sum_{j=1}^K|c_j|$ and $\theta_i:=\frac{|c_i|}{C}$.
These weights are positive and sum to one.
Since $\operatorname{sgn}(c_i)=(-1)^{K-i}$, the signs of the $c_i$
alternate just as those of the $e_i$ do.
Consequently, there is a common sign $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ such that
$e_i=\sigma E_t\operatorname{sgn}(c_i)$ for every $i$.
Thus $\theta_i e_i=\frac{\sigma E_t}{C}c_i$, and the preceding
interpolation identity yields
$\sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i e_i s(\lambda_i)=0$
for every $s\in\Pi_t$.

Now fix $q\in\Pi_t$ and put $h:=q-q^\star\in\Pi_t$.
Since $\lambda_i^{-1}-q(\lambda_i)=e_i-h(\lambda_i)$,
expanding the square gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i
 \left|\frac{1}{\lambda_i}-q(\lambda_i)\right|^2
 &=
 \sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i e_i^2
 -2\sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i e_i h(\lambda_i)
 +\sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i|h(\lambda_i)|^2\\
 &=
 E_t^2+\sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i|h(\lambda_i)|^2
 \geq E_t^2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here the cross term vanishes by the orthogonality relation with
$s=h$, and the first term equals $E_t^2$ because
$|e_i|=E_t$ and $\sum_i\theta_i=1$.
\end{proof}


The weights from Fact~\ref{fact:drhs-weighted-approximation}
may be arbitrarily small and need not correspond to integer
multiplicities. The following fact addresses both issues.

\begin{fact}[\bf Regularizing and rounding the weights]
\label{fact:drhs-integer-multiplicities}
Suppose that $K\leq\frac{\kappa}{4}$ and that $M\geq2\kappa$
is an integer. For any positive weights
$\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_K$ summing to one, there exist positive
integers $n_1,\ldots,n_K$, summing to $M$, such that
\[
 n_i\geq\frac{M}{2\kappa},
 \qquad
 \frac{n_i}{M}\geq\frac{3}{8}\theta_i
 \qquad(i\in[K]).
\]
\end{fact}

\begin{proof}
Define
$\omega_i:=\left(1-\frac{K}{\kappa}\right)\theta_i
+\frac{1}{\kappa}$.
Then $\sum_{i=1}^K\omega_i=1$.
Moreover, $K\leq\frac{\kappa}{4}$ implies both
$\omega_i\geq\frac{1}{\kappa}$ and
$\omega_i\geq\frac{3}{4}\theta_i$.

Start with $n_i=\lfloor M\omega_i\rfloor$ and distribute the
remaining $M-\sum_i\lfloor M\omega_i\rfloor$ copies arbitrarily
among the $K$ indices.
The resulting integers sum to $M$.
Since $M\omega_i\geq\frac{M}{\kappa}\geq2$, they satisfy
\[
 n_i
 \geq\lfloor M\omega_i\rfloor
 \geq M\omega_i-1
 \geq\frac{M\omega_i}{2}.
\]
In particular, every $n_i$ is positive.
Combining this bound with
$\omega_i\geq\frac{1}{\kappa}$ gives
$n_i\geq\frac{M}{2\kappa}$, while combining it with
$\omega_i\geq\frac{3}{4}\theta_i$ gives
$\frac{n_i}{M}\geq\frac{3}{8}\theta_i$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-spectrum}]
Choose $c_0>0$ as in
Fact~\ref{fact:drhs-uniform-approximation}.
Since $K=t+2\leq c_0\sqrt{\kappa}+2$, we may choose
$\kappa_0\geq4$ sufficiently large that
$K\leq\frac{\kappa}{4}$ whenever $\kappa\geq\kappa_0$.

Take the spectral points $\lambda_i$ and weights $\theta_i$
from Fact~\ref{fact:drhs-weighted-approximation}, and apply
Fact~\ref{fact:drhs-integer-multiplicities} to obtain
positive integers $n_i$ summing to $M$.
These integers satisfy $n_i\geq\frac{M}{2\kappa}$.
Furthermore, for every $q\in\Pi_t$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{i=1}^K\frac{n_i}{M}
 \left|\frac{1}{\lambda_i}-q(\lambda_i)\right|^2
 &\geq
 \frac{3}{8}\sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i
 \left|\frac{1}{\lambda_i}-q(\lambda_i)\right|^2\\
 &\geq\frac{3}{8}E_t^2
 \geq\frac{3}{512\mu^2},
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the last two inequalities follow from
Facts~\ref{fact:drhs-weighted-approximation}
and~\ref{fact:drhs-uniform-approximation}, respectively.
This proves \eqref{eq:drhs-flat-spectrum}.

Finally, every $\lambda_i$ belongs to $[\mu,\bar L]$, so
$D:=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1I_{n_1},\ldots,\lambda_KI_{n_K})$
satisfies $\mu I\preceq D\preceq\bar L I$.
\end{proof}
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- fact-5: body_md -->
\label{fact:drhs-uniform-approximation}
Suppose that $\kappa=\bar L/\mu\geq4$ and
$t\leq c_0\sqrt{\kappa}$, where $c_0>0$ is a sufficiently small
numerical constant. Then $E_t\geq\frac{1}{8\mu}$.
<!-- end fact-5 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Suppose, toward a contradiction, that there exists $q\in\Pi_t$
such that
$\|\lambda^{-1}-q(\lambda)\|_{\infty,[\mu,\bar L]}
<\frac{1}{8\mu}$.
Since $\kappa\geq4$, both $\mu$ and $4\mu$ belong to
$[\mu,\bar L]$. Evaluating the approximation bound at these points gives
$q(\mu)>\frac{7}{8\mu}$ and
$q(4\mu)<\frac{3}{8\mu}$.
Thus $q(\mu)-q(4\mu)>\frac{1}{2\mu}$, and the mean-value theorem yields
$\|q'\|_{\infty,[\mu,\bar L]}>\frac{1}{6\mu^2}$.

On the other hand, the same approximation bound implies
$\|q\|_{\infty,[\mu,\bar L]}\leq\frac{9}{8\mu}$.
Markov's inequality for polynomials, rescaled from $[-1,1]$
to $[\mu,\bar L]$, therefore gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|q'\|_{\infty,[\mu,\bar L]}
 &\leq
 \frac{2t^2}{\bar L-\mu}
 \|q\|_{\infty,[\mu,\bar L]}\\
 &\leq
 \frac{9t^2}{4(\kappa-1)\mu^2}
 \leq
 \frac{9c_0^2\kappa}{4(\kappa-1)\mu^2}
 \leq
 \frac{3c_0^2}{\mu^2},
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the last inequality uses
$\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-1}\leq\frac{4}{3}$.
Choosing $c_0$ so that $3c_0^2<\frac{1}{6}$ contradicts
the preceding derivative lower bound.
Hence $E_t\geq\frac{1}{8\mu}$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- fact-6: body_md -->
\label{fact:drhs-weighted-approximation}
Let $K:=t+2$. There exist distinct points
$\mu\leq\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_K\leq\bar L$
and positive weights $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_K$, with
$\sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i=1$, such that
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i
 \left|\frac{1}{\lambda_i}-q(\lambda_i)\right|^2
 \geq E_t^2
 \qquad\text{for every }q\in\Pi_t.
\]
<!-- end fact-6 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Let $q^\star\in\Pi_t$ be a best uniform approximant to
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{-1}$ on $[\mu,\bar L]$.
By the Chebyshev alternation theorem, there exist
$K=t+2$ ordered points $\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_K$ such that
the residuals
$e_i:=\lambda_i^{-1}-q^\star(\lambda_i)$
satisfy $|e_i|=E_t$ and alternate in sign.

For each $i\in[K]$, define
$c_i:=\prod_{j\neq i}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)^{-1}$.
We first observe that
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^K c_i s(\lambda_i)=0
 \qquad\text{for every }s\in\Pi_t.
\]
Indeed, the $i$th Lagrange basis polynomial
$\ell_i(x):=\prod_{j\neq i}\frac{x-\lambda_j}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j}$
has leading coefficient $c_i$.
Comparing the coefficients of $x^{K-1}$ in the interpolation identity
$s(x)=\sum_{i=1}^K s(\lambda_i)\ell_i(x)$
gives the claim, since $\deg(s)\leq t=K-2$.

Set $C:=\sum_{j=1}^K|c_j|$ and $\theta_i:=\frac{|c_i|}{C}$.
These weights are positive and sum to one.
Since $\operatorname{sgn}(c_i)=(-1)^{K-i}$, the signs of the $c_i$
alternate just as those of the $e_i$ do.
Consequently, there is a common sign $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ such that
$e_i=\sigma E_t\operatorname{sgn}(c_i)$ for every $i$.
Thus $\theta_i e_i=\frac{\sigma E_t}{C}c_i$, and the preceding
interpolation identity yields
$\sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i e_i s(\lambda_i)=0$
for every $s\in\Pi_t$.

Now fix $q\in\Pi_t$ and put $h:=q-q^\star\in\Pi_t$.
Since $\lambda_i^{-1}-q(\lambda_i)=e_i-h(\lambda_i)$,
expanding the square gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i
 \left|\frac{1}{\lambda_i}-q(\lambda_i)\right|^2
 &=
 \sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i e_i^2
 -2\sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i e_i h(\lambda_i)
 +\sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i|h(\lambda_i)|^2\\
 &=
 E_t^2+\sum_{i=1}^K\theta_i|h(\lambda_i)|^2
 \geq E_t^2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here the cross term vanishes by the orthogonality relation with
$s=h$, and the first term equals $E_t^2$ because
$|e_i|=E_t$ and $\sum_i\theta_i=1$.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- fact-7: body_md -->
\label{fact:drhs-integer-multiplicities}

<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
Let \(q_0,q_1\in\mathbb N_{+}\), \(j_\star:=q_0+1\), and
\(m:=q_0+q_1+2\), and suppose \(m^2<M\).
Every deterministic two-stage algorithm above admits a
joint-law-preserving orthogonal coupling with
\(\widehat A=\widehat U^\top D\widehat U\), where
\(\widehat U\sim\operatorname{Haar}(O(M))\), and with
\(h_1,\ldots,h_m\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,I_M)\), independent of
\(\widehat U\).

Write \(\widetilde\xi,\widetilde y\) for the coupled input and output, and
set
\(\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}
 :=\operatorname{span}\{\widehat A^a h_j:
 1\leq j\leq q_0,\ a\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0},\
 a+j\leq q_0+1\}\).
Then, almost surely,
\begin{align}
 \widetilde\xi
 &=
 P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}}\widetilde\xi
 +\beta
 \frac{(I-P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}})h_{j_\star}}
      {\|(I-P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}})h_{j_\star}\|_2},
 \qquad
 \beta:=\|(I-P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}})\widetilde\xi\|_2>0,
\\
 \widetilde y
 &\in
 \operatorname{span}
 \{\widehat A^a h_j:
 1\leq j\leq m,\ a\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0},\ a+j\leq m\},
\\
 \widehat A^a h_{j_\star}
 \text{ appearing in \eqref{eq:drhs-flat-output-span}}
 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 a\leq m-j_\star=q_1+1.
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:drhs-adaptive-gaussian-lifting}
Let $B=U^\top D U$, where $D$ is a fixed positive diagonal
$M\times M$ matrix and $U$ is Haar distributed on $O(M)$.
Suppose that $m^2<M$.
For each $1\leq k\leq m$, let $v_k$ be a unit vector in
$\mathcal S_{k-1}^\perp$, chosen as a deterministic Borel
function of $H_{k-1}$.

The joint law of $(B,v_1,\ldots,v_m)$ admits a coupling with
a Haar matrix $\widehat U$, standard Gaussian vectors
$h_1,\ldots,h_m$, and an orthogonal matrix $R$ such that
$\widehat U,h_1,\ldots,h_m$ are mutually independent and,
with $\widehat B:=\widehat U^\top D\widehat U$, almost surely,
\[
 \widehat B=RBR^\top,
 \qquad
 Rv_k=
 \frac{(I-P_{\mathcal K_{k-1}})h_k}
      {\|(I-P_{\mathcal K_{k-1}})h_k\|_2}
 \quad(1\leq k\leq m),
 \qquad
 R\mathcal S_k=\mathcal K_k
 \quad(0\leq k<m).
\]
In particular, every terminal vector
$y\in\mathcal S_{m-1}+\operatorname{span}\{v_m\}$ satisfies
\[
 Ry\in
 \operatorname{span}\bigl\{
 \widehat B^a h_j:
 1\leq j\leq m,\quad a\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0},\quad
 a+j\leq m
 \bigr\}.
\]
No response to the final innovation $v_m$ is needed.
The construction can be chosen jointly Borel in any fixed
auxiliary parameter on which the innovation rules depend
jointly Borel measurably.
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- fact-8: body_md -->
\label{fact:drhs-triangular-augmentation}
Fix $B\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ and set
$\mathcal S_0:=\{0\}$.
For $1\leq k\leq m$, let $x_k$ be a candidate and write
$s_k:=P_{\mathcal S_{k-1}}x_k$,
$r_k:=x_k-s_k$, and $\alpha_k:=\|r_k\|_2$.
If $\alpha_k>0$, set $v_k:=r_k/\alpha_k$;
otherwise, choose a unit vector
$v_k\in\mathcal S_{k-1}^\perp$ by a fixed Borel rule.
For $k<m$, form $H_k$ and $\mathcal S_k$ as above.

Then, for every $1\leq k<m$,
\[
 \mathcal S_{k-1}+\operatorname{span}\{x_k,Bx_k\}
 \subseteq\mathcal S_k,
 \qquad
 \dim(\mathcal S_k)\leq\frac{k(k+3)}{2}.
\]
Moreover, $x_k$ and the ordered augmented transcript $H_k$
determine $Bx_k$ measurably.
The terminal candidate satisfies
$x_m\in\mathcal S_{m-1}+\operatorname{span}\{v_m\}$.
Under $m^2<M$, every dummy direction required in the
construction exists.
<!-- end fact-8 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
For $k<m$, the definition of $H_k$ gives
$\mathcal S_{k-1}\subseteq\mathcal S_k$ and
$B\mathcal S_{k-1}\subseteq\mathcal S_k$:
every preceding generator remains present, together with
one additional power of $B$.
The vectors $v_k$ and $Bv_k$ also belong to $\mathcal S_k$.
Since $x_k=s_k+\alpha_kv_k$, including when $\alpha_k=0$,
both $x_k$ and $Bx_k=Bs_k+\alpha_kBv_k$ belong to
$\mathcal S_k$.

To reconstruct the response, let $W_{k-1}$ be the matrix
whose columns are the ordered vectors in $H_{k-1}$.
Choose measurably coefficients $c_k$ satisfying
$W_{k-1}c_k=s_k$, for example using the Moore--Penrose
pseudoinverse.
Every column of $BW_{k-1}$ occurs in $H_k$, so the augmented
transcript determines
$Bs_k=(BW_{k-1})c_k$.
It also contains $Bv_k$, and therefore determines
$Bx_k=Bs_k+\alpha_kBv_k$.
For $k=1$, the term $Bs_k$ is zero.

For each $j\leq k$, the family $H_k$ contains $k+2-j$
powers generated by $v_j$.
Its total number of vectors is therefore
$\sum_{j=1}^k(k+2-j)=k(k+3)/2$, which bounds
$\dim(\mathcal S_k)$.
Consequently, before every slot $k\leq m$,
$\dim(\mathcal S_{k-1})\leq (k-1)(k+2)/2<m^2<M$.
Thus the required orthogonal complements are nontrivial,
and measurable dummy directions can be selected by a fixed
Gram--Schmidt rule.
Finally, $x_m=s_m+\alpha_mv_m$ proves the terminal inclusion.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Temporarily fix the delayed input at $\xi=z$.
We construct an augmented experiment with $m$ candidate slots.
The candidates at slots $1,\ldots,q_0$ are the original
preprocessing queries.
At slot $j_\star=q_0+1$, the candidate is $z$.
The candidates at slots $j_\star+1,\ldots,m-1$ are the
$q_1$ original post-disclosure queries.
The candidate at slot $m$ is the terminal output $y$.

At every slot $k<m$, the analyst applies
Fact~\ref{fact:drhs-triangular-augmentation} with $B=A$,
obtaining the innovation $v_k$ and the augmented transcript
$H_k$.
For a genuine query, the analyst reconstructs $Ax_k$ from
$H_k$ and returns only this response to the original procedure.
All additional Krylov vectors remain private.
At the forced slot $j_\star$, the analyst privately forms
the next triangular layer but returns no matrix-vector
response.
Only at this slot is $z$ disclosed to the procedure.
At the terminal slot, the analyst forms $v_m$ from the
residual of $y$ without exposing any additional matrix
products.

For fixed $z$, each innovation $v_k$ is a deterministic
Borel function of $H_{k-1}$.
Indeed, the ordinary transcript can be reconstructed
recursively from $z$ and the augmented transcript.
Given the preceding ordinary transcript, the original
query rule determines the next genuine candidate;
Fact~\ref{fact:drhs-triangular-augmentation} then recovers
its response from the next augmented transcript.
The forced candidate is the fixed vector $z$, and the
terminal candidate is determined by the completed ordinary
transcript.
Projection, normalization away from zero, and the fixed
dummy-direction rule are all Borel.
Thus the innovation rules satisfy the hypotheses of
Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-adaptive-gaussian-lifting}.

Apply that lemma for each fixed $z$, using its construction
jointly Borel in $z$.
We may therefore sample $\xi$ uniformly on the unit sphere,
independently of $\widehat U,h_1,\ldots,h_m$, and use the
coupling corresponding to $z=\xi$.
For each fixed $z$, the original-coordinate matrix and
augmented transcript have the same joint law as in the
original experiment with input $z$.
Integrating this identity over the spherical law of $z$
preserves the full joint law of $A$, $\xi$, the ordinary
transcript, and $y$.
In this coupling, write
$\widehat A:=\widehat U^\top D\widehat U$,
$\widetilde\xi:=R\xi$, and $\widetilde y:=Ry$.

Let $\mathcal S:=\mathcal S_{q_0}$ and
$\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}:=\mathcal K_{q_0}$.
The preprocessing query rules do not use $\xi$.
We also choose all preprocessing dummy directions using
only the preceding augmented transcript.
Hence $\mathcal S$ is a function of $A$ alone and is
independent of $\xi$ in the original experiment.
The coupling preserves this independence.
Furthermore,
$\dim(\mathcal S)\leq q_0(q_0+3)/2<M$.
Since a proper linear subspace has zero spherical measure,
$\beta:=\|(I-P_{\mathcal S})\xi\|_2>0$ almost surely.

The innovation at the forced slot is therefore
$v_{j_\star}=(I-P_{\mathcal S})\xi/\beta$.
The lifting lemma gives
$R\mathcal S=\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}$ and identifies
$Rv_{j_\star}$ with the normalized Gaussian residual
associated with $h_{j_\star}$.
Since
$RP_{\mathcal S}=P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}}R$,
rotating the decomposition
$\xi=P_{\mathcal S}\xi+\beta v_{j_\star}$ yields
\[
 \widetilde\xi
 =
 P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}}\widetilde\xi
 +
 \beta
 \frac{(I-P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}})h_{j_\star}}
      {\|(I-P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}})h_{j_\star}\|_2}.
\]
Orthogonality of $R$ also gives
$\beta=\|(I-P_{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{pre}}})
\widetilde\xi\|_2$.
This proves \eqref{eq:drhs-flat-fresh-input}.

At the terminal slot,
$y\in\mathcal S_{m-1}+\operatorname{span}\{v_m\}$.
The terminal assertion of the lifting lemma therefore gives
\[
 \widetilde y\in
 \operatorname{span}\bigl\{
 \widehat A^a h_j:
 1\leq j\leq m,\quad a\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0},\quad
 a+j\leq m
 \bigr\},
\]
which is \eqref{eq:drhs-flat-output-span}.
For the distinguished column $j_\star=q_0+1$, the triangular
constraint gives $a\leq m-j_\star=q_1+1$, proving
\eqref{eq:drhs-flat-degree}.
Finally, $\widehat A=RAR^\top$ and
$\widetilde\xi=R\xi$ imply
$\widehat A^{-1}\widetilde\xi=RA^{-1}\xi$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
We apply the delayed-information-chain construction directly,
choosing its upper spectral scale as part of the hard instance.
This allows all constants below to depend only on $p$.
Set
\[
 R_\varepsilon
 :=
 \frac{\Delta^{\frac{p}{p+1}}L_p^{\frac1{p+1}}}{\varepsilon},
 \qquad
 \alpha_p
 :=
 \begin{cases}
  \frac74,&p=2,\\[1mm]
  \frac53,&p\geq3.
 \end{cases}
\]
We will obtain a query lower bound of order
$R_\varepsilon^{\alpha_p}$ in dimension
$O_p(R_\varepsilon^{1+\frac1p+2\alpha_p})$.
By decreasing the accuracy constant in the theorem, we may
assume throughout that $R_\varepsilon\geq2$.

Let $C_{\mathrm{reg},p}$ and $C_{\mathrm{gap}}$ be the constants
in Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-regularity}.
Choose positive constants $c_{\mu,p}$ and $c_N$ such that
$C_{\mathrm{reg},p}c_{\mu,p}^p\leq1$ and
$C_{\mathrm{gap}}c_N\leq1$.
Choose also
$C_{\kappa,p}\geq\max\{\kappa_0,4/c_0^2\}$.
Define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mu&:=c_{\mu,p}(L_p\varepsilon^{p-1})^{\frac1p},
 &\qquad
 \rho&:=\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu},\\
 \kappa&:=C_{\kappa,p}
 R_\varepsilon^{\,2(\alpha_p-1-\frac1p)},
 &
 \bar L&:=\mu\kappa,
 \end{aligned}
\]
and let
$N:=\lfloor c_N\Delta\mu/\varepsilon^2\rfloor$,
$t:=\lfloor c_0\sqrt{\kappa}\rfloor$, and $T:=Nt$.
The choice of $\mu$ gives
$\Delta\mu/\varepsilon^2
=c_{\mu,p}R_\varepsilon^{1+\frac1p}$.
Thus, after decreasing the accuracy constant further,
$c_N\Delta\mu/\varepsilon^2\geq2$.
Since $\alpha_p>1+\frac1p$, our choice of $C_{\kappa,p}$
also ensures $\kappa\geq\kappa_0$ and
$c_0\sqrt{\kappa}\geq2$.
Using $\frac a2\leq\lfloor a\rfloor\leq a$ for $a\geq2$,
we obtain
\[
 N\asymp_p R_\varepsilon^{1+\frac1p},
 \qquad
 t\asymp_p R_\varepsilon^{\alpha_p-1-\frac1p},
 \qquad
 T\asymp_p R_\varepsilon^{\alpha_p}.
\]

Define the phase dimension $M$ and the total hard dimension
$d_0:=NM$ as in \eqref{eq:drhs-calibrated-dimension}, with
$C_{\mathrm{dim}}\geq\max\{C_0,2\}$.
This ensures $M\geq2\kappa$ and the dimension hypothesis of
Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-sequential}.
To bound $d_0$, first note that
$\kappa/T=O_p(R_\varepsilon^{\alpha_p-2-\frac2p})=O_p(1)$,
because $\alpha_p<2+\frac2p$.
Moreover, $N\leq T$, so
$\log(12NT(T+2))\leq\log(12T^2(T+2))=O(T)$.
Substituting these estimates into
\eqref{eq:drhs-calibrated-dimension} gives
\[
 M=O_p(T^2),
 \qquad
 d_0=O_p(NT^2)
     =O_p\!\left(
       R_\varepsilon^{1+\frac1p+2\alpha_p}
     \right).
\]
Hence a sufficiently large constant $C_p$ ensures
$d\geq d_0$ under the dimension assumption of the theorem.

For such a dimension $d$, construct the hard chain with
spectral interval $[\mu,\bar L]$.
Let $F$ denote an unshifted realization.
The estimates in Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-regularity} are uniform
in $\bar L$ and give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Lip}(D^pF)
 &\leq
 C_{\mathrm{reg},p}
 \frac{\mu^p}{\varepsilon^{p-1}}
 =
 C_{\mathrm{reg},p}c_{\mu,p}^pL_p
 \leq L_p,\\
 F(0)-\inf F
 &\leq
 C_{\mathrm{gap}}N\frac{\varepsilon^2}{\mu}
 \leq
 C_{\mathrm{gap}}c_N\Delta
 \leq\Delta.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Every realization is also $C^\infty$ and coercive.

To ensure nonnegativity, use the pointwise lower bound from
the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:drhs-regularity}:
$F(x)\geq-C_{\mathrm{sh}}N\varepsilon^2/\mu$ for all $x$,
where $C_{\mathrm{sh}}:=6B_0C_R$.
Define
$f:=F+C_{\mathrm{sh}}N\varepsilon^2/\mu$.
Then $f\geq0$, all derivatives are unchanged, and
$f(0)-\inf f=F(0)-\inf F$.
Consequently, the law $\mathcal D_d^+$ of these shifted
functions is supported on
$\mathcal F_p^{(d)}(\Delta,L_p)$.
The shift depends only on the calibrated parameters and
not on the phase realization.
An exact value-and-gradient oracle for $f$ can therefore
be simulated using an oracle for $F$ by adding this fixed
constant to each returned function value and leaving the
gradient unchanged.

Fix a deterministic algorithm making at most $T-1$ oracle
calls.
Apply Lemmas~\ref{lem:drhs-certification} and
\ref{lem:drhs-sequential} to the corresponding algorithm
on the unshifted chain.
Writing $z_s^{\mathrm{out}}$ for the $s$th hard block of
its output, we obtain
\[
 \Pr_{f\sim\mathcal D_d^+}
 \bigl(\|\nabla f(x^{\mathrm{out}})\|_2\leq\varepsilon\bigr)
 \leq
 \Pr\bigl(
   \|z_s^{\mathrm{out}}-x_s^\star\|_2<3\rho
   \text{ for every }s\in[N]
 \bigr)
 \leq\frac1{12}.
\]
The distribution $\mathcal D_d^+$ is independent of the
algorithm.
For a randomized algorithm with the same hard query budget,
condition on its internal seed and apply the preceding
bound to each resulting deterministic algorithm.
Averaging over the seed shows that its average success
probability under $\mathcal D_d^+$ is at most $\frac1{12}$.
Thus some fixed
$f\in\mathcal F_p^{(d)}(\Delta,L_p)$ has success probability
at most $\frac1{12}$, and hence
\[
 T_{\varepsilon,\mathrm{FO}}^{\mathrm{rand}}
 \bigl(\mathcal F_p^{(d)}(\Delta,L_p)\bigr)
 \geq T
 \gtrsim_p R_\varepsilon^{\alpha_p}.
\]

For $p=2$, we have
$\alpha_p=\frac74$ and
$1+\frac1p+2\alpha_p=5$.
For $p\geq3$, we have
$\alpha_p=\frac53$ and
$1+\frac1p+2\alpha_p=\frac{13}{3}+\frac1p$.
Substituting the definition of $R_\varepsilon$ and adjusting
$c_p$ and $C_p$ proves the two claimed bounds.
